go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 4 -json /tmp/ch04-cli/ch04
dotnet build solutions/edition-3/main/Examples/Consumer/Consumer.csproj

The component suite tests real tools and PTYs with fake HTTP at the provider boundary. The consumer exercise additionally verifies successful, correlated custom output—not merely the presence of a result marker—and the timestamped root diagnostic. No real-provider acceptance follows from either fake.

The numeric result has limits. Independent source review still checks actual parent relationships, Ensemble-owned logging, behavior in the correct package and absence of mutable global application state. The original logger check rejected a working multi-hop parent path because it expected a direct field selector. Its globals check depended on variable names. Neither can establish those architectural properties. Keep the source findings alongside the runtime results; do not label a printed log line proof of ownership.

The weights. jobmodel is 25 because it is the chapter, and because the common wrong answer, special-casing run_command instead of changing the dispatch site, passes a naive test and fails the moment a tool you do not own wedges. Both negative controls, the read_file legs in jobmodel and bigoutput, are measured load-bearing: delete either and the “it’s a shell problem” student scores 100. toollimits is 10 because it grades three properties and a forward reference in one fixture. debugger is 5 rather than more because sendinput already grades the mechanism; the five points buy the proof that the mechanism reaches a real program. shutdown is 5 because it is one behavior, and because without it the never-returning job is a leak the grader would otherwise have to hunt with kill -0.

What would still pass if I deleted this?

Same audit as the last three chapters: delete each protected behavior from the reference and confirm the score drops, and treat a row reading 100 → 100 as the finding. One row was killed-job-reported-as-done, and it scored 100 on the first run.

Here is how. The killed process died. Its goroutine ended the job as done with exit_code -1, and the waiter was told job 1 done, exit_code -1 … [job 1 killed: kill_job]. The check searched the report for the word “killed”, and the kill note supplied it. A text regex can be satisfied by the very message that documents the failure. The fix is to grade structure: job_killed carries a status, which must be killed, and the post-kill report must not claim done, finished, completed, succeeded, or an exit_code.

Three more findings from this chapter’s audit, each of them a shape you will meet in your own grader. Assert every mutation actually landed and changed bytes; this project has now been bitten three times, and the Chapter 4 rig refuses a regexp that matches other than once or whose replacement is a no-op. A mutant of a module with dependencies needs the dependency: the mutant go.mod carries the creack/pty require and the course go.sum, or the mutant fails to build and the failure is misread as detection. And treat a skipped check as a failed check. A t.Skip on an empty fixture is a vacuous pass with better manners, which is why debugger fails rather than skips when dlv is absent.

The first-edition audit deliberately omitted two mutants, with the reason recorded. Pipes-for-PTY, because the textual change is too large for a regexp and the evidence is the measured refusal plus debugger passing. And pattern-never-wakes, because the session would exceed the forty-five second harness timeout and leak a dlv process; the two pattern mutants that exist cover the semantics.

The second-edition review found another timing trap: starting a waiter goroutine does not prove it is waiting when Kill happens. Removing the notification still passed the initial test 20 times. Releasing a blocked file read likewise does not prove its late completion has reached Finish before the assertion. The corrected tests establish those orderings around the real job code. Their first repair then raced while cleaning up a failing test; a buffered result channel made both successful and defective paths finish cleanly. Check the complete failure output. The intended assertion does not make a race warning beside it disappear.

One environmental assumption, stated so a failure elsewhere is diagnosable. ch3parity holds because Chapter 3’s fixtures finish inside the three-second wake; go run ./testdata/exit7 measured 0.05 to 0.3 seconds warm and 1.3 cold. A machine where a cold go run of a one-line program exceeds three seconds fails ch3parity with a running report where an exit code was expected. The fixture assumed blocking; the wake is behaving. Run exit7 once before grading to warm the build cache. The PTY library is measured on macOS; Linux is assumed.

What you are not building

No mailbox, no interrupts, no Interrupted turn state. Jobs do not outlive the process, because one transcript is one process and Shutdown runs at exit. A tool served by somebody else’s process is named in §4.1 as the worst case and tool_limits is built for it, but you are not connecting to one yet. The custom consumer uses the same dispatch site; it does not add another scheduler. Four supervision tools and one ordinary-job path.

4.9 Drive it yourself

Ungraded, and the one to do first, because this is the chapter where the frustration from the end of Chapter 3 gets its answer.

Rebuild your own binary from its module directory. Configure the provider, discovered model, endpoint and selected key as in Chapter 3, keeping the key out of command arguments and tool subprocesses. Then go back to a disposable project:

dotnet publish solutions/edition-3/main/Cli/Ch04.csproj -c Release -o /tmp/ch04-cli
cd /path/to/scratch/project
CH02_LOG=session.jsonl /tmp/ch04-cli/ch04 chat

Ask it to run the test suite that took ninety seconds. Three seconds in, it comes back: job 3 still running after 3s. no new output; 0 bytes total at cr/io/3, and a line telling it what it can do next. Watch what the model does with that. Most of them wait again with a longer delay. Some of them go read a file while they wait, which is a thing your Chapter 3 agent could not have conceived of. Then ask it to start the development server, the request that never came back last chapter, and watch it start the server, get a handle, and carry on with the conversation while the server runs.

Then do the demonstration from §4.8 by hand, in chat. Ask it to debug something small with dlv. Watch the (dlv) pattern do the waiting. If you have never seen a language model sit at a debugger prompt, set a breakpoint, and read a variable back, it is worth the fifteen minutes on its own.

The second-edition student drove those paths with all three providers on October 9. Each started a delayed job, waited for its end, answered a NAME> PTY prompt with Ada, observed hello Ada, and killed a running sleep job. The retained student record links the actual event logs and distinguishes model summaries from inspected output:

live model plain input cache read output
claude-haiku-5-5 29,113 0 985
gpt-5.4-mini 7,215 6,272 593
gemini-3.8-flash 30,236 0 1,437

No cache writes were recorded. OpenAI also set a 256-byte cap: the job stored 564 bytes and the report named 308 omitted bytes. The Gemini session includes the successful debugger sequence from §4.8. These totals belong to the actual sessions, not a cost forecast or new runs of the enhanced chapter.

Shutdown needs its own observation. In the first attempt, a sleep 60 job expired before EOF, so it demonstrated no shutdown kill. A bounded repeat checked that a sleep 300 process existed immediately before EOF and was gone immediately after; the log recorded killed with reason shutdown. The repeat used 4,444 input and 139 output tokens. The unnecessary debugger repeat used 11,578 input and 728 output; both remain in the record rather than disappearing from the account because their lessons were inconvenient.

For free plumbing checks, use the revised grader and Chapter 3’s serve-only fake with your own binary. The original convenience launchers build first-edition answers; they do not validate yours. The simple fake script demonstrates ordinary calls, while the jobs grader supplies the wait, input, kill, output and debugger scenarios.

Take the library outside

Build the separately compiled C# example from Examples/Consumer. Its local exercise reads the established environment and refuses a non-loopback endpoint, so accidentally inherited provider settings cannot turn a plumbing check into a paid request. Registering shout preserves the built-ins. A local fake should request shout, read_file, and run_command, then verify all three results, job files, and the timestamped shout called diagnostic before sending its final reply. The application has no private access to the library.

The earlier Edition 2 external-consumer provider runs are historical evidence, not C# acceptance. Real-provider exercises require current permission and budget. Record blocked portions as incomplete; do not replace model judgment with a scripted fake and describe the two as equivalent.

Then try what the original external-use exercise proposed: a small application with a tool that knows something about your project. A tool that queries your database, checks CI status or reads a monitoring dashboard. The framework does not know those operations and does not need to. These are ideas for using the library, not additional tools required by this exercise.

Preserve a runnable chapter endpoint and record actual results and limitations. Commit or tag only with the repository owner’s authorization. Keep the actual scores and accepted exceptions; original Chapter 4 scored 90/100 FAIL, and original Chapter 5 scored 110/120 FAIL with nested Chapter 4 still 90/100. Those accepted student checkpoints retain their history separately from the revised grader’s results.

Now the thing this chapter cannot fix, and you should feel it before the next chapter names it. Start that ninety-second test suite again, and while the job is running, type something. Anything. “Stop, wrong directory.” Nothing happens until the wake returns. Your agent can run a job without dying, and it still cannot hear you while it does, because the loop that dispatched the tool is the only thing that would notice your message, and it is parked waiting for the answer. A supervised job fixes the freeze and leaves the deafness.

Fixing that is not more job machinery. It is a different shape: one inbound queue carrying prompts, interruptions, and job completions as the same kind of thing, drained by a loop that never blocks on a tool. This chapter has earned that by making the pain specific. On 10 August the agent could not be told anything at all. After this chapter, it can be told anything, three seconds from now.

Chapter 5: Two Seams and a Loop

The historical CodeRhapsody incidents below retain the first edition’s measurements. The exercise and ownership rules below describe the C# implementation. Historical Go runs are not evidence that this endpoint used a real provider.

The agent framework from Chapter 4 is good enough to write an author-editor orchestrator. Imagine what it could do with a GUI built exactly the way you want it. Your layout, your keybindings, your idea of what coding with AI should feel like. That is where this book is headed. But the tools that shipped GUI-first paid for it: the GUI imported the framework, the framework imported the GUI, and by the time anyone noticed the cycle it was load-bearing. CodeRhapsody made the same mistake, and refactoring it out took weeks of focused work. This chapter exists so you do not repeat it. By the end, your framework will have an API clean enough to host any GUI, any gateway, any agentic application. Streaming comes next, followed by the GUI. This one builds the surface it plugs into.

That surface is two seams and a loop. Right now, ask a question while a tool runs and the agent does not notice until the tool finishes. Send a hint and it arrives one round too late. Run two agents through one blocking application loop and the second waits until the first is done. The package structure is right and the engine is deaf.

This chapter fixes the deafness. Three additions and one retirement: an outbound seam so the framework tells the world what happened instead of the world reaching in to ask; an inbound queue so prompts, hints, tool completions, and interrupts enter through one door; and a loop between them that drains the queue and notifies observers on every event. Retire the old synchronous orchestration loop; keep its public API as an adapter to the actor. Two loops over one engine are two owners of mutable state, not backward compatibility. A framework is two seams and a loop. By the end, the same core runs a three-agent workflow where each agent has its own tools, its own prompt, and its own observers, and a hint mid-tool-call arrives before the tool finishes.

TL;DR

Give each Agent one mailbox and one asynchronous loop that owns its conversation. Callers send typed requests; model and tool workers return immutable outcomes. Only the Agent applies those outcomes to History and decides what starts next. A private completion task reliably completes each admitted request. A separate, bounded observer stream reports progress without being allowed to stall work.

Pause stops scheduling, not background jobs. Interrupt ends the current turn, not the Agent. Shutdown closes admission, drains workers and jobs, then destroys the owning relationships. The old synchronous SendAsync becomes a convenience wrapper over this same actor; it must not remain a second implementation.

The actor also gives local media and a small multi-Agent workflow one consistent entry point. They are clients of the framework, not reasons to add a second orchestrator in the CLI. Common declares the actual C# types, relationships, and operations; partial implementations provide their bodies in the functional modules.

Shared contracts

The library remains one compiled C# assembly. Common declares the actual partial objects, their persistent fields, and every operation used across modules. Agent supplies orchestration; Engine renders and performs one frozen HTTP exchange; History owns recorded facts and reduction; Jobs owns execution. Neither the CLI nor a GUI belongs in Common or in the Agent’s loop.

The public entry points have different promises:

Operation Promise
SubmitAsync(parts) Queue a distinct request; return its reliable final text or error.
SendAsync(text, cancellation) Submit text and wait; cancelling this wait does not cancel the turn.
PostAsync(input) Acknowledge admission of a live message, hint, or control.
DispatchAsync(call, cancellation) Dispatch a host tool through the actor; return its reliable report.
RunAsync(input, cancellation) Sequential channel-based facade over the same actor.
WaitAsync(predicate, cancellation) Consume matching lossy Agent progress.
FlushAsync(cancellation) Wait for foreground quiescence without closing admission.
ShutdownAsync() Close admission, cancel and join owned work; do not resurrect the actor.

AgentInput is an immutable value carrying Kind and Text. InputKind contains Message, Hint, Pause, Resume, InterruptNow, InterruptAfterTool, and Ephemeral. A live message while busy becomes input to the current turn; concurrent submissions remain distinct queued requests. The private mailbox also carries HTTP/tool/control completions and lifetime operations.

Observation is a value with kind, event sequence, optional part, text, state transition and nullable admission outcome. Kinds are Input, StateChanged, PartFinal, TurnEnd, and Error. Each public submission, live input and direct dispatch publishes exactly one accepted/refused input outcome, including validation failures. A request’s eventual completion is a separate fact. Progress publication is nonblocking and bounded; the reliable request task does not depend on progress being read.

Ensemble owns named or anonymous Agents and a merged progress stream. AgentObservation contains the actual Agent reference and its observation. FindAgent(name) searches the root’s actual children, with ordinal unique names within that root. WaitAnyAsync watches merged progress, not a group of results. Each Agent retains independent History, Engine, Tools, Jobs and mailbox.

BlobRef and ModelFeatures are value-like declarations. Exact selected-model capabilities govern local-file media projection. Logs retain locators; requests inline bytes. Unknown models may send text, but not undeclared attachments. URI and job-handle rendering remain deferred. See §5.9 for the one authoritative capability policy.

Verification is scoped. The full retained Go grader includes Go consumer imports and dependency checks. It is not a C# architecture test. The C# endpoint uses the unchanged executable replay/media checks through:

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 5 -executable-only \
  -media-models /your/owned/media-models.json -json /your/owned/build/ch04

This is a 25-point report: replay 15 and media 10. It excludes Go consumer, workflow, topology and inherited Chapter 4 parity checks. The mapping selects fixture models; it does not add production aliases or prove live capability:

{"anthropic":"claude-3-haiku-20240307","openai":"gpt-4o","gemini":"gemini-2.5-flash"}

Separately test held HTTP, busy hints, both interrupt modes, pause, reliable replies under observation loss, shutdown joins, complete ownership operations, and the real external C# workflow. Inspect Common and the functional call paths; compilation alone cannot enforce the spoke dependency rule. A marker check cannot prove that stored edits reached the reviewer or that every manuscript tool ran. Keep actual CLI exercises and source review alongside—not inside—the score.

§5.1 The idea in plain words

Chapter 2 separated recorded facts from derived conversation context and vendor requests. Chapter 4 lets a command keep running while the model receives a job handle. But the Agent itself still follows a synchronous loop: ask the model, wait for a tool, ask the model again. A second caller cannot reliably say “pause” or add useful information while that loop is waiting.

The fix is not to scatter locks around that loop. Give conversation decisions one owner, with three pieces that work together.

An observer is a one-way window. The Agent publishes state transitions, completed parts, and progress. A display or logger watches them without owning the conversation. Slow observation must not stop work. A bounded delivery queue may discard a progress update; it must never be the only path by which a waiting caller receives its answer. Each admitted request has its own reliable completion task and exactly one terminal outcome.

A mailbox is a one-way door. Prompts, hints, controls, and worker completions enter one ordered queue. In C# a Channel provides the ordinary asynchronous queue and wake-up behavior. Posting does not wait for the tool or model to finish. The queue synchronizes delivery; it does not give a sender permission to edit History. A hint arriving during a request cannot rewrite the bytes already sent, but it can affect the next safe scheduling decision.

An actor loop drains the mailbox. The Agent makes short decisions: record an input, freeze a model request, admit a tool, apply a returned result, or settle a turn. Work that waits on the network or a process runs outside that loop. Its completion is another message, not a worker-side History write. The Agent’s old blocking API waits for a reply from this same actor. It is not an alternative execution engine.

Ownership remains the model from Chapter 4. Ensemble owns Agents. Each Agent owns its History, Engine, Tools, and Jobs; Jobs owns the running Job objects. Pause and interrupt do not destroy that graph. A paused Agent still accepts controls and worker completions. An interrupted turn must distinguish a tool that started from a call that never reached dispatch: preserve the real job’s handle, and pair each skipped call with an explicit not-executed result. Do not invent effects or silently replay the skipped tail on a later turn.

Shutdown is different. It closes admission, accounts for admitted work, drains owned workers and processes, and only then detaches the children. That ordering keeps the parent paths available while workers finish. Garbage collection cannot perform this logical cleanup for us.

The media and multi-Agent examples use these same paths. Vendor requests may contain inline media bytes, but the canonical log keeps the original locator. A role tool reaches another Agent through its actual owning Ensemble and waits on a private reply. There is no hidden workflow engine in the command-line host.

§5.2 The framework that imported its own GUI

CodeRhapsody built the GUI before it had a framework seam. The React frontend connected to a Go server, the Go server imported the framework, and the framework reached back into the server for test scaffolding. test_support.go built a real GUI server for the twenty-three tests that needed a UI attached. The import graph formed a cycle, and the cycle hid inside convenience: nobody noticed because every test passed.

The dependency surfaced as a question: can the framework run without the GUI? No. It compiled without it, but tests could not run. Untangling it took five commits across two days. The load-bearing commit was titled “Test scaffolding takes a UIObserver, not a GUI server.”

The fix was not deletion. The GUI was demoted to an observer. Instead of the framework importing the GUI, the framework broadcasts events, and the GUI subscribes to them. The import arrow reversed direction. After the fix, the framework does not know the GUI exists, the GUI is one of several observers, and tests run without building a server.

The guard that enforces this boundary exempts test files and ratchets them downward, on the principle that a guard that fails today guards nothing. Twenty-three tests needed a GUI server. Now thirteen do, and the ratchet prevents the number from climbing back. The boundary found problems, it did not create them: two encapsulation reaches appeared as compile errors the moment the internal/ wall went up, one where a tool file grew a method on a job type and another where the engine called an unexported function on a job.

The fix’s shape is this chapter’s thesis. The GUI went from a component the framework knows about to an observer the framework broadcasts at. The first-edition facade measured who actually used its framework: two-thirds of the API surface serves tool authoring, five percent serves agent lifecycle. Design the observer seam for the ninety-five percent of the world that is not the engine.

§5.3 The outbound seam

The actor publishes an immutable observation after recording the corresponding fact. A display may receive a completed text, tool call, or result as a PartFinal, not merely a string stripped of its arguments and correlation. StateChanged reflects the reducer’s actual transitions; TurnEnd describes a terminal outcome. History remains the durable source for prompts, hints, request boundaries and completed content. Observations cannot reconstruct it.

Each Agent owns a bounded channel configured to drop old progress when full. Ensemble has a separate bounded merged channel. Publishing to both is a direct, nonblocking operation through the Agent’s real parent. It does not call an arbitrary observer, create a task per event, or retain an unbounded callback queue. A slow display may miss progress, but cannot delay recording or request replies.

This endpoint offers shared consuming streams, not broadcast subscriptions. Two WaitAsync callers compete for Agent observations. A waiter also consumes nonmatching values while looking for its predicate. Root and Agent streams are separate views, but two readers of either one are not two subscribers. If a later requirement needs independent subscribers, each needs its own bounded queue; sharing a channel reader would not implement broadcast.

Admission publishes an Input outcome with Accepted true or false. This includes invalid inputs and refusals after shutdown. The reliable task carries the actual exception; an observer may miss its diagnostic. Shutdown closes work admission, while observations remain readable until logical destruction. Calls after destruction are disposed-object errors, not new events from a live Agent.

Chapter 5 does not stream HTTP tokens. Its external workflow displays a complete text part as one delta followed by a finalizer. That is a presentation choice, not evidence of incremental provider delivery. Chapter 6 supplies streaming.

§5.4 The inbound seam

Chapter 4 already put a tool’s execution outside the conversation loop. The remaining deafness came from awaiting its report in the same loop that should hear human input. Moving execution was not enough; move the wait too.

Use one Channel<Mail> with one reader. Public messages and private worker outcomes enter that same queue. Channel delivery preserves enqueue order; it does not invent a global physical order for simultaneous callers. Each message is handled before the next scheduling decision.

The public vocabulary is intentionally smaller than the private mailbox:

await agent.PostAsync(new AgentInput(InputKind.Hint, "Keep the examples short."));
await agent.PostAsync(new AgentInput(InputKind.Pause));
await agent.PostAsync(new AgentInput(InputKind.Resume));

These tasks acknowledge admission, not completion of a model turn. The actor validates before changing conversation state or queuing effects. Refused input must leave it usable for the next valid request. One lazy-started mailbox reader belongs to the Agent; no separately owned Actor wrapper is needed.

HTTP and foreground-observation workers return immutable outcomes to this mailbox. They do not append History, select the next tool, or schedule another model request. A running Job owns its independent execution/output state; its report is a snapshot, not evidence that execution has finished.

§5.5 The actor loop

The implementation in Agent/Actor.cs follows three readable steps: receive a mail message, apply its facts, then advance if scheduling is allowed. All lasting scheduling fields are declared in Common/Actor.cs. Async methods provide waits; there is no second scheduler framework hidden beside the Agent.

Start a turn. Record the message, render a frozen request string, record RequestSent, then release HTTP to Engine’s SendAsync. There is at most one model request per Agent. Engine returns immutable, unnumbered response events; the actor assigns their place in History. Engine neither reads live History nor writes it. A hint received after freezing cannot change those request bytes.

Apply a response. Record returned facts before publishing progress. Validate duplicate call IDs before any effect. Dispatch tool calls serially in response order. Jobs reserves an ordinary job and records ToolCalled before starting its handler. That synchronous admission prefix runs on the actor; the subsequent observation wait runs outside it and posts its report back. Controls that do not allocate jobs retain their Chapter 4 contracts.

Record a report. The actor appends ToolReturned, including the actual job locator where applicable, before asking the model to consume it. Host-invoked direct tools instead record ToolObserved: a real audit outcome that does not invent an assistant tool call in model dialogue. Both preserve output evidence. A returned running snapshot does not mean the worker ended.

Apply a hint. Record HintReceived without changing the active turn’s reducer state. During HTTP it affects the next request. During foreground tool observation it cancels only that observation, obtains the real running/completed report, and pairs every undispatched batch-tail call with its exact-ID not-executed result. No skipped effect is replayed later. The next request sees the hint and paired results. Idle hints are retained until a proper trigger; pause still prevents new scheduling.

Finish a turn. Record terminal facts before completing the request task. TurnEnded restores the reducer to Idle; TurnInterrupted records interruption. These are replayable facts, not a fabricated error used to force a state change. The Chapter 2 states remain Idle, InputPending, InFlight and ToolsPending. Scheduling flags are transient actor control, not another canonical transcript.

Reliable completion is not observation

SubmitAsync creates a TaskCompletionSource<string> with asynchronous continuations and places it in the request message. The actor settles it exactly once. A slow or cancelled caller cannot block the actor while it delivers the outcome. Concurrent submissions queue separate turns; they do not read a shared last-answer field or watch for an arbitrary Idle transition.

SendAsync waits on that same task. Caller cancellation detaches its wait; explicit interrupt is how an application ends the turn. RunAsync is a sequential input-channel adapter over submission, not a preserved copy of the old tool loop. With logging enabled, append/flush precedes publication and completion. An append failure cannot be reported as durable success; fault cleanup still joins workers and detaches the graph.

Limits and lifetime

A positive ToolRoundLimit permits that many tool batches per human turn. Zero selects the named default of 200; a negative value disables the cap. After the last permitted batch, the model may consume its results and answer. If it requests another batch, execute none of it, pair every call as not executed, and return a distinguishable limit error. Do not edit signed assistant content or leave dangling results. The immutable Configuration supplies one policy per Agent.

Pause blocks new model/tool scheduling but continues processing inputs and completions. Resume continues automatically. Handle-free job controls can act while foreground work is held; they do not start a competing conversation turn.

Immediate interrupt cancels HTTP and the current foreground observation, not independent Jobs. after_tool retains the current HTTP response or dispatched tool boundary, then refuses the remaining calls. Both modes end the active turn and leave the same Agent available. A late completion cannot dispatch stale calls or settle a newer request. The actor collects its outstanding completion before starting the next turn; independent Jobs keep their own output and handles.

Shutdown closes admission, cancels in-flight transport/observation and controls, settles admitted requests, stops Jobs with reason shutdown, and joins workers. History and the parent paths remain attached until this cleanup finishes. Repeated shutdown joins the same lifetime. Destroy then removes relationships through the owning parents’ methods, even when a joined fault must propagate.

.NET cannot forcibly stop an arbitrary managed callback. The callback receives cancellation and must cooperate; one that ignores it can delay shutdown. PTY processes can be killed and drained. Do not claim a callback has vanished merely because a cancellation token was signalled or its Job status is killed.

§5.6 Wait and flush

Use WaitAsync(predicate, cancellation) for display progress. Use the relevant request task for orchestration. A lossy state event cannot identify which of several queued prompts completed. Ensemble.WaitAnyAsync applies the same rule to the merged stream; it does not gather a group of reliable answers.

FlushAsync is useful at a CLI’s EOF: wait until active/queued turns and foreground controls settle. It does not close admission, resume paused work, or wait for independent background Jobs. Later inputs may extend the wait. Cancelling the waiter does not cancel those turns. Shutdown that discards unfinished work faults the pending flush rather than claiming it drained.

This is deliberately less machinery than a workflow engine. The application retains the author request task, then starts the editor after success, then the reviewer. Observations explain progress; reliable tasks decide transitions.

§5.7 Hints and interrupts

A hint changes information for the next safe decision. An interrupt ends the current turn. Neither is permission to delete the Agent or kill independent work. The same mailbox accepts both while HTTP or a tool observation is waiting.

This distinction is easiest to test with a held real Job and two model calls in one batch. Send a hint or interrupt after the first Job starts. Assert its real handle and output remain accessible, the second call never runs, and its result says not executed. Then submit a fresh prompt and prove the Agent still answers. Repeat at the HTTP boundary: release a late response containing calls and prove that an ended turn cannot cause their effects. Use gates rather than sleeps to establish which boundary the test actually reached.

The stdin protocol

The CLI reads stdin asynchronously and posts to the Agent’s mailbox. The protocol is JSON lines:

{"kind":"prompt","text":"Write a haiku about refactoring"}
{"kind":"hint","text":"Use a metaphor about gardens"}
{"kind":"interrupt"}

Backward compatibility with the Chapter 1 format:

{"user":"Write a haiku about refactoring"}

A message with a "user" key and no "kind" key queues a separate reliable request. The CLI continues reading stdin and emits {"assistant":"..."} replies in request order. Optional parts uses the public Part JSON format and takes precedence over user text, including an empty array. Media bytes are resolved only when projecting a request. Live prompt and hint inputs instead use the actor’s current turn state; they can become hints while the Agent is busy.

The C# CLI also accepts these direct actor operations:

{"kind":"pause"}
{"kind":"resume"}
{"kind":"interrupt","mode":"after_tool"}
{"kind":"tool","id":"host-1","name":"list_directory","arguments":{"path":"."}}
{"kind":"shutdown"}

Interrupt mode defaults to now. Direct tool dispatch returns tool_result; its audit result is not an invented model-requested call. Live inputs have an ack after admission; direct tools acknowledge queuing and return their outcome later; shutdown acknowledges after joining. Live mode additionally emits lossy observation records with kind, sequence, text, accepted flag, state transition and optional part. These are progress, not request replies. Explicit interrupt/shutdown produces an error outcome for an unfinished reliable request.

EOF calls FlushAsync: wait for active/queued turns and foreground controls, not independent background Jobs. Then shutdown cancels and joins remaining Jobs. Flush does not resume paused work; send resume or shutdown before EOF if work is paused. Explicit shutdown cancels instead of draining queued turns. Cancelling a flush waiter detaches only that waiter. New inputs may extend a flush wait; it is a quiescence wait, not a frozen-prefix barrier.

§5.8 Managing multiple agents

Ensemble already owns the peer Agents. It is not supplemented by another coordinator root or mutable name registry. Construction supplies the real parent and optional name; AddAgent validates ownership and name uniqueness before changing either relationship end. RemoveAgent completes both ends. Destroying one root cannot touch a same-named Agent belonging to another root.

var author = new Agent(app, authorConfiguration, name: "author");
var editor = new Agent(app, editorConfiguration, name: "editor");
var reviewer = new Agent(app, reviewerConfiguration, name: "reviewer");

Each immutable Configuration supplies its role’s PrimaryInstructions. Installing tools appends tool-use guidance; it must not erase that role prompt. Each Agent owns its own concrete Tool objects, History, Engine, Jobs and mailbox. Two held requests on different Agents may progress concurrently; one Agent never has two model requests in flight.

The merged observation envelope carries the actual source Agent. A hint addressed to author uses app.FindAgent("author"), not a global fleet lookup followed by filtering. A callback reaches diagnostics through Job → Jobs → Agent → Ensemble. Application data such as the manuscript has one authoritative home, not one copy per role.

This chapter’s peers are constructed by application code. They are not children spawned by a model tool. Adding the reviewer must not require a new library workflow API; the application simply constructs another Agent and awaits its reliable request. Sub-Agent ownership and spawning contracts remain later work.

§5.9 Media capabilities

Image, audio, video, and document support are independent facts. ModelFeatures uses separate flags for them. Do not infer audio support from image support, or silently omit a part the selected model cannot accept.

Engine.LookupModel(vendor, model, out features) is an exact lookup. The small Chapter 5 table declares images for claude-3-haiku-20240307, gpt-4o, and gpt-4o-mini, and image/audio/video/PDF input for gemini-2.5-flash, each under its own vendor. These are the renderer’s supported declarations, not a claim that a paid live request was run or that a model remains available indefinitely. An unknown identifier still works for text; there is no default attachment row.

The renderer checks capabilities before reading a file or starting HTTP. An unsupported attachment produces an error such as:

Model 'claude-3-haiku-20240307' does not support audio media.

BlobRef is value-like: it has no owning parent because it describes an address, not an owned file. Its Kind and Locator remain in canonical events and survive as a locator when a blob is redacted. Rendering calls Data() only on local-path references and creates disposable vendor JSON containing the actual bytes:

  • Anthropic uses an image block with a base64 source and MIME type.
  • OpenAI Chat Completions uses an image_url block containing a data URI.
  • Gemini uses inlineData with its MIME type and base64 data.

The surrounding text parts retain their order. History does not acquire base64 content or a second authoritative file cache. A missing file is an error; a saved locator cannot guarantee that external content remains available forever.

URI and job-handle attachments remain deferred. Unsupported tool-result media placements also fail explicitly: this adapter cannot turn a blob into empty text and pretend the model received it. Anthropic’s nested result blocks can carry supported images; the current OpenAI and Gemini tool-result projections are text/structured-result projections, not media containers.

§5.10 Exercise: Author, Editor, Reviewer

Build Examples/Workflow/Workflow.csproj as a separate C# assembly referencing the public library, as the Chapter 4 consumer did. Three agents, three roles:

The author receives a topic and writes a first draft. Its tools are write_draft (stores text) and word_count (returns the count).

The editor receives the author’s draft and improves it. Its tools are read_draft (retrieves text) and edit_draft (replaces text).

The reviewer receives the editor’s draft and approves or rejects it. Its tool is review (returns accept or reject with notes).

The accepted example uses string text arguments for write_draft and edit_draft, empty objects for word_count and read_draft, and string decision (accept or reject) plus notes for review. Its word count counts whitespace-separated words in the stored manuscript. These are small application-level choices to document in the tool schemas, not new framework builtins. The stored draft is shared application data; synchronize access because a tool worker can outlive the turn that launched it.

The slow-tool fixture also calls think with this argument object:

{"seconds":3,"thought":"composing draft"}

It waits the numeric number of seconds and returns the thought. Register it only on the author in this application; it is not an Ensemble builtin or a substitute for the actual manuscript tools.

The workflow is sequential: author writes, editor edits, reviewer reviews. The application advances through reliable SendAsync or SubmitAsync completions. PostAsync delivers live hints; WaitAsync watches progress. Each agent uses the same vendor (the fake from Chapter 2) with a different system prompt. The workflow is ordinary C# application code. Every new collaboration pattern is a new application program. That is the limit this chapter reaches; agent-created collaboration remains later work. The framework works; the rigidity is in the glue code, not in the framework itself.

Three agents prove the cost was paid once. The first agent might work because the framework was tested with it. The second might work because the code was debugged for two. The third works because the framework is general. If adding the reviewer required a single line inside the framework package, the seam is wrong.

The binary reads JSON events on stdin, writes observations as JSON lines on stdout, and logs to the path in CH06_LOG. The grader drives the fake vendor to script specific responses for each agent.

The C# workflow is in solutions/edition-3/main/Examples/Workflow. Keep the historical CH06_LOG environment name for protocol compatibility. Build that project separately. This offline exercise requires a loopback endpoint; it does not grant paid-provider access. The local provider fake supplies the ordinary Anthropic adapter environment (LLM_VENDOR=anthropic, a model, a dummy LLM_API_KEY, and its loopback LLM_BASE_URL), not a new vendor enum. The grader starts the application without arguments in a disposable directory. It sends a prompt, a hint addressed to the author during think, then EOF:

{"kind":"prompt","text":"Write about the ocean"}
{"kind":"hint","text":"make it vivid","agent":"author"}

Emit observations with the observation discriminator and external agent tag. The kinds are state_changed, part_delta and part_final; their payload fields are specified in the exercise walkthrough below. A hint acknowledgment is a delta whose chunk begins hint:. After each actual request completes, the application emits its completion record and stage marker:

{"observation":"turn_ended","agent":"author"}
{"pipeline":"author_done"}

Use the corresponding editor/reviewer names for their stages. These extra records belong to the application protocol, not new sealed core observation types. Log them and the observations to CH06_LOG; keep each Agent’s durable conversation history separately so one Agent’s sequence numbers do not become another’s. EOF waits for the submitted workflow before shutdown.

§5.11 What this chapter does not build

There is no streaming transport, GUI, model-driven spawning, grouped-results API, URI fetching, or job-handle attachment resolver here. The workflow’s whole-part delta is not a token stream. BlobRef can describe URI and handle locators, but this renderer rejects them explicitly. These omissions are boundaries, not silent fallbacks.

The actor and progress seam provide foundations for later chapters. They do not turn a lossy Wait into a future supervision contract. Keep the current surface small and teach its exact promises before adding new ones.

Taking it for a spin

Build the actual library tests, CLI and separate consumer using the approved .NET 10 SDK. The working CLI project retains the historical Ch04.csproj and ch04 assembly names; that is a filename, not the chapter boundary.

dotnet run --project solutions/edition-3/main/Tests/Tests.csproj
dotnet build solutions/edition-3/main/Cli/Ch04.csproj
dotnet build solutions/edition-3/main/Examples/Workflow/Workflow.csproj

Use an owned loopback fake and dummy credentials for local exercises. Set LLM_VENDOR, LLM_MODEL, LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, and an owned CH06_LOG path for the workflow, then run its compiled DLL. The exercise fake must actually call think, write_draft, word_count, read_draft, edit_draft, and review; a fake that merely returns final prose does not test manuscript sharing.

Send the topic, wait until the author’s real think Job starts, then send the addressed hint shown in §5.10 and EOF. Inspect all three captured role prompts and tool declarations. The next author request must contain the hint, the first Job’s real running report and the skipped tail’s not-executed result. Verify the stored author’s text reaches the editor, the edited text reaches the reviewer, and the review decision and notes are actually returned by review. The three reliable pipeline markers must occur in order before exit zero. Tagged progress may be dropped; those markers do not depend on it.

Illustrative output shape, not a captured provider transcript:

{"observation":"state_changed","agent":"author","from":"idle","to":"input_pending"}
{"observation":"part_delta","agent":"author","part_id":1,"chunk":"A draft about the ocean."}
{"observation":"part_final","agent":"author","seq":3,"part_id":1,"part":{"type":"text","text":"A draft about the ocean."}}
{"observation":"turn_ended","agent":"author"}
{"pipeline":"author_done"}

The consumer’s state_changed fields are from and to; whole-text part_delta carries part_id and chunk; part_final carries seq, part_id and the complete serialized part. Display IDs are unique within this consumer run; they are not durable History identities. Agent sequence numbers remain local to that Agent. The shared application log records the same output lines, while CH06_LOG.author.jsonl, .editor.jsonl and .reviewer.jsonl preserve separate canonical histories.

Also exercise the single-Agent CLI: queued legacy replies, a live prompt and hint during held HTTP, pause/resume, both interrupt modes, direct host tools, explicit shutdown and EOF. Do not use a sleep alone as proof that a tool has started. Check its real dispatch event or gated handler before sending the control.

For local media, parts takes precedence over fallback text. kind:1 below is the public codec’s local-path Ref kind:

{"user":"ignored fallback","parts":[{"type":"text","text":"Describe this."},{"type":"blob","mime":"image/png","ref":{"kind":1,"locator":"/your/owned/image.png"}}]}

With a declared image-capable model, inspect the captured request’s actual bytes, not just its MIME label. The saved event must retain only the locator. Unsupported media on a text-only/unknown model must fail before a network request. Replay the logged prefix preceding each RequestSent through the same vendor/model renderer and compare it byte-for-byte with the live request. Replay must need no provider key and must not rewrite canonical History.

The local verification of this C# endpoint covers actor/component behavior, three-vendor image projection, Gemini WAV/PDF byte projection, representative video-container bytes, the scoped executable grade, and the external three-role workflow. Video bytes do not prove a decodable movie. Loopback fixtures do not prove current model availability, remote acceptance, or live-provider behavior. Real-provider exercises remain incomplete because the authorized allowance is exhausted. No installation into the working Ensemble follows from these tests.

Historical context, not carried evidence

The retained Go chapter described a Gemini ocean-writing workflow and an Anthropic cartoon-image test, and linked a historical ocean conversation. Those runs motivated the exercise, but they are not runs of this C# endpoint. The important lesson survives: application code supplies roles and manuscript tools; the actor handles transport, hints, jobs and reliable completion without knowing what an author or editor is. Streaming, the GUI and model-created collaboration still come later.

Chapter 6: Streaming, or the Same Answer in Pieces

Ask the Chapter 5 Agent something difficult and the cursor stops. Behind the HTTP connection, the provider may be producing text or tool arguments already. Our client waits for the completed body before showing any of it.

This chapter removes that unnecessary wait. It does not turn half a tool call into permission to execute it. The display can be provisional; the conversation and effects cannot.

TL;DR

Streaming changes delivery, not the authoritative answer.

  • Common declares Chunk, ParsedResponse, and the Engine’s parsing operation. Engine implements SSE framing and vendor translation. The Agent’s existing mailbox remains the sole conversation owner.
  • Engine.ParseAsync(HttpResponseMessage, Action<Chunk>?, CancellationToken) accepts either plain JSON or SSE. Both paths use the existing completed-body decoder for canonical parts, provenance, exact arguments, and usage.
  • A chunk carries a response-local part ID, kind, and display fragments. The parser returns the matching IDs with the completed events. The actor never guesses final identity from array position.
  • Deltas enter the mailbox, then the bounded observation queues. They are not recorded in History. Final events are appended before their parts are published to observers.
  • A declared model streams by default unless Configuration.DisableStreaming is true. Unknown models use plain delivery. Plain delivery publishes finals but no synthetic deltas.
  • Partial arguments are display-only. Missing terminators, malformed frames, provider errors, and interrupted requests cannot authorize tool effects.
  • The root optionally writes sanitized request/frame payloads to a caller-owned trace writer. Engine reaches it through Engine → Agent → Ensemble.
  • Examples/Observer measures the delivered stream. Examples/Workflow tags real chunks with their Agent, response ID, and part ID. Both are separate assemblies using the public library.

The runnable endpoint is solutions/edition-3/ch06. Working development uses solutions/edition-3/main. These C# sources compile with C# 14 and .NET 10.

6.1 The idea in plain words

An HTTP response body is already a stream of bytes. Reading the whole body before parsing is a client decision, not an inherent property of HTTP.

Three responsibilities change:

  1. Transport hands an open response to the parser after headers arrive.
  2. Parsing recognizes complete SSE frames and emits transient chunks as their data arrives.
  3. The actor receives those chunks through the same mailbox as controls and completions, then publishes optional progress.

One responsibility deliberately does not change: History owns finalized conversation facts. Replaying a saved response does not require stitching hundreds of display fragments back together. The recorded ResponseEnded event contains the completed parts and usage, just as it did in Chapter 5.

The HTTP worker cannot append History, start tools, or finish the user’s turn. It sends chunks and then an immutable completion back to the actor. Pause, hint, interrupt, and shutdown therefore continue to use the existing owner rather than a parallel streaming control loop.

Upgrading from Edition 2: the old “non-streaming is streaming with a length of one” rule no longer applies to observer notifications. A non-streaming response emits zero deltas, not one synthetic delta per part. Final parts are authoritative in both modes: a display must be able to create a part from its final notification even if no delta preceded it, and must not append the final text to an already displayed partial copy. Streaming changes how soon content can be shown, not what belongs in the conversation. Compare final content and usage across modes; do not require a positive plain-mode delta count.

A slow observer still cannot stall that owner. Observation queues remain bounded and lossy. A reliable request task, not a quiet screen or a final-looking chunk, tells the application whether its request completed.

6.2 The shared vocabulary

Read Common/Streaming.cs and Common/Actor.cs before their implementations. The essential declarations are:

// Value-like parser output, not an independently owned runtime service.
public enum ChunkKind { Reply, Thinking, ToolCall }

public sealed record Chunk(
    int PartID,
    ChunkKind Kind,
    string Text = "",
    string ToolName = "",
    string ArgsText = "");

public sealed record ParsedResponse(
    ImmutableArray<Event> Events,
    ImmutableArray<int> PartIDs,
    bool ToolBeforeText = false);

The Engine declares its required partial operation in Common:

public partial Task<ParsedResponse> ParseAsync(
    HttpResponseMessage response,
    Action<Chunk>? onChunk = null,
    CancellationToken cancellation = default);

This callback carries transient parser output for this invocation. It is not a constructor service bag, a second owner, or an alternative route to logging. The actor’s HTTP worker uses it only to post a delta message to the mailbox. Final events and identities return together in ParsedResponse.

Observation carries the resulting Delta, or a finalized Part with its PartID, plus ResponseID. At the root, AgentObservation also retains the actual originating Agent. A string label in JSON is a display of that relationship, not a substitute for it.

The accumulation state is per parse and value-like. Its declaration lives in Common; Engine/Streaming.cs supplies the algorithms. It is not another persistent transcript. Once the complete native response is decoded, those scratch dictionaries and JSON objects can be reclaimed normally.

6.3 One transport entry, shared final construction

The trap is two independent semantic decoders: one for JSON and one for SSE. They inevitably acquire different rules for arguments, opaque signatures, usage, and errors.

Our single HTTP entry is ParseAsync. It inspects the response content type:

  • Plain JSON: read the completed body and call the existing Parse(status, body) decoder. Derive final identities and explanation order, but emit no transient chunks.
  • SSE: frame and accumulate the provider’s native response, emitting chunks along the way. At terminal success, pass that native response through the same completed-body decoder and return its events with the accumulated identity mapping.

Retaining the completed-body decoder is intentional. It is the shared semantic operation, not a competing transport implementation or a new ParseStream service. Canonical JSON numbers, provenance, signatures, and nullable usage still have one decoding home.

A plain response could manufacture one delta per part. This C# implementation does not: an event called a delta should mean something arrived incrementally. Consumers already need final parts to correct lossy previews, so final-only plain delivery does not require a second conversation model. A plain run has zero deltas and the same authoritative parts.

Do not infer success from partial visible text. The parser requires terminal success and complete arguments. Expected protocol failures become a fixed, credential-safe ErrorOccurred, not a partial ResponseEnded. Explicit cancellation propagates to the actor. Previously displayed chunks may remain on a terminal, but cannot enter History as a successful response or cause a tool to run.

6.4 Server-sent events, and the reader that survives them

SSE is ordinary HTTP with text framing:

event: content_block_delta
data: {"type":"content_block_delta","index":0,"delta":{"type":"text_delta","text":"Hello"}}

event: content_block_delta
data: {"type":"content_block_delta","index":0,"delta":{"type":"text_delta","text":" world"}}

A blank line ends a frame. Each data: line contributes to its payload. StreamReader.ReadLineAsync handles the line endings; the small shared loop handles the framing before vendor interpretation begins.

Case Required behavior
Multiple data: lines Join with newlines; do not silently discard later lines.
Comment beginning : Ignore it, including keepalive comments.
CRLF Recognize the same boundaries as LF.
[DONE] Treat it as OpenAI’s terminator, not a JSON object.
Last frame without a blank line Process its pending data at EOF.
EOF without required protocol completion Refuse success, even if text was visible.
Missing/null required members Return a safe protocol error, not an accidental null-reference fault.

A frame boundary is not a part boundary. One part may span many frames; one frame may contain several parts. Shared framing does not make the vendors’ content semantics identical.

Tests use real HttpResponseMessage bodies and a held loopback HTTP response. They include comments, multiline data, CRLF, missing terminators, invalid JSON, missing members, and incomplete arguments. No provider account is needed to establish these deterministic rules.

6.5 Part IDs: who is allowed to name a part

Within one response, a part ID identifies exactly one part. A part never changes IDs, and one ID never crosses kinds.

A fresh ID for every chunk tells a consumer that forty things happened, not which chunks belong to the same paragraph. A final array position is no better: it may not exist when the first chunk arrives.

OpenAI makes this concrete. A tool fragment can arrive before the text that will precede it in the final decoded response. Sorting final parts and then numbering them cannot recover the identity used earlier.

The code that chose an ID must repeat it on finalization.

  • Anthropic keeps its nonnegative block indices, including gaps.
  • OpenAI maps wire tool indices to parser-local IDs and allocates text/thinking IDs on first appearance. Final decoder order may differ from arrival order; PartIDs explicitly maps the finished parts back to their original IDs.
  • Gemini infers continuation from content kind, explicit part boundaries, and signature closure. It has no Anthropic-style block index to borrow.

Zero is valid. IDs may restart on the next response. The display key is (response_id, part_id), or (agent, response_id, part_id) for several Agents. The actor uses the recorded RequestSent sequence as ResponseID; it does not ask the CLI to infer response boundaries from a state transition it might miss.

Part IDs themselves remain transient parser identities, not a new persisted widget schema. Later replay or reconnect code must not assume a fresh parser run will reproduce the same display mapping without an explicit contract.

The actor first appends each final event, then publishes the corresponding PartFinal observations using those stored parts and parser IDs. An observer that reads History on finalization therefore sees the event already present. Human input and Job results have no parser part ID and must not masquerade as model finals.

Tests group deltas by identity before comparing them with finals. Concatenating all text in a turn would let meaningless IDs pass. Tool fragments need a slightly different assertion: decode the completed argument JSON and compare values, because canonical formatting may differ from the incoming fragments. The large integer 9007199254740993 must not become a rounded floating-point value on the way through that comparison.

6.6 Three vendors, three local translations

Vendor Request selection Stream interpretation
Anthropic stream: true Message start, block start/delta/stop, usage updates, message stop.
OpenAI chat completions stream: true, stream_options: {include_usage: true} Choice deltas, tool-index mapping, finish reason, optional usage-only frame, [DONE].
Gemini :streamGenerateContent?alt=sse Response-shaped frames; infer continuation locally and retain signatures.

Anthropic

Block start creates identity. Text and thinking deltas append visible content; input-JSON deltas append raw argument text. Block stop decodes the complete argument value. A stream cannot succeed while a block remains open. Signatures and opaque blocks survive into the shared final decoder.

OpenAI

Only choice zero belongs to this single-answer API. Tool indices identify calls even when several calls are interleaved. Names can also arrive in pieces; show them, but do not dispatch by a partially received name.

Usage can arrive after the finish reason in a frame with no choices. Allow that accounting frame, but reject new choice content after completion. Requesting include_usage does not make missing counts measured zeros: the existing nullable usage rules still apply.

Gemini

A first same-kind entry can continue the current part. Additional explicit entries start distinct parts; function calls are complete parts; a signature closes the part it signs. Empty signed text is meaningful replay material and must not vanish merely because it paints no characters.

Readable thought content and ordinary text remain different kinds. Preserve signatures on thought, text, and tool-call parts according to the existing provenance codec. Do not invent a uniform wrapper shape just for a streaming test; replay semantics, not a convenient fixture assertion, govern the value.

Arrival order is policy evidence

The strict explanation policy asks whether substantive assistant text preceded the first tool fragment. Later text cannot retroactively explain an earlier call. ToolBeforeText records this decision during parsing, before final parts are rearranged by the shared decoder.

The actor uses that fact together with its existing explanation check. A refusal still produces a paired result for the complete call and no effect. Neither an explanation nor a complete-looking argument fragment permits execution before terminal success.

6.7 Capabilities: conservative delivery, strict content

ModelFeatures.Stream is a Boolean permission to request streaming. It does not promise incremental text, thought, and arguments from every model. The adapters emit only what actually arrived: a complete Gemini function object may produce one display chunk while text arrives in many pieces.

This makes a per-kind capability bitmask unnecessary for this implementation. A future requirement to negotiate individual stream kinds could justify one; the current HTTP APIs and display consumers do not need it.

Configuration.DisableStreaming defaults to false. A caller can opt out without changing the selected model. Effective selection requires both a known stream-capable row and no explicit opt-out. Stream capability is declared separately from media capability; adding an image type must not silently change HTTP delivery.

The small offline-rendering table includes claude-3-haiku-20240307, gpt-4o, gpt-4o-mini, and gemini-2.5-flash. These declarations are not current model availability checks or proof of real-provider acceptance.

An unknown model falls back to plain delivery. An unsupported media attachment still fails before HTTP. That difference is deliberate: choosing slower delivery preserves content; silently dropping an image would corrupt it. A new wire format needs parser work and evidence, not merely another table row.

6.8 Three records, three purposes

History retains complete events. Deltas never become extra dialogue or extra token accounting. Successful responses preserve the established replay contract; interrupted or malformed attempts retain their actual terminal facts.

API trace retains sanitized payloads for diagnosis. The root accepts an optional TextWriter and serializes writes. The caller owns that writer’s lifetime and closes it after the root has stopped its children. Engine reaches it through its real parents; no copied logger is injected into the parser.

Requests and received frame payloads are traced as they arrive. The configured key and its JSON-escaped representation are redacted before writing. Headers and endpoint URLs are not traced. This is not a byte-for-byte HTTP capture: SSE comments and framing are not response payloads. It is also not a general secret detector—prompts, file content, opaque signatures, and other private material may remain. Keep traces outside version control and review them before sharing.

Observers receive provisional chunks and stored-part final notifications. They can update a display, but neither progress loss nor a display exception changes the reliable request reply. Counts from a bounded observer describe received observations, not an authoritative accounting ledger.

6.9 The terminal, and the flush that makes streaming real

The JSON CLI emits one flushed record per delivered observation:

{"observation":"part_delta","response_id":2,"part_id":0,"kind":"text","chunk":"Hello"}

A model part_final includes the same identity and a typed part. State and turn observations remain distinct. Human input uses input_part; Job results use tool_result. A successful posted turn produces a completed assistant record; a blocking request already has its own reliable answer and must not print it twice.

Use kind: prompt for live JSON output. Legacy user requests retain their reliable reply-only compatibility behavior. -no-stream or EN_DISABLE_STREAMING=1 forces plain delivery. CH06_API_LOG selects the trace; CH02_LOG retains its earlier name for the canonical CLI event log.

In interactive chat, streamed text, thinking, and tool fragments are a stderr preview. Thinking is dim and tool arguments yellow only when stderr is a terminal; redirected output has no ANSI codes. The reliable completed answer is written once to stdout. Prompts and usage go to stderr too.

This differs deliberately from the older Go terminal’s streamed-answer stdout. A lossy preview cannot guarantee a complete redirected answer. Rather than add an unbounded queue or a second reliable streaming protocol, this example keeps stdout reliable and makes the preview explicitly provisional. Both file descriptors are visible in an ordinary terminal. The GUI chapter can replace a preview from authoritative finalized content instead of merely appending it.

Each preview or JSON record is flushed immediately. Otherwise every stage may be logically correct while the user still sees nothing until EOF. The gated exercise holds the provider’s remaining frames until the application’s first meaningful chunk appears. That proves visibility before completion, unlike counting stdout reads after the provider has already finished.

Hint acknowledgments are separate records, not strings recognized by a hint: prefix. A model may legitimately begin its answer with that text. Display content is never a protocol discriminator.

On EOF, the JSON CLI first flushes accepted turns, then stops work, closes the Agent, and drains queued display records. It captures usage before destruction. Cancelling the display reader immediately after the reliable answer would lose already-published finals and create a misleadingly incomplete transcript.

6.10 Two separate applications

Aggregate observer

Examples/Observer builds one Agent, installs its tools, starts one observation reader, and awaits SendAsync. Local counters measure:

  • chunks and UTF-8 display bytes per kind;
  • finalized model parts, keyed by response and part ID;
  • state transitions and model-request steps;
  • time to first delivered delta and total reliable-turn duration.

After completion it destroys the root and drains the observation task, then prints one stream_stats record. The report also includes the reliable answer, measured History usage, and effective streaming selection. Plain mode reports zero deltas, has_delta: false, and first_delta_ms: 0; that zero means no delta was delivered, not zero-latency network service.

CH07_NO_STREAM=1 disables streaming in this example. CH07_LOG selects the aggregate JSONL file; CH07_AGENT_LOG, when supplied, selects its event log. The historical environment names remain for compatibility. Both example applications require an explicitly configured loopback endpoint in this permitted offline exercise.

Three-role workflow

Examples/Workflow retains Chapter 5’s one manuscript and real named Agents. Reliable author, editor, and reviewer tasks drive the pipeline. Its root observer only displays activity; an Idle transition is not permission to advance the workflow.

Deltas come directly from Observation.Delta; finals use the parser’s IDs. The example no longer invents a whole-part delta or increments a local counter on finalization. Every output record identifies the actual Agent. A hint_accepted record is not a fabricated model chunk. CH06_LOG duplicates output records to a file, and CH06_HISTORY_DIR optionally stores each Agent’s canonical events. EN_DISABLE_STREAMING=1 selects plain delivery.

The local exercise holds the author’s first streamed tool-name chunk until that chunk is displayed. It then sends a busy hint during a real Job, verifies the untouched batch tail is paired, and lets the reliable three-role pipeline finish at EOF. Finals and assembled text/tool arguments are checked by (agent, response_id, part_id), including noncontiguous IDs.

Taking it for a spin

Build from the endpoint directory with the approved SDK and an owned CLI home:

dotnet build Cli/Ch04.csproj
dotnet build Examples/Observer/Observer.csproj
dotnet build Examples/Workflow/Workflow.csproj
dotnet run --project Tests

The CLI project retains the name Ch04.csproj to preserve existing executable references; it compiles this endpoint’s current library. Run from an owned scratch directory so job files and traces stay outside the source tree. Configure LLM_VENDOR, LLM_MODEL, LLM_BASE_URL, and LLM_API_KEY for the owned fake. Never put a real credential in a command argument or transcript.

printf '%s\n' '{"kind":"prompt","text":"Describe the lighthouse."}' |
    dotnet /absolute/endpoint/Cli/bin/Debug/net10.0/ch04.dll

printf '%s\n' '{"kind":"prompt","text":"Describe the lighthouse."}' |
    dotnet /absolute/endpoint/Cli/bin/Debug/net10.0/ch04.dll -no-stream

dotnet /absolute/endpoint/Cli/bin/Debug/net10.0/ch04.dll chat

dotnet /absolute/endpoint/Examples/Observer/bin/Debug/net10.0/Observer.dll \
    'What does the configuration say?'
CH07_NO_STREAM=1 dotnet /absolute/endpoint/Examples/Observer/bin/Debug/net10.0/Observer.dll \
    'What does the configuration say?'

Use identical scripted responses for exact on/off comparisons. Two independent live generations need not choose the same words or chunk boundaries. Real provider exercises require separate authorization; this endpoint’s offline work does not claim them completed.

Scoped executable grading

The existing grader has language-independent streaming fixtures. The C# route accepts a compiled CLI launcher and the separate observer launcher:

grade-edition2 -ch 6 -executable-only -json \
    -stream-model claude-3-haiku-20240307 \
    -stream-exercise /absolute/observer /absolute/cli
Check Points Meaning
stream-deltas 20 Genuine multiple chunks, not just completed parts.
deltas-match-final 20 Response-scoped text identity and reconstruction.
thinking-streamed 15 Thinking chunks remain separate from reply text.
tool-params-streamed 15 Tool names and argument fragments correlate with complete calls.
delivery-not-content 10 On/off finals and usage agree; unknown models fall back; external aggregate reports real measurements.
Scoped total 80 Excludes inherited Chapter 5 and Go consumer/topology checks.

The full Go route remains intact. The scoped grade is not a claim of full Go consumer parity. Source review, all-vendor parser fixtures, gated delivery, interruption tests, and the three-role application are separate evidence.

The first C# scoped grade misclassified opaque finals because its adapter read a generic observation text label before the typed part. Correcting that adapter preserved the actual typed-part contract. A green number still cannot replace inspection of parser IDs, ownership, cleanup, or real output timing.

Lessons retained from earlier editions

Earlier demonstrations and mutation tests are historical, not C# integration receipts. Their useful lessons remain:

  • A no-stream request can return identical content while failing every meaningful incremental-delivery assertion. Content equality alone does not test streaming.
  • A fresh ID per chunk can look plausible in logs. Grouping before comparing is what exposes the mistake.
  • A test waiting on file modification time can mislabel a busy hint as a new turn. Reliable completion, not timestamps, defines the boundary.
  • A working provider model outside an explicitly authorized selection still does not satisfy the exercise. Successful output does not expand permission.
  • Chunk counts and OS read counts are not token counts. A few rapid reads may establish incremental writes without proving perceptibly paced typing.

What this chapter does not build

No execution from fragments. Only a successful complete response can supply a tool batch. Interrupted streams cannot dispatch a late call.

No durable delta transcript. History retains canonical facts, not a second conversation assembled from previews.

No lossless progress guarantee. Reliable answers and canonical History remain available when a bounded display drops optional observations.

No polished redraw. The terminal appends previews. Replacing a partial widget with its authoritative final, handling reconnects, and giving several Agents usable screen space belong to Chapter 7.

The vocabulary is ready for that next step: actual origins, response-local identity, typed chunks, and stored-before-published finals. The GUI will project those facts; it must not become another owner of the conversation.

Chapter 7: Everything Is an Artifact

The terminal from Chapter 6 is honest but limited. Text, thinking, and tool arguments compete for the same screen. A tool the human cannot comfortably follow is a tool the human cannot steer. This chapter adds a browser view without making the Agent depend on that view.

TL;DR

Build the browser as an optional application over the public C# API. The Agent still owns conversation, scheduling, tools, and jobs. The GUI owns presentation and connection lifetime, not a second transcript or actor loop.

  • A locked History.Snapshot() supplies immutable events and context from one instant. Appending to a list is not a synchronization strategy.
  • Final response events retain Chapter 6’s response sequence and parser part IDs. A response-local ID of zero is valid. Provider call IDs and opaque signature data remain unchanged.
  • Browser IDs combine Agent, response, and part identities. Historical records without parser metadata get deterministic event/position IDs instead.
  • The host sends canonical history plus current partials on connection, then live frames. An internal history frontier is not a cursor supplied by the browser.
  • Progress observations are bounded and lossy. Periodic snapshot catch-up recovers finalized facts. Each WebSocket has its own bounded output queue; a slow browser is disconnected, not allowed to block the actor.
  • ToolCalled is an audit of a request. ToolStarted means admission succeeded and execution was permitted. A refused call must never look dispatched.
  • Typing and queued speech cause edge-triggered pause/unpause requests. Pause is Agent-wide. An unchanged local condition is not a tab’s permanent veto over an explicit unpause from elsewhere.
  • Full-content speaker buttons are separate from automatic narration. Collapsed or scrollable presentation must not discard the rest of the text.

The implementation is Examples/Gui, a separate .NET 10 web project using the installed ASP.NET Core shared framework. The core library references neither that project nor ASP.NET. No package installation is required.

7.1 Why the browser is outside the Agent

The earlier chapters established the useful boundary: submit inputs through an Agent’s public operations, await reliable completion when completion matters, and consume observations when displaying progress.

The browser adds no new scheduling authority. A button sends an input to the same mailbox that a non-GUI caller uses. HTTP workers still return immutable outcomes. Only the actor records conversation facts and schedules the next step. Closing a tab does not cancel a turn, terminate a job, or destroy the Agent.

The optional application’s composition root constructs the Ensemble, Agent, selected-model configuration, tools, logs, and hosting operation. Its Common directory declares the GUI functions and value-like projection. Server implements them. Static browser files live in wwwroot.

The server operation holds its connection queues and partial text locally for that operation’s lifetime. It does not introduce a persistent GUI owner into the core graph. Those values are derived display and transport state, not alternative authoritative conversation objects. Core destruction remains the existing Ensemble → Agent → owned children cascade.

This distinction also limits the claim: the GUI is a trusted local control surface, not a security sandbox for the tools. Choose a suitable workspace. Binding to loopback and rejecting foreign origins does not make arbitrary model-generated commands safe.

7.2 Give reconnect a trustworthy source

A browser can miss progress. It may disconnect during a response, reconnect after completion, or simply consume its bounded queue too slowly. A list of recent observations cannot reconstruct completed history reliably.

Use two sources:

  1. Recorded facts: finalized response parts, human messages, tool admission and results, pause/resume, and terminal facts. These come from History.
  2. Transient partials: accumulated chunks for an unfinished response. These belong only to the hosting operation and disappear when finalized or ended.

History exposes a value-like atomic read:

public sealed record HistorySnapshot(
    ImmutableArray<Event> Events,
    Context Context);

// Declared in Common; implemented by History.
public partial HistorySnapshot Snapshot();

History locks its mutation and snapshot boundaries. Append still validates, sequences, writes, and flushes before publishing the new state. Only afterward does it publish an EventRecorded observation. That observation can be dropped; the recorded event cannot be replaced by a claim that the observer saw it.

The host serializes subscriber registration, replay construction, and queueing under one short handoff lock. It never holds that lock during a network send. A connection receives its replay before becoming eligible for subsequent frames. Its internal frontier prevents already-replayed durable facts from being delivered again as newly recorded history.

There is a subtle ordering trap. By the time an old delta reaches the display reader, History may already contain the response’s final. Taking the newest snapshot on every delta would publish that final first and erase genuine live progress. The live path therefore projects through the observation’s recorded sequence. Full catch-up happens on idle polls and connection establishment. A reconnect that already received the final must not receive old queued chunks as if the part were unfinished again.

On a quiet observation stream, a short cancellable poll catches up finalized facts. This is display recovery, not an Agent timer or turn deadline. It does not schedule model work or cancel it.

Writing an event log does not implement application restoration. This chapter reconnects to the same live Agent. Loading a saved application after process restart belongs to later chapters.

7.3 One identity from streaming through replay

Chapter 6’s parser IDs are local to one response. Part 0 in the next response is a different part. A tool provider’s call ID is a different kind of identity again: it correlates a call with a result and must retain its provider meaning.

For finalized responses, Event now has:

public readonly long ResponseID;
public readonly ImmutableArray<int> PartIDs;
public partial Event WithDisplay(long responseID, IEnumerable<int> partIDs);

ResponseID is the actual RequestSent sequence. PartIDs follows canonical part order and contains the parser’s IDs, not inferred array indices.
