Metadata must describe every part, use nonnegative distinct IDs, and belong to a response event. Numbering and serialization preserve it. Older logs without this metadata remain valid.

The GUI combines these facts into a string such as:

root:r27:p0

Human messages, results, and historical responses without metadata use a separate event/position namespace. They never collide with a streamed response. No global mutable display counter, identifier registry, or signature rewriting is needed.

The browser uses the ID as the card key. A final replaces that card’s partial text; replay reconstructs the same card, not a duplicate. Repeated final frames are idempotent. The server and browser both reject resurrection of completed content by stale chunks.

7.4 Truthful tool cards

There are three distinct claims:

  1. The model requested a call.
  2. The application admitted execution.
  3. An observation of the job or control returned.

ToolCalled records the first. It is not proof that a handler ran. The dispatcher validates schema arguments after separating observation options, preserves explanation-policy refusals, and records ToolStarted only when admission succeeds. It records that permission before starting effects. If recording fails, the effect must not start.

A started fact does not mean an operating-system command succeeded. A command may fail to start, a file may be missing, or a tool may report an expected error. Those are outcomes, not reasons to falsify the admission history.

The GUI projects admitted execution as tool_dispatched. Refused calls have no such frame. They still get their paired result and visible error status. The browser’s plan card can therefore change from planned to started to finished/error, without portraying a refusal as real execution.

tool_finished means the foreground observation returned. A running-job report can be a legitimate result: waiting stopped, while the independent job remains alive. Preserve the job handle and locator. Do not relabel that observation as process termination.

turn_ended carries the completed answer when the turn completed normally, or an explicit terminal reason otherwise. It is not inferred from a transient return to Idle between tool rounds. The GUI derives the answer from the last recorded response; it does not keep another authoritative answer field.

7.5 The wire protocol

The server sends JSON over /ws. The page and static assets are served from the same loopback host. There is no SSE parser in the browser: vendor streams have already passed through the core Engine.

Important outbound frames are:

Type Purpose
replay recorded display frames, current partials, and Agent state
part_delta Agent ID, part ID, kind, and a chunk string
part_final stable part ID and a typed finalized part
tool_dispatched admitted call ID, name, arguments, and job metadata
tool_finished result identity, corresponding call card, result/error/job
state_changed recorded effective-state transition
agent_state current effective state, including pause
turn_ended completed answer or terminal reason
lifecycle / error interruption or other visible control/error information

An empty chunk is a real empty string, not an omitted chunk property. Part zero is equally real. Streamed tool names and arguments remain distinct at the core boundary; their GUI projection includes readable name fragments.

Inbound commands are small mappings to existing public operations:

{"type":"subscribe"}
{"type":"prompt","text":"Explain the selected function."}
{"type":"hint","text":"Keep the public signature unchanged."}
{"type":"pause"}
{"type":"unpause"}
{"type":"interrupt","mode":"now"}
{"type":"interrupt","mode":"after_tool"}
{"type":"shutdown"}

Connection registration queues replay automatically. subscribe is idempotent; it does not start a new Agent or replay work. The wire spelling is unpause, although the core operation is InputKind.Resume and the button says “Resume.”

The host validates message shape and bounds input size. It rejects foreign WebSocket origins and non-loopback hostnames. The configured listener is loopback-only. This is not permission to expose it on a public interface.

Each connection has a bounded outgoing queue and one network writer. If the queue fills, disconnect that client rather than blocking all clients or the actor. Reconnect uses the same replay path. Dropped progress is not repaired by inventing extra deltas; finalized content is repaired from History.

7.6 Render one kind of card well

Every message is an artifact: a stable card that may stream and then finalize. Use one card map and vary rendering through type and role, not through separate conversation models for chat, tools, and thinking.

  • Human and assistant text use safe Markdown: headings, paragraphs, lists, links, inline code, and fenced code.
  • Thinking and tool details are collapsible. Their complete text remains in the backing card and a scrollable details view.
  • Tool plans show arguments and lifecycle status. Results retain full readable output; terminal escape sequences do not become browser control syntax.
  • Successful edit_file results can show the applied exact replacement from the admitted arguments. Label it accurately: it is not a whole-file diff.
  • Search results keep their path/line output readable. Do not delete content merely to make a card short.

Build DOM nodes and assign textContent; never interpolate provider or tool text into innerHTML. A filename, fetched document, or source fragment may contain hostile markup. Fenced HTML must appear as code, not execute.

Display limits are acceptable only if the rest remains reachable. Collapsing or scrolling is different from truncating the stored value. A speaker button uses the full backing text, not the visible summary or the first screenful.

The layout must work at narrow widths. Controls wrap, code can scroll, and focus remains visible. Geometry checks and browser DOM assertions are useful, but they do not establish every person’s visual comfort or screen-reader experience.

7.7 Speech is part of steering

For someone who cannot comfortably read a busy transcript, speech is a control surface, not ornamental animation.

Speak this artifact is always available when the browser supports speech:

  • human and assistant text: full readable text;
  • thinking: full readable thought text, never signatures or opaque metadata;
  • tool call: full name and formatted arguments;
  • tool result: full readable result, not a collapsed preview.

Clicking the active artifact again stops it. Choosing another artifact cancels the old queue and starts the new request. A global Stop speech button and Escape from an empty input provide explicit escape paths. Speech failures are not allowed to strand the Agent in a permanently queued-speech state.

Automatic narration is a separate opt-in preference. It narrates new assistant text and thinking as complete clauses arrive, then flushes the final remainder. It announces a concise tool-call summary. It does not automatically read human messages, tool results, or reconnect history.

A single queue owns pending utterances and the current utterance. Both onend and onerror settle the current item and advance the queue. A callback from a cancelled utterance is ignored by identity. Queue state counts as busy before the browser actually starts audio; relying on speechSynthesis.speaking alone creates a pause race.

The earlier browser implementation recorded a Chrome visibility workaround: when the page becomes visible, issue an empty zero-volume utterance through speechSynthesis.speak. Preserve it as a local compatibility measure, outside the narration queue. It is not a claim about every browser version, and it must not itself cause a busy-speech pause.

A fake speech boundary can verify selected text, queue transitions, and error cleanup. It cannot prove audible output, voice quality, or human hearing. Those remain separate user exercises.

7.8 Pause scheduling, not the mailbox

Chapter 5 already supplies the right C# mechanism. Pause prevents new model requests and tool dispatch, while the actor continues processing controls and worker completions. Do not add a second GUI-specific gate or block the actor thread while it waits for unpause.

A request already in flight may finish while paused. Its response is recorded; a planned tool remains undispatched until unpause. A hint is accepted promptly. Immediate interrupt still cancels the active turn without killing independent jobs, and remains usable while paused. The two interrupt modes retain Chapter 5’s different boundary semantics.

The browser has a local cause:

input is nonempty OR speech is active OR speech is queued

Only its transitions send controls:

  • false → true: send pause;
  • true → false: send unpause.

The server’s effective state is authoritative. Another tab or application caller can explicitly unpause even while this tab is still typing. Unchanged typing must not immediately reassert pause on every key or state frame. Only a later local cause transition sends another request.

This is why the model is not a distributed set of tab-owned veto tokens. The human needs a dependable explicit escape, not a hidden AND of every browser’s local conditions.

Enter submits a prompt; Shift+Enter inserts a newline. Ctrl+Enter or Alt+H sends a hint. Input clearing updates the local pause cause. Buttons provide the same operations without requiring keyboard shortcuts.

7.9 Build and inspect locally

Build the optional project separately from the core:

dotnet build Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj

Run it from an owned workspace, selecting a provider and model explicitly:

dotnet run --project /path/to/Examples/Gui -- \
  --port 8097 --workspace /path/to/owned-work \
  --vendor anthropic --model SELECTED-MODEL --base-url PROVIDER-URL \
  --event-log event.log

Credentials come from the existing LLM_API_KEY environment contract, not from page content or command-line arguments. LLM_VENDOR, LLM_MODEL, and LLM_BASE_URL provide defaults for their flags. --no-stream disables streaming; unknown stream capability still follows Chapter 6’s plain fallback. --gui-dir selects static assets when not using the copied build output.

Keep four kinds of evidence distinct:

Log Contents
event.log / --event-log / CH02_LOG canonical recorded facts
api.log / CH06_API_LOG existing sanitized request/payload trace
gui.log / CH07_GUI_LOG UTC timestamp, direction, and GUI JSON frame
debug.log ordinary application diagnostics

GUI tracing writes > for received and < for sent frames. API and GUI traces redact the configured credential. They are still private working artifacts: conversation and tool output can contain other sensitive information. Do not publish them merely because one key was redacted.

Use an owned port, workspace, browser profile, and fake provider while developing. Do not borrow another running Agent or change someone’s connected browser. Closing the browser leaves work running. Stopping the host explicitly tears down connections, stops observation, and lets the composition root destroy the Agent graph. The existing cooperative-callback shutdown limitation still applies.

7.10 Verification and taking it for a spin

Test real components with small external fakes. Important cases include:

  1. Round-trip finalized display IDs, including zero and noncontiguous IDs; reject malformed metadata and retain historical-log compatibility.
  2. Read snapshots during concurrent appends and verify one coherent frontier.
  3. Refuse malformed and policy-disallowed tool calls without a started fact; admit a valid tool and inspect its real effect and recorded result.
  4. Gate a provider after a meaningful delta. Observe it in the browser before releasing completion, then reconnect during the partial response and after finalization. IDs must remain stable and cards must not duplicate.
  5. Pause an active turn before a tool plan completes. Verify that no tool effect occurs until unpause, while hints and interrupts still work.
  6. Verify a fresh prompt works after interruption. Reject a foreign WebSocket origin without granting it actor input capability.
  7. Inspect actual narrow-layout controls and safe rendering of hostile-looking code. Exercise full-content speaker buttons through a fake speech boundary.
  8. Exercise queued speech, interrupted-utterance cleanup, automatic typing pause, cross-tab explicit unpause, and silent visibility wakeup.

The existing executable grader can test the optional server without compiling Go consumers:

grade-edition2 -ch 7 -executable-only \
  -gui /absolute/path/to/wwwroot -gui-model SELECTED-STREAM-MODEL \
  /absolute/path/to/gui-launcher

This route covers 80 points: wire behavior, reconnect replay, GUI trace, and pause semantics. It excludes inherited Chapter 6 scoring and Go topology checks. The full historical Go route remains available and unchanged in scope. Neither route establishes accessible speech quality or real provider acceptance.

For a human exercise, use a bounded task in the owned workspace. Watch a response stream, inspect thinking and tool details, send a hint, pause and unpause, and interrupt while paused. Reconnect while work continues. Listen to individual full artifacts and try automatic narration if authorized. Keep the actual logs and describe failures honestly.

The C# endpoint’s offline protocol, browser, and fake-speech evidence is recorded in docs/edition-3-csharp-progress.md. Paid-provider work and audible-user verification must remain explicitly incomplete when they have not been done. A green grade is evidence for its checks, not a replacement for these boundaries or for an inspection of the ownership and call paths.

Chapter 8: Build Your Dream GUI

TL;DR

Make the optional GUI comfortable to use without giving it a second Agent loop. The server owns presentation preferences; the Agent owns its next-turn tool budget. A browser sends a patch, the server validates and saves a complete snapshot, and only then does it publish that snapshot to every connected client. An active turn keeps the budget it captured when it began.

The deliverable is a working settings panel: theme, narration, speech rate, font size, speech-related pausing, and tool batches per turn. Preferences survive browser reload and server restart. A failed save changes neither live behavior nor the visible acknowledged settings. This is a C#/.NET 10 extension of the Chapter 7 endpoint, not another runtime or a Go-package translation exercise.

In plain language

A setting is a small promise. If the page says the font is 24 pixels or the next turn allows three tool batches, the running application should agree. If a write fails, the page must not pretend the preference was saved.

There are three different lifetimes:

  1. The browser displays the last server-acknowledged snapshot. Its controls propose changes; local storage is not a second source of truth.
  2. The GUI server loads and saves presentation preferences and shares them with all clients. It reaches the actual Agent to read or change its budget.
  3. The Agent turn captures its effective budget once. A later settings change applies to the next turn, not halfway through this one.

Theme and font changes affect existing transcript content immediately. Speech rate changes affect the next utterance constructed, not audio already speaking. Turning off “Pause Agent while speaking” releases the speech-related pause cause without cancelling speech. Typing is still an independent reason to pause.

These distinctions are small enough to explain and important enough to test.

8.1 Keep the existing ownership model

Continue from solutions/edition-3/ch07; advance main and preserve earlier endpoints. Core remains independent of ASP.NET, browser APIs, settings paths, and user-interface types. The optional Examples/Gui assembly references core.

Core Common/Actor.cs declares the runtime policy and its public operations:

// Agent owns the next-turn policy. The actor alone uses capturedToolLimit.
private int nextTurnToolLimit;
private int capturedToolLimit;
public partial int MaxToolRounds();
public partial void SetMaxToolRounds(int value);

The matching implementations are in Agent/Agent.cs; scheduling stays in Agent/Actor.cs. The getter returns the configured runtime value, including zero. The setter accepts zero or a positive integer and rejects a negative integer without changing anything. Synchronize reads and writes with the Agent’s ingress lock. Do not add a service wrapper or have the GUI inspect actor-private state.

Chapter 5’s immutable constructor configuration seeds this live policy; it is not updated as a competing settings object. Its existing library-only negative limit continues to mean unlimited. The new runtime setter and GUI accept only nonnegative values. This distinction preserves the older constructor contract without making negative numbers a new public preference.

At turn start, the actor reads the current policy and resolves zero to the default 200 batches. Keep that captured value until the turn ends. A queued turn captures when it actually starts, not when the prompt first arrives. A hint that continues an active turn does not create a new budget.

A batch is one model response containing tool calls, regardless of how many calls are in it. After the last admitted batch, let the model consume its results. Add a short request-only instruction to answer without more tools. Extend Engine.Render(Context context, string requestInstruction = "") for this purpose; do not append the instruction to History or modify opaque/signed replay parts. If the model still requests another batch, pair its calls with refused results before any effects. The limit is a scheduling boundary, not merely advice.

8.2 Preferences are values, not another owner graph

Examples/Gui/Common/Settings.cs declares a value-like Preferences record and partial parse/load/save operations. It contains presentation facts only:

public sealed record Preferences(
    string Theme = "system",
    bool TtsEnabled = false,
    double TtsSpeed = 1,
    int FontSize = 18,
    bool PauseWhileSpeaking = true);

A record is appropriate because a preference snapshot is a value. It needs no parent links or logical destruction. The Agent budget deliberately is not a field in this record: read it from the Agent when making a wire or disk snapshot. A candidate parsed from JSON may temporarily include a budget value while being validated and saved; that is not another authoritative live store.

The host’s existing composition scope owns its current preferences, settings path, sockets, and transport synchronization. Do not invent a global settings registry, browser-owned Agent state, or a second scheduler.

One validation policy for disk and wire

Use these concrete rules in this endpoint:

Field Default Accepted value
theme "system" system, light, or dark
tts_enabled false JSON Boolean
tts_speed 1.0 finite number, clamped to 0.25–4.0
font_size 18 32-bit integer, clamped to 12–32 pixels
pause_while_speaking true JSON Boolean
max_tool_rounds 0 nonnegative 32-bit integer; zero means auto/200

Wrong types, invalid enum values, negative budgets, out-of-range integer representations, and unknown fields leave their prior values unchanged. A patch must be an object. On load, merge valid fields into defaults using the same validation. Missing, unreadable, or malformed files fall back to defaults without rewriting or deleting the original file. Do not coerce "true", 1, and true into interchangeable values.

This deliberately changes Edition 2’s recovery policy: malformed saved JSON used to stop startup with an error. Here preferences can fail without locking the human out of the GUI. Leaving the file untouched on load gives you a chance to inspect or recover it; this is not a backup system, and a later successful settings edit can replace that file. A failed save still leaves the accepted in-memory values unchanged, as the next section requires.

Preserve zero on disk, in snapshots, and in the input control. Do not replace it with 200 in the user-facing state. Only the actor’s captured effective limit normalizes zero.

8.3 Save before publication

The default path is $HOME/.ensemble/settings.json; --settings PATH supplies an explicit path, useful for owned local exercises. These are application preferences, not conversation events. Do not put credentials in this file.

For a patch:

  1. Under the host’s short settings/connection lock, merge it with current values and the Agent’s current policy.
  2. Serialize the complete candidate to a unique temporary file in the destination directory. Create the parent directory when necessary.
  3. Replace the destination with that completed file.
  4. Only after replacement succeeds, update the Agent policy and presentation preferences, then queue the same full snapshot to every connected client.

The lock serializes concurrent patches and their publication order. Network sends remain outside it; the existing per-connection bounded queues carry frames. This small file write is ordinary blocking I/O, not an invitation to build a persistence service. Same-directory replacement prevents exposing partial JSON; it does not promise power-loss durability, a backup archive, or recovery from arbitrary filesystem damage.

If writing or replacing fails, send an error to the requester. Do not change live values, broadcast success, or overwrite the previous good file with a partial candidate. Clean up the owned temporary file. A later valid request may try again; do not silently change the persistence path.

8.4 WebSocket contract

Keep the existing /ws protocol and add:

{"type":"get_settings"}
{"type":"update_settings","settings":{"theme":"dark","tts_speed":1.5}}

A newly connected client receives a full snapshot automatically. Explicit get_settings returns the same shape:

{
  "type":"current_settings",
  "settings":{
    "theme":"system",
    "tts_enabled":false,
    "tts_speed":1,
    "font_size":18,
    "pause_while_speaking":true,
    "max_tool_rounds":0
  }
}

After successful persistence, all connected clients, including the requester, receive settings_updated with the complete merged settings object. Do not broadcast only the patch. New connections and reconnects obtain current values from the server, not from another tab. Ignore unknown fields for compatibility. The older Go grader used the label settings_changed; that historical label is not a requirement to add a second product message.

8.5 Build a useful settings panel

The second edition built three panes, drag bars and a sidebar agent tree. This C# endpoint keeps one transcript and adds settings to the Chapter 7 page. There are no drag bars or agent-tree controls in this endpoint. Start with this smaller page, then judge whether it is comfortable enough for your work.

Open Examples/Gui/wwwroot/index.html, style.css and app.js in the preserved solutions/edition-3/ch08 endpoint. They divide the work without a UI framework:

  • The header holds connection and Agent state, Pause/Resume/Interrupt buttons, and a native details element for Settings. Its summary opens the controls without a custom panel widget.
  • The main element, #transcript, holds conversation cards. The notice below it reports connection and settings errors; it has role="status" so the message is not merely a color change.
  • The #compose form holds the labelled textarea and Send message/Send hint buttons. Keep these separate actions visible even though keyboard shortcuts also exist.

The layout is ordinary document flow. The body is centered with a maximum width of 70rem; the transcript grows with its cards, and the composer follows it. The .controls rows use wrapping flex layout, so buttons can move onto another row instead of widening the page. Cards use overflow-wrap: anywhere, and code blocks use white-space: pre-wrap, keeping long arguments and code lines from forcing horizontal page scrolling. At widths below 420 pixels, the page padding shrinks and buttons can grow to fill a row. Check those choices with real long output, not just an empty page.

Theming changes shared CSS variables rather than recoloring each card. The root provides the light palette; data-theme="dark" selects the dark one. A prefers-color-scheme media query supplies the system palette only when neither explicit light nor dark is selected. Font size is another root variable, --font-size, used by the page font and inherited by inputs. Existing content therefore changes along with the controls.

Follow one edit through the page. Selecting Dark sends the sparse patch {"theme":"dark"} through patchSettings. The control can show the proposed choice while “Saving settings…” is displayed, but the acknowledged settings remain authoritative. When settings_updated arrives, applySettings updates the root theme attribute, font variable and every settings control. Another tab uses the same path. An error restores the acknowledged values and displays the failure; it does not pretend the proposed change was saved. This is why the page needs both a control value and the last accepted settings snapshot.

Put the panel in the existing optional GUI. Provide clearly labeled controls for every table entry. Numeric input steps are integral for font and batch count; label zero as auto/default. Keep controls usable on a narrow screen and at the largest supported font. Group secondary preferences in a collapsible panel so they do not dominate the transcript.

Use CSS variables for theme colors and font size. Apply them to the root so existing messages, input, controls, and code blocks update together. Explicit light/dark settings override the operating system. System mode follows prefers-color-scheme, including changes while the page is open. Syntax colors, links, focus indicators, and notices must remain readable in both themes.

The browser retains only its last acknowledged settings snapshot. A control sends a patch and may retain its proposed edit while saving. Actual presentation and speech policy change only when the server acknowledges a snapshot. If the connection is unavailable, show a notice rather than pretending to save. A save error restores the acknowledged control values. Remove any old local-storage copy of these preferences.

Speech and pause are related, not identical

Keep Chapter 7’s one active utterance and FIFO pending text. When constructing an utterance, read the current acknowledged speech rate. Do not recreate or cancel the utterance already speaking just because its rate setting changed. Automatic narration is opt-in; speaker buttons still read selected content.

Both queued and active speech count as busy. The local pause cause is:

typing OR (pause_while_speaking AND speech_busy)

Send pause/unpause only when that cause changes. Turning speech pausing off immediately removes that cause, even with queued audio, but must not override a remaining typing cause. Turning it on while audio is queued or speaking pauses immediately. Preserve symmetric onend/onerror cleanup, cancellation identity checks, cross-tab explicit unpause, and the separate silent visibility wakeup. Speech settings must not introduce another owner of Agent lifecycle.

8.6 Test the behavior, not a screenshot of a slider

Use real components and working external-boundary fakes. The following evidence answers different questions; none substitutes for the others.

Core budget test

Hold a real loopback HTTP response after the turn has begun. Change the runtime policy while it is held. Release it and count actual tool effects: the current turn must keep its old limit and the next turn must use the new one. Check the request-only stop-tools instruction, paired refusals, negative setter rejection, zero preservation, and unchanged History after rendering. Check the instruction projection for all three provider dialects without contacting those providers.

Protocol and persistence test

Use two real WebSocket connections to the GUI server. Test full snapshots, partial merges, invalid fields, clamps, explicit zero, concurrent patches, new-client state, and actual server restart. Load malformed JSON and a file with invalid fields. Force a write failure using an owned temporary path; verify the error, unchanged live snapshots, no success broadcast, and preserved prior file. Never damage a real user’s configuration to create this fixture.

Browser exercise

Use an isolated browser profile, not another user’s connected browser. Operate the real visible controls and verify both tabs update. Check system theme changes, existing transcript font, narrow-screen geometry, and reload from server state. At a fake speech boundary, inspect each constructed utterance’s rate, queue two items, change rate between them, and toggle pause while the queue is busy. Test error cleanup as well as normal completion. Such a fake establishes wiring and selection—not audible quality, correct pronunciation, or human accessibility.

Executable grading

The existing Go grader can launch the compiled C# GUI; its language does not make HTTP/WebSocket tests Go-only. Use the Chapter 8 -executable-only route with -gui pointing to the static asset directory and a GUI executable wrapper as the positional target. It reuses four settings checks totaling 80 points: round trip (25), initial snapshot (20), broadcast (20), and persistence (15). Inherited Go topology/Chapter 7 scoring is excluded, not silently awarded. Budget execution, validation/rollback, and browser checks remain separate proof. Require parsed passed:true and process exit zero before reporting a pass.

8.7 Use it and report honestly

With authorized provider access, launch the GUI on an owned loopback port and ask the Agent to perform a small useful programming task. Adjust theme, speech, font, and the next-turn budget while it works. Inspect the resulting code and run its tests. Use the existing four private logs to diagnose behavior; do not publish credentials or raw conversation data.

Without provider authority, exercise the real application against a local fake and leave the provider-dependent task explicitly incomplete. Fake HTTP, WebSockets, and speech do not prove remote model compatibility or human hearing. Do not restart or deploy a shared application merely to demonstrate this chapter.

Preserve a source-only endpoint, explain the ownership and captured-budget choices, record corrections and evidence limitations in the progress record, and continue to Chapter 9. The goal is a GUI whose small promises are dependable—not an elaborate settings framework.

Chapter 9 — Skills

TL;DR

A skill is a small manual that grants a named set of tools. Each Agent owns a concrete Skills manager. The manager validates a dependency closure, renders its manuals, and records the entire activation in History before making it visible. Request rendering and tool admission read the same recorded grants. A tool that is not granted cannot execute, even if the model guesses its name.

The primary manual is rendered once at creation. Later manuals enter provider instruction context, not ordinary tool-result prose. Loading never rewrites the primary. Unloading in this chapter records a pending marker: instructions and tools remain usable until a later chapter implements compaction-time removal.

The runnable endpoint is solutions/edition-3/ch09. Its library, CLI, optional GUI, and separate public-API example use C# 14/.NET 10 without downloaded packages.

9.1 In plain language

A constitution and a shelf of manuals

The primary skill is the Agent’s constitution. It says how to work and lists which additional manuals the Agent may request. A loaded manual supplies both instructions and the tools needed to follow them. Dependencies are supporting manuals loaded automatically before the requested manual.

There are two different questions:

  1. Can this tool run? Its name must be granted by an active skill.
  2. Has the model been told how to use it? The corresponding rendered manual must be present in the request’s instruction context.

Satisfying only one question is not enough. A prompt saying “you may write files” does not enable a handler. Adding a handler does not teach the model the manual. The recorded activation ties both facts together.

Load once, record what was taught

Suppose a manual contains $CUSTOM_VAR. The manager substitutes the current registered value when loading that manual, then keeps the resulting text. A later variable update does not rewrite what the Agent was already taught. The primary receives the same treatment at creation.

History stores these rendered snapshots. Replay therefore does not depend on whether a Markdown file was subsequently edited, moved, or deleted. The files are the catalog; History records this Agent’s actual activations.

Pending does not mean gone

Immediate revocation would leave a conversation describing tools that suddenly cannot run. This chapter does not solve compaction. unload_skill therefore marks a non-primary skill pending removal and says so honestly. The manual and its tools remain active. Test this with a tool granted by the loaded skill, not one that was already granted by the primary.

9.2 Ownership and the authoritative facts

Keep the existing hub-and-spoke organization:

  • Common/Skills.cs declares Skills, immutable skill values, parent links, fields, and callable partial members.
  • Skills/Parser.cs implements the documented front-matter subset and value construction. Skills/Skills.cs implements catalog resolution, variable rendering, activation, provenance, and pending removal.
  • Agent/Skills.cs implements complete two-way attachment and removal. The manager reaches History and the handler catalog through its actual Agent parent, not copied service references.
  • History owns activation and pending-removal events. Engine projects their immutable snapshots into provider requests. Jobs performs admission through the Agent before starting effects.
  • CLI and GUI composition roots choose the skill directory, primary name, and environment-derived variables. The core library never reads the environment.

The relevant public vocabulary includes:

// Value-like configuration: it does not own an Agent or need holder back-links.
public sealed record SkillSpec(
    string Directory,
    string Primary,
    IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>? Variables = null);

// Value-like provenance: the earliest activation granting a tool.
public readonly record struct ToolSource(string Skill, long Sequence);

SkillPart is also value-like. It contains a skill’s name, rendered body, granted tool names, and whether it is primary. Its immutable arrays are not another mutable capability database. There is no parallel active-tool set: active manuals and grants are derived from the skill parts in History’s Context. Pending markers remain events; they do not remove those parts.

The manager retains only its catalog definitions, registered variables, and lifecycle state. The Agent’s ordinary Tools() collection remains the handler catalog. In a skill-configured Agent, registration alone is not permission to run. In a library Agent without skills, the earlier explicit tool-installation behavior remains available.

Complete relationship operations

new Skills(agent, specification) validates its catalog, attaches through agent.AddSkills, installs the two control definitions, and activates the primary closure. A failed activation removes the added controls and detaches the manager. No half-created manager is returned.

RemoveSkills validates membership before changing either end and clears both links before returning. Skills.Destroy is idempotent and removes that link; it does not destroy its parent. Agent destruction first drains jobs while History is available, then destroys its manager, tools, Engine, and History through the existing protected cleanup path. A retained loader called without a manager returns an explicit refusal, not a null-reference fault.

9.3 The skill file format

A host supplies one explicit directory. The manager reads SKILL.md files recursively in sorted path order and rejects duplicate names. There is no implicit home-directory fallback or precedence between competing roots.

---
name: ensemble
description: The default careful coding assistant.
type: primary
tools: read_file list_directory search_files
loadable-skills: code-tools
---
Explain what you will do and why before using tools.
Inspect actual files and report failures honestly.

Enabled tools:
$TOOLS

Additional manuals:
$SKILLS

The parser trims front-matter lines, but deliberately does not implement general YAML nesting. The supported fields are:

Field Meaning
name Required unique identifier: letters, digits, _, or -.
description Optional plain single-line text for discovery.
type Required primary, loadable, or dependency.
tools Tool names granted by this manual.
depends Manuals activated before this one.
loadable-skills Loadable manuals this manual offers explicitly.

The three name-list fields accept either whitespace-separated names or a YAML-style dash list:

tools:
  - write_file
  - edit_file
  - run_command

This is a small documented subset, not a general YAML implementation. Unknown fields, duplicate fields, malformed identifiers, and missing boundaries are errors. Quoted scalars, flow arrays, and multiline YAML values are not part of the contract. The first closing --- ends front matter; later separators remain literal body text. Empty lines and comment lines in front matter are ignored.

Catalog syntax is checked at construction. Activation then validates the chosen closure: missing dependencies, cycles, wrong primary placement, invalid offered names/types, or unknown handlers refuse the operation. A dependency is not independently discoverable unless an active manual explicitly offers it as a loadable skill; dependency-typed entries cannot be offered as loadable entries. A loadable manual may offer further manuals, making discovery progressive.

Both load_skill and unload_skill are always enabled controls for a configured primary, even if it offers no additional manuals. They are not ordinary jobs.

9.4 Variables and transactional activation

Built-in substitutions are:

Variable Snapshot value
$TOOLS Sorted enabled tool names after the proposed activation.
$SKILLS Currently offered, not-yet-active skill names and descriptions.
$CUSTOM_VAR, or another registered uppercase name Host-supplied value at activation.

Unknown variables remain visible. Substitution makes one pass: text supplied as a variable value is not recursively interpreted. Variable names must match [A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*; hosts cannot replace the built-ins TOOLS and SKILLS.

RegisterVariable updates the manager’s explicit variable map under its lock. It does not mutate existing skill bodies. This is configuration for the next activation, not a new conversation event.

A successful load performs these steps on the Agent’s actor:

  1. Require that an active skill currently offers the requested name. An already active name is an idempotent success, including while pending unload.
  2. Resolve dependencies first, checking the entire closure before publication.
  3. Calculate the prospective active names, grants, and discoverable manuals.
  4. Render all new bodies against that prospective snapshot.
  5. Append one SkillLoaded event containing all new SkillPart values.
  6. Return a concise successful tool result naming the loaded manuals.

History’s append is durable before publication. A validation failure grants nothing. A persistence failure propagates as a real failure through the actor; it is not converted to a successful load or a harmless validation message.

The initial event contains the primary and its dependencies. Primary grants also include the two controls. Later events contain only newly activated manuals. Source(tool) walks these entries in activation order and reports the earliest granting skill and sequence. A tool shared by two manuals has one effective permission, not two mutable copies.

unload_skill refuses the primary, marks another active skill pending once, and returns text explaining that its instructions and tools remain active. This chapter adds no replacement primary, file watcher, reload command, or compaction framework.

9.5 Instructions, dialogue, and dispatch

Loading a file is not enough. A successful activation must reach the outgoing request in the correct instruction location:

Adapter Instruction location
Anthropic Top-level system.
OpenAI Chat Completions The initial system message.
Gemini systemInstruction.parts.

The primary body is emitted first, followed by the other rendered bodies. Each occurs once. Skill entries are excluded from ordinary dialogue projection, so a loaded body does not also appear as tool-result text. Ordinary human, assistant, and tool exchanges retain their existing roles and correlation IDs. Signed or opaque provider content is not rewritten to carry instructions.

The primary body stays fixed; the complete instruction block grows as manuals are activated. Do not assert that the entire block remains byte-identical after loading. The loader’s result reports success or failure; it is not the only carrier of the instructions. Clearing ordinary tool-result text must not silently remove a manual or revoke a grant.

The actor renders from a captured immutable Context before starting HTTP. Declarations use that snapshot’s grants rather than consulting a second live enabled set halfway through rendering. Tool dispatch checks the recorded active grants before reservation or effects. A guessed disabled tool call receives a paired error with its real call ID and cannot create a job or file.

The skill controls run synchronously at the actor’s admission point. They still consume one-shot observation options, validate arguments, and record call/result facts, but allocate no independent job. The next model request sees the new manual and permissions. All other scheduling, hint, interrupt, and reliable reply behavior remains owned by the existing actor.

Optional Anthropic deferred declarations

Portable mode sends full declarations for enabled tools. That is the default. For a selected Anthropic model known to support tool search, a host may explicitly set Configuration(..., deferredTools: true). The executable equivalent is EN_DEFERRED_TOOLS=1; other vendors refuse this option. The Boolean is the host’s capability assertion, not a model-name guess or proof of provider support.

In this mode:

  • Initial tools, including the loader, remain eager.
  • Tools reachable through the primary’s catalog but granted only later are sent with defer_loading: true. A catalog declaration does not grant dispatch.
  • A successful load records newly granted tool names as result metadata.
  • Anthropic projects those names into the correctly paired loader result:
{
  "type": "tool_result",
  "tool_use_id": "load-1",
  "content": [
    { "type": "tool_reference", "tool_name": "write_file" }
  ]
}

The declarations stay deferred after activation; references reveal their schemas to the model. Other adapters and ordinary mode retain textual load results. Result metadata survives event serialization, numbering, replay, and ordinary result redaction. It is not reconstructed by searching response text.

Anthropic requires the deferred schemas in every request. Deferral saves model context, not outbound wire bytes. The official tool-search documentation describes this client-side custom-search path and its reference format. The local tests verify our projection against that contract, not a real provider exchange. With no live manager/catalog during offline rendering, use the portable enabled declarations; do not invent a deferred catalog from missing files.

9.6 Constructing and running the C# applications

A library host supplies values directly:

var specification = new SkillSpec(
    "/absolute/path/to/owned/skills",
    "ensemble",
    new Dictionary<string, string> { ["CUSTOM_VAR"] = "example" });

var configuration = new Configuration(
    Vendor.Anthropic,
    "selected-model",
    "https://api.anthropic.com",
    apiKey);

var agent = new Agent(app, configuration, skillSpec: specification);

The constructor installs the ordinary handler catalog before activating skills. A host with custom handlers can instead construct an Agent, register its tools, and then construct Skills before accepting input. If logging is required, open the log before constructing the manager: its initial activation is a real event and must be recorded too. The CLI and GUI use that order.

For example, from a chapter endpoint:

dotnet build Cli/Ch04.csproj
dotnet build Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj
dotnet run --project Examples/Skills/Skills.csproj -- /new/owned/exercise-directory

The separate Examples/Skills assembly exercises public construction, disabled writes, load-time variables, provenance, pending removal, and a real write. It uses no reflection, internal API grant, or model provider. It leaves its output file for inspection and explicitly destroys the Agent graph.

The applications copy the shipped manuals from Skills/*/SKILL.md beside their executables. They default to that output skills directory and primary ensemble. The primary permits read/inspect tools and offers code-tools for editing and job control. full is an explicit full-capability primary for trusted local exercises, not a reason to grant all tools by default.

Both composition roots accept:

Setting Environment Explicit flag
Skill root EN_SKILLS_DIR --skills-dir PATH
Primary name EN_PRIMARY_SKILL --primary-skill NAME
Example variable EN_CUSTOM_VAR None; register other variables in a library host.
Deferred Anthropic mode EN_DEFERRED_TOOLS=1 None.

Flags override environment values. Existing LLM_* connection settings and streaming options remain unchanged. Credentials never belong in a skill file, variable value intended for model instructions, or committed request capture.

9.7 Exercises and evidence

Use an owned scratch directory and a working local provider fake first. Give a small primary read_file and an offered writer skill write_file, with a list_directory dependency. Set $CUSTOM_VAR to a harmless marker. Then:

  1. Request a write before loading. Check both the paired error and absence of the file; merely hiding a declaration is not enforcement.
  2. Load the writer. Inspect the next actual request for the primary’s unchanged body, the newly rendered manuals in instruction context, and enabled tools.
  3. Write a file, mark the writer pending, then write a second file with the dynamically granted writer. Verify bytes, not just the final answer.
  4. Read the result and let the CLI reach normal EOF. Inspect its exit and usage.
  5. Render the log offline with the original skill directory unavailable. Loaded instruction snapshots and control declarations must survive without HTTP.
  6. Repeat through the GUI. Expand the real tool-result cards, check the pending explanation, reload the page, and verify stable replay without duplicates.

Also test cycles, missing dependencies, unknown handlers, malformed metadata, idempotent loading, primary unload refusal, variable snapshot timing, two-Agent isolation, and both directions of manager removal. A held-turn or fake-provider test must use the real Agent and its actor, not invoke private handlers and call that an integration test.

The Chapter 9 executable-only grader reuses the existing eight skill checks for 85 points. It excludes the inherited Chapter 8/Go topology campaign; it is not a full Go grade. Component tests, the separate C# consumer, and actual CLI/browser exercises cover different boundaries and must be reported separately.

Real-provider runs require their own authorization and evidence. Historical Go sessions and demonstrations do not verify this C# implementation, deferred-tool support on an account, audible speech, or human accessibility. Keep blocked integration work explicitly incomplete rather than borrowing an earlier pass.

The next chapter gives recorded conversations a life beyond a single process. This chapter provides the prerequisite: the actual manuals and grants are facts in History, not an accidental consequence of whichever files happen to exist when replay begins.

Chapter 10 — Persistence and Replay

TL;DR

Give an Agent a durable conversation without giving yesterday’s configuration authority over today’s runtime. Save one reduced Context, its as_of event sequence, a credential-free description of effective configuration, and an optional diagnostic log. Validate a complete candidate before replacing live state or a save file. On restart, load the snapshot, fold only the newer tail, and number new events above the recovered boundary.

The C# endpoint is solutions/edition-3/ch10. It uses the existing Agent → History relationship. There is no second transcript, persistence service bag, or replacement actor loop.

10.1 In plain language

Think of a snapshot as a notebook whose contents have already incorporated events through page number N. Keeping copies of those old events beside the notebook is useful for diagnosis, but reading them into the notebook again would duplicate the conversation.

An event newer than N is different: it has not yet been incorporated and must be applied once. If the snapshot is absent, start with an empty notebook and replay the complete event log instead. If the log is absent, the snapshot must still stand on its own.

The notebook records what happened. It does not choose which provider, credentials, model, skills, or tools you are allowed to use now. Those come from the current application’s explicit runtime configuration.

A backup is another candidate, not permission to ignore validation. A corrupt primary must never displace a known-good backup. If neither candidate is usable, stop without rewriting either one.

10.2 Ownership and the save contract

Common declares the shared vocabulary; functional modules provide the bodies:

  • Common/Persistence.cs declares immutable PersistenceOptions and SaveDocument, plus the operations on Agent, History, Engine, and JsonCodec.
  • History/Persistence.cs owns capture, replay, candidate selection, replacement, and diagnostic retention.
  • Serialization/Persistence.cs owns the neutral JSON format and validation.
  • Engine/Persistence.cs projects effective configuration without credentials or endpoints.
  • Agent/Persistence.cs performs startup loading and arms automatic saving. The existing actor’s joined shutdown performs the save.
  • CLI and GUI composition roots choose paths and policies. Core code does not read environment variables or standard input.

PersistenceOptions is value-like. It contains paths and a retention count, not a service, owner, or mutable conversation. It needs no parent back-pointer.

A save has exactly these four top-level fields:

{
  "context": {},
  "as_of": 42,
  "config": {},
  "log": []
}

The empty objects above are schematic, not valid complete Context or configuration values.

context contains dialogue entries, the current ephemera slot, reducer phase, and measured usage. Each entry carries its sequence, actor, parts, and any finalized display identities. Text, tool calls, tool results, exact JSON numbers, blob locators, opaque provenance, signatures, redaction stubs, and skill instruction values use the existing neutral part codec. Saving does not resolve media files, fetch URIs, or convert the conversation into provider wire JSON.

as_of is the event boundary already incorporated into Context. History owns this fact explicitly. It cannot infer it from the last retained diagnostic event: a valid snapshot-only save has no such event.

config documents the effective vendor, model, system prompt, and normalized tool declarations. Engine derives it through the existing request projection, using only the captured skill instruction entries. Keys, authorization headers, provider endpoints, and unrelated runtime settings are not configuration fields in the save. Conversation text is still private user data; excluding credentials from configuration does not make a session file public.

log contains canonical events retained for diagnosis and, when needed, newer tail replay. It is not a second mutable conversation authority.

10.3 Capture and replay

History.Snapshot() obtains Events, Context, and Sequence under the same short lock. All three describe one committed instant. Readers never copy an unsynchronized list, and a save does not hold that lock across filesystem I/O.

The loader validates a candidate into local values before publishing anything:

  1. Decode the document and required fields.
  2. Validate Context entries, usage, phases, display identities, and event shapes.
  3. Require strictly increasing positive event sequences.
  4. If Context exists, start with it and skip events at or below as_of.
  5. Fold each newer event in sequence. A gap in the required tail is an error, not an invitation to manufacture missing state.
  6. If Context is null, fold the complete log from empty Context instead. The complete log must start at event 1.
  7. Set the new numbering boundary to the larger of the saved as_of and the replayed sequence.
  8. Publish the recovered Context, retained events, and sequence together.

A failed load leaves the prior live state and file bytes unchanged. Loading is a startup operation, before opening an output event log or accepting actor work. Agent.StartPersistence enforces that startup boundary. The lower-level History operations are also available for explicit import/testing by a caller that owns the startup sequence.

There are three useful equivalent representations:

Representation Context Log
Snapshot plus diagnostics Complete through N May include events ≤ N
Snapshot plus tail Complete through N Includes required events > N
Log-only null Complete from event 1

A snapshot-only save is the first row with an empty log. It must restore both conversation and future numbering correctly.

10.4 Safe replacement and recovery

History serializes save operations with a save lock distinct from its short state lock. An append can continue while a captured candidate is being written. A later append is not part of that candidate and must not be removed during its diagnostic trimming.

Saving follows this order:

  1. Normalize and validate the save/archive paths. The archive cannot be the primary or its .bak file.
  2. Capture one coherent snapshot and derive its credential-free configuration.
  3. Build the selected diagnostic suffix and validate the serialized candidate by decoding and replaying it.
  4. If enabled, write the dialogue archive from that captured Context.
  5. Read and validate the previous primary before rotating it into save.json.bak. Never promote corrupt primary bytes over a good backup.
  6. Write the new primary through a same-directory temporary file, flush its contents, and replace the destination.
  7. Only after successful publication, trim the captured diagnostic prefix in live History. Preserve every event appended after the capture.

Temporary files are cleaned up on failure. Same-directory replacement avoids publishing a partially written JSON document. This is not a claim that every filesystem or power failure preserves all metadata; the chapter does not implement a write-ahead journal or directory-fsync recovery protocol.

Startup tries the primary and backup independently. Missing files allow a new session only when neither candidate exists. Parse, replay, access, or shape failures are reported safely; corrupt file contents are not copied into diagnostics. Successful backup recovery reports its saved sequence. It does not claim to recover events that were never durably saved.

If both candidates fail, construction/startup is refused and saving is not armed. Do not “repair” an unreadable save by silently overwriting it with an empty conversation.

10.5 Reapply the current runtime

Saved configuration is documentary. The application still supplies the current Configuration, skill catalog, primary skill, variable values, and tool handlers.

Agent.StartPersistence captures the freshly constructed runtime’s skill instruction values before loading. After a successful restore, it records RuntimeConfigured:

  • remove saved skill instruction/grant entries;
  • append the current runtime’s initial skill values;
  • reset the reducer phase to Idle;
  • preserve ordinary historical system entries and all other reduced conversation.

Skill source and pending-unload queries use the reduced skill entries. A pending flag is part of the immutable skill value, so trimming diagnostic events cannot erase it during the current session. Runtime reconfiguration replaces those old values rather than reviving their flags. Yesterday’s dynamically loaded skill does not become today’s permission merely because its tool result remains in the conversation. The new primary is rendered from today’s inputs, then remains frozen for this Agent as Chapter 9 requires.

RuntimeConfigured is a durable explanation, not an out-of-band mutation. Log-only replay reaches the same runtime state. The GUI also treats it as a new live-session boundary, clearing old pause/shutdown projection flags without deleting the transcript.

Hints retain their recorded actor. In particular, a human hint is not a skill instruction or a system message. Anthropic’s broad user projection can conceal a role error that OpenAI exposes, so cross-vendor restoration tests must check actual roles, not only whole-request text.

10.6 Retention and the optional archive

RetainLog has three meanings:

  • negative: retain all available diagnostic events;
  • zero: retain none;
  • positive N: retain the newest N diagnostic events.

A newly opened diagnostic event log writes the retained/bootstrap prefix, not a fabricated complete event history. After retention, use the save document—not a standalone truncated event log—to recover the full conversation.

This controls diagnostics, not conversation. Context, usage, redaction state, and as_of are always saved. Retention applies to both the saved diagnostic array and the corresponding captured prefix in memory. It never renumbers events or recreates previously discarded diagnostics.

An optional ArchivePath receives a dialogue-only JSONL projection from Context before trimming. It excludes runtime skill instruction entries and is not a recovery authority. It is neither the primary event log nor Chapter 14’s full archive/journal design. Rewriting that projection preserves the current reduced conversation, including summaries and redactions; it does not promise to retain removed raw material forever.

The archive, primary, and backup are not one multi-file atomic transaction. If a later primary write fails, the archive may already be newer. Live diagnostics are still untrimmed, and primary recovery follows the validated primary/backup contract. Do not load the derivative archive as a substitute save.

10.7 Public C# usage

The library defaults to no automatic filesystem persistence until its caller configures a policy. This prevents unrelated embedded Agents from accidentally sharing the process working directory. The CLI and GUI opt in by default.

var root = new Ensemble.Ensemble(Console.Error);
try
{
    var configuration = new Configuration(
        Vendor.Anthropic,
        model,
        baseUrl,
        apiKey);

    var agent = new Agent(root, configuration);
    agent.InstallTools();
    _ = new Skills(agent, new SkillSpec(skillsDirectory, primarySkill));

    bool resumed = agent.StartPersistence(
        new PersistenceOptions(savePath, RetainLog: 200));

    // This writes the restored/bootstrap diagnostic prefix before new facts.
    agent.History().StartLog(eventLogPath);

    // Accept messages through the same actor API as earlier chapters.
    await agent.FlushAsync();
    await agent.ShutdownAsync();
}
finally
{
    root.Destroy();
}

Configure persistence once, before actor admission. A second configuration or configuration after actor startup is refused. Explicit History.Save and History.LoadSave support callers that manage their own lifecycle, but they do not authorize replacing an active Agent’s conversation concurrently.

Shutdown first joins the owned work and destroys Jobs while History remains attached. It records completed shutdown, then saves. Logical destruction follows. A save error remains a failure; it cannot be relabeled as successful shutdown persistence. The destruction-in-progress guard prevents repeated teardown while keeping real parent paths usable until saving is finished.

Examples/Persistence is a separate assembly demonstrating snapshot-only save/load, runtime model change, continuous sequence numbers, and automatic shutdown saving. It takes a new output directory and performs no network request.

10.8 CLI and GUI behavior

Both applications default to save.json in their working directory. Use a distinct directory or explicit path for each independent session.

CLI/GUI option Environment fallback Meaning
--save PATH EN_SAVE_PATH Primary save; backup is PATH.bak
--save-log N EN_SAVE_LOG Diagnostic retention; default -1
--archive-log PATH EN_ARCHIVE_LOG Optional dialogue projection
--no-save EN_DISABLE_SAVE=1 Disable automatic load/save

Explicit options override the corresponding environment defaults. The library reads none of these variables. Invalid numeric values or unusable save candidates fail startup rather than silently selecting another session.

The CLI drains accepted work at EOF and joins shutdown before exiting. The GUI saves after its owned host lifetime ends and shutdown completes. A force kill cannot run that code; this chapter does not promise to recover unsaved work after SIGKILL.

GUI replay uses reduced Context for finalized transcript content, plus retained event facts for lifecycle and direct-tool diagnostics. It can therefore restore a snapshot-only save. Context entries retain actual response/part IDs; legacy entries still use deterministic replay IDs. Projection does not append synthetic history or restart old jobs.

Live capture bounds both events and Context entries by the same observed sequence. Otherwise a current snapshot could publish a later final before older queued deltas. Reconnect uses a complete consistent snapshot and must not create duplicate cards or revive a saved shutdown state.

10.9 Exercises and verification

Use an owned directory, loopback fake provider, dummy key, and isolated browser profile. Do not point exercises at another running Ensemble session.

  1. Send several turns, exit normally, restart without replay flags, and inspect the actual next provider request for each prior human turn exactly once.
  2. Change vendor, model, primary skill, variable values, and allowed tools. Check that saved conversation survives while current configuration governs the next request and save.
  3. Compare snapshot-plus-log, snapshot-only, log-only, and older-snapshot/newer-tail representations. Require equal effective conversation and continuous event numbering.
  4. Save opaque values, exact-number arguments, media locators, usage, redacted results, summaries, and display identities. Test the real codec and reducer, not a substitute persistence model.
  5. Corrupt primary alone, then both candidates. Isolate invalid cases so a valid backup cannot hide decoder rejection. Verify file and live-state nonmutation on refusal.
  6. Block an archive or replacement path. Require a visible failure, no false success, and no diagnostic trimming. Verify a corrupt primary is not rotated over the good backup.
  7. Exercise all retention modes and confirm snapshot-only restart works without the optional archive.
  8. Restart the real GUI, inspect visible restored cards and their IDs, submit a new prompt, and refresh. Confirm the saved shutdown does not disable the new session.

The reusable executable Chapter 10 grade covers six CLI persistence checks for 85 points. Its C# -executable-only route excludes inherited Go checks and the old stdin-driven GUI probe. The GUI is a WebSocket host; its restart behavior is exercised separately through the actual host and an isolated browser, not credited as another stdin client.

Passing local fakes establishes the persistence and protocol behavior exercised here. It does not establish real-provider integration, audible accessibility, or recovery of events never saved. Those limits belong in the progress record alongside implementation and offline evidence.

Chapter 11 — MCP Tools and a Browser That Can Answer

Until now, a tool has lived inside the application. This chapter adds tools that live in another process or in the browser. The Agent still owns admission, execution records, Jobs, and conversation. A remote server supplies a capability; it does not become a second Agent scheduler.

We use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for discovery and calls. Its JSON-RPC messages give us a small, inspectable boundary: initialize a connection, discover tools, call one, and correlate its reply. We use that boundary in both directions. An Agent can call a skill’s server, and a peer can ask the Agent to execute an enabled local tool.

The purpose is not merely to make a remote function return a string. We must preserve the architecture built in earlier chapters:

  • Common declares the vocabulary and persistent relationships; functional partial classes implement operations.
  • A discovered name is not a grant to execute it.
  • The actor remains the only publisher of conversation and skill state.
  • A Job’s lifetime is independent of a caller’s observation wait.
  • Destruction closes admission, joins owned work, and removes both ends of every relationship.
  • Browser inspection is on demand, not an unsolicited attachment to every request.

1. Put the boundary in the right place

The core remains one C# assembly. Common/Mcp.cs and Common/McpBrowser.cs declare the MCP vocabulary. The Mcp/ directory implements transport, RPC, discovery, content conversion, and connection ownership. Skills/ prepares and commits skill activations; Agent/ schedules requests and receives worker completions; Jobs/ runs remote calls through the existing Job machinery.

The optional GUI project has its own Common declaration and server implementation for the WebSocket tunnel. Neither the MCP library nor the Agent depends on ASP.NET or JavaScript.

The small IMcpTransport interface is a real external I/O boundary, not glue between partial classes. It sends and receives JSON messages and disposes its transport resources. Production implementations cover line-oriented streams, an owned child process, and a connected WebSocket. Tests use working peers at those same boundaries.

The relationship graph

Object Parents and responsibility
Mcp Belongs to one Agent; owns its connections and optional browser registration.
McpClient Belongs to the manager; a skill connection also belongs to Skills under its SkillName; a browser client also belongs to its McpBrowser registration. Owns the RPC reader, pending replies, reverse-request work, transport, and remote Tools.
Remote Tool Belongs to the Agent and the client that supplies it. Calls still execute as Agent-owned Jobs.
McpBrowser Belongs to the manager; owns one browser transport and at most one claimed client.
McpToolDefinition Immutable, value-like discovery data: name, description, schema, and optional automatic frequency. It needs no holder back-pointers.

These are actual object references. A client does not rediscover its Agent by a global ID lookup or receive a copied bag of services. It reaches the Agent through its manager and reaches its granting owner through SkillOwner().

Parent add/remove methods validate before mutation and update both ends. Removing a relationship is not the same operation as destroying the child. Destroying a connection destroys its remote Tools, closes the transport, releases pending callers, joins reader and reverse work, and detaches the client from all its parents. Repeated destruction calls join the same cleanup task.

Admission closes when destruction is requested, not when a background cleanup task happens to run. Otherwise a caller could start another RPC or reattach an object that is already being dismantled.

2. One protocol, two explicit roles

Do not confuse an application that serves a pipe with an outgoing MCP client. This chapter supports both roles, but not both reader modes on the same connection.

Outgoing skill connection

For a skill server, Ensemble initiates the handshake:

  1. Send initialize with protocol version 2024-11-05.
  2. Validate the reply.
  3. Send notifications/initialized.
  4. Request tools/list and validate the complete catalog.
  5. Install only the ordinary tools granted by the owning skill.

A connected transport is not yet a successfully initialized skill. Missing schemas, duplicate names, incompatible protocol replies, process exit, or a failed catalog cause preparation to fail and its resources to be joined and removed.

Requests use integer IDs and a pending-reply table. A reply completes its matching request, not whichever caller happens to be waiting first. The outgoing reader must also recognize peer requests while it awaits replies: a server may reverse-call the Agent during initialization or a tool call.

Cancelling a reply wait removes that wait without corrupting correlation when a late reply arrives. A failed or cancelled write is different. It may have emitted half a frame, so the connection is closed rather than reused as though framing were intact.

Incoming CLI service

The CLI’s --mcp-pipe mode exposes enabled Agent tools on stdin/stdout. Here the external client sends initialize, receives the reply, and sends notifications/initialized before discovery or calls.

# After building Cli/Ch04.csproj; use your approved dotnet executable.
dotnet Cli/bin/Debug/net10.0/ch04.dll --mcp-pipe --no-save

Normal skill and log startup still happens first. Stdout contains JSON-RPC frames only; diagnostics use stderr. ServeAsync uses the existing reverse-tool admission path, not an independent tool dispatcher or fabricated model turn. EOF returns from serving; the application then joins connection destruction and Agent shutdown. An incoming service cannot initiate outgoing RPC on that same transport.

This distinction resolves an easy testing mistake: an outgoing fixture waits for Ensemble to initialize it, whereas an incoming-service fixture must initialize Ensemble itself. Reversing those roles produces a deadlock, not useful protocol evidence.

3. Reverse calls must not wait behind themselves

Suppose the Agent is waiting for a server’s tools/call reply. The server asks the Agent to read a file before it can finish. If that reverse request is queued behind the waiting model turn, neither side can proceed.

Reverse calls therefore enter a nonblocking actor control lane. The actor still validates the name, current skill grants, and arguments, and executes through ordinary Jobs. A disabled tool remains disabled; being on a trusted transport is not a grant.

Discovery exposes enabled local tools, excluding automatic snapshot tools. Remote tools are not reflected back as local reverse capabilities. A successful reverse call records a host observation, not an assistant tool-use exchange that never occurred. Unsupported methods return JSON-RPC errors. Expected bad arguments and denied calls return controlled failures; invariant and persistence faults must not be disguised as successful tool results.

The important test is a real held operation: leave a model turn or server call waiting, issue a reverse write_file, verify the file and its host observation, and only then release the original operation. A mocked assertion that a callback was invoked would not establish progress through this cycle.

4. Skill activation is a transaction

A skill may declare servers in its front matter:

---
name: notes
description: Read and update project notes
type: loadable
tools: notes_read notes_write
mcp_servers:
  - name: local
    transport: stdio
    command: /absolute/path/to/notes-server
    args: ["--format", "json"]
---
Use these tools for project notes. Read before replacing existing content.

This is the supported front-matter subset, not arbitrary YAML. Server names, transport spelling, field types, and JSON string-array arguments are validated. Use literal argument elements; this is not a shell command string. The process inherits the configured working directory and a small credential-free environment, not the application’s provider secrets. Stderr is drained separately from protocol stdout.

For a browser server, the declaration is simply:

mcp_servers:
  - name: browser
    transport: websocket

A browser does not need a process command. Server names are unique within their real skill owner. Two unrelated skills may both name their server local; Agent-wide tool-name collisions are still refused.

Prepare outside the actor; commit on the actor

Loading a server-backed skill requires asynchronous I/O, but I/O continuations must not publish grants or instructions. Activation proceeds as follows:

  1. Resolve and validate the dependency closure on the actor.
  2. Capture the variables and working directory needed by preparation.
  3. Start or claim the connections, initialize them, and discover their catalogs off the actor.
  4. Send one reliable commit message back to the actor.
  5. Revalidate the closure, cancellation, providers, and collisions; render the frozen manuals; install only explicit allowlisted ordinary tools; append one dependency-first activation event.
  6. On failure, destroy and join the prepared connections without publishing a partial activation.

Once a commit is queued, preparation awaits its definite outcome. Cancelling an observer must not race successful publication and destroy clients the actor has just committed.

The server’s catalog cannot broaden the skill’s tools list. A declared name must resolve unambiguously; discovery is evidence of availability, not authority. $TOOLS is rendered from usable ordinary capabilities. Loaded manuals remain in provider instruction context, not buried only in a tool-result body.

Primary startup

Local-only primary skills keep their synchronous initialization path. A server-backed primary requires explicit Skills.InitializeAsync after persistence loading and diagnostic-log setup, before user work is accepted. Concurrent callers join one initialization; cancelling one observer does not cancel shared startup.

Until the primary commits, the manager is unready and grants no provisional tools. Input and direct tool work are refused; actor controls remain responsive. Reverse calls during initialization see only actually committed grants. Startup is tracked control work, not a fake load_skill call with an invented call ID.

A GUI must listen before a browser-backed primary can connect. RequiresBrowserStartup() examines the primary dependency closure: only a closure containing a WebSocket server needs that wait. A stdio-only primary initializes without any browser connection. The Agent’s readiness gate remains authoritative in both cases.

Unload and persistence

Unloading closes the selected skill’s clients, processes, and remote Tools immediately. The manual’s pending-unload state remains under the earlier chapter’s conversation policy; retaining a manual does not retain executable authority. Independently owned dependency connections are not destroyed merely because another skill used them.

Chapter 10’s saved configuration is documentary, not executable state. Shutdown may save a configuration projection after remote Tools have been removed. A later startup rebuilds connections and grants from current configuration and manuals; it does not resurrect a process or browser connection from saved tool JSON. Failed primary startup must not overwrite a previous good session save.

5. Remote results remain structured

An ordinary MCP call is still a Job. Observation timeouts report that it is running; they do not cancel execution. Explicit Job cancellation cancels the remote request and sends the cancellation notification. A reverse call or ordinary wait does not borrow ownership of the Job lifetime.

MCP content is an ordered array, not one lossy string. The codec maps supported text, image, and audio blocks into the existing neutral parts, preserving order and isError. Inline media uses validated base64 and MIME information. Unsupported blocks, including general resource blocks, are refused explicitly rather than silently dropped or fetched.

The Job retains an atomic structured result separately from incremental process-output bytes. Its diagnostic output is written before completion publication. The first completed ordinary observation returns the structured parts and error flag; later observations do not replay the same result. Automatic collection uses a separate completion read that does not consume the public observation cursor.

Provider rendering is a separate boundary. An adapter supporting inline media in tool results can render those parts; another adapter may explicitly refuse that placement. Passing an MCP codec test does not establish that every provider accepts every media form. This chapter does not add remote URI fetching or Job-handle media resolution.

6. Automatic tools: wait for the snapshot, not the handle

Some external tools provide changing context rather than a model-chosen action. This implementation recognizes per_turn_ and per_round_ name prefixes, and compatible discovery annotations:

  • per_turn_: collect once at the start of a turn and retain its value only for that turn.
  • per_round_: collect before each model request, including a later request after ordinary tool results.

Conflicting prefix and annotation frequencies are refused. Only definitions granted by their actual active skill owner are eligible.

Automatic tools are not ordinary callable tools. They never appear in provider declarations, $TOOLS, deferred catalogs, or discovery references. Guessed model calls and reverse calls cannot invoke them. Filtering happens at both admission and request emission, including references replayed from older recorded results.

Collection uses real Jobs

A dangerous shortcut is to treat a timeout-limited observation as the snapshot. That returns a handle or “running” text, then sends the model request without the data it was supposed to contain.

Instead, the collector reserves and starts a real Job, records execution through the actor, and waits for its completed result. It does not replace tool_limits with a hidden foreground timeout. While collection is pending, the actor remains responsive to hints, pause, interrupt, and shutdown.

Interrupt abandons the collector’s wait; it does not kill an independent Job. That Job can finish later and remain inspectable. Its late result is not inserted into an interrupted turn or allowed to contaminate a later one. Shutdown has the separate authority to terminate and join owned work.

Pause also matters after collection: even if all results are ready, the actor must not start HTTP until scheduling resumes.

Ephemera is request context, not dialogue

Completed automatic values are combined with the current manual ephemera slot immediately before the request is frozen. The actor records system ephemera; the reducer replaces the slot rather than appending durable conversation. Each request consumes the slot.
