Diagnostic events may record what arrived, but saved reduced dialogue and provider instruction bodies must not accumulate snapshots.

The per-turn value is reused within that turn; per-round values are replaced each round. The next turn collects fresh values. Failed rendering or HTTP must not leave a stale slot waiting to leak into an unrelated request. Rendering refusal still occurs before the transport-attempt event.

A server-reported snapshot failure is nonfatal context failure, not successful snapshot data. The request receives a short diagnostic naming the automatic tool and real Job handle. Full error content remains in the Job and host observation for inspection. Do not promote failed output into facts the model is asked to rely on.

7. The browser is an on-demand MCP server

The GUI already has one WebSocket for display and controls. MCP shares that socket through envelopes:

{"type":"mcp","agent_id":"root","data":{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}}

The reply uses the same envelope and Agent identity. The actual identity comes from the server’s replay frame; it is not guessed from a tab title. All GUI controls must match that identity before dispatch. Nonmatching controls and MCP envelopes are refused without reaching tools or the model.

There is one socket writer. The tunnel owns a bounded inbound MCP queue and uses the existing outbound queue. It must not silently drop reliable RPC replies. Closing MCP on skill unload does not close unrelated conversation traffic on the socket.

Registration is not activation

The first eligible browser connection registers its transport. Connecting alone installs no tools and grants no capabilities. Loading the browser skill claims that registration, performs the outgoing handshake, discovers the browser catalog, and commits the skill’s explicit allowlist.

The registration is one-shot. It cannot be reused as a fresh RPC session after unload. Disconnect removes its claimed client and Tools; a new connection can establish a new registration. Observer tabs may view the conversation but cannot inject replies into another tab’s active browser session. A stopped Agent may still accept a replay-only observer, without constructing new MCP ownership.

Browser replies remain tied to the socket that received the request. A delayed callback from an old connection must not send its response through a newly connected socket.

The shipped browser tools

The shipped skill offers five explicit tools:

Tool Purpose
gui_snapshot Return a bounded description of visible DOM content and usable selectors, with truncation reported.
gui_click Click a uniquely selected visible element.
gui_input Set an editable element’s text and notify the page through its input events.
tts_queue Inspect current and queued speech from the page’s existing speech state.
tts_say Add speech; with interrupt:true, cancel current speech and clear queued speech before the replacement.

Inspect before acting, use selectors actually observed, and inspect again to confirm the result. A DOM snapshot is not pixel vision. A queued utterance is not proof of sound or hearing. The tools omit password values from inspection, but page content can still be sensitive; callers must choose what context to expose deliberately.

There are no automatic per_turn_* or per_round_* browser snapshots in this skill. The browser can be idle and connected without sending the page or speech queue into model requests. Automatic collection remains available to a different skill with an explicit need for it.

8. Build and exercise the actual boundaries

From solutions/edition-3/main, use the approved .NET 10 SDK:

dotnet build Ensemble.csproj
dotnet run --project Tests/Tests.csproj
dotnet build Cli/Ch04.csproj
dotnet build Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj

Use an offline restore source and controlled environment when network access is not authorized. Keep test homes, persistence files, ports, and browser profiles separate from a person’s running application. Never infer permission to use a paid model or restart another instance from permission to run local tests.

A useful verification sequence is:

  1. Transport and correlation. Use a real pipe peer to return replies out of order, close during pending RPC, send reverse requests, and emit a partial failed write. Check callers and ownership cleanup.
  2. Skill transaction. Hold initialization, verify no provisional grants, then release it. Fail a later dependency and verify earlier prepared processes are gone without published manuals.
  3. Primary startup. Test stdio without a browser, browser-backed startup after listener creation, concurrent initialization observers, shutdown during startup, and preservation of a previous save on failure.
  4. Remote Jobs. Verify ordered parts, exact error status, one-time observation, explicit kill, and denied/colliding names without effects.
  5. Automatic context. Capture real loopback model requests across two rounds and another turn. Check cadence, declaration exclusion, pause, interrupt, retained Job output, and ephemera consumption on rendering and HTTP failure.
  6. Incoming service. Send the handshake over actual streams, list enabled tools, read a real file with an integer correlation ID including zero, refuse a disabled write, and close stdin normally. No model HTTP should be needed.
  7. Browser. Use an isolated real page, load the skill, inspect and change a known element, inspect speech state, unload, and test a second observer tab’s isolation. Exercise a browser-backed primary and stopped-Agent replay too.
  8. Public consumer. Reference Ensemble from a separate C# project. Construct the graph through public APIs, activate and unload a process-backed skill, use the incoming service, then join destruction and inspect both parent collections.

Use small working fakes for external boundaries, not mocks of the components under test. Preserve failed runs and distinguish fixture mistakes from product defects. A timeout that reveals an incorrect fixture selector is not evidence that a protocol is broken; a green CLI grade is not evidence that a hidden browser tab worked.

What this endpoint establishes

The C# chapter has offline component, executable, separate-consumer, and isolated real-browser evidence. Its scoped CLI grader covers incoming pipe behavior, MCP discovery and calls, reverse calls, model-directed skill use against local peers, and automatic context. The optional GUI is exercised separately; the scoped grade does not certify Go package topology or browser appearance.

No live paid-provider interoperability or audible/human-accessibility acceptance is claimed. Fake speech verifies queue wiring, not sound. General MCP resource mapping and broad provider media support are not silently credited. Those limits matter even when every permitted check passes.

9. What to carry forward

A remote boundary changes latency and failure modes, not ownership. Keep the actor responsible for publication, the Job responsible for execution lifetime, the skill responsible for grants, and the client responsible for its connection.

The most useful questions in review are concrete:

  • Can a discovered or detached tool gain authority without a committed owner?
  • Can shutdown leave a reader, process, pending reply, or reverse parent link behind?
  • Can a snapshot wait return a handle instead of data and still allow HTTP to start?
  • Can interruption consume or destroy a Job that it merely observes?
  • Can a stale tab, foreign Agent identity, or old socket deliver an accepted reply?
  • Does saved configuration describe state, or accidentally masquerade as authority to recreate it?

Answer those questions in code and working exercises, not by trusting an architectural diagram or a passing grade. The next chapter can build on this boundary because its responsibilities remain explicit.

Chapter 12: The Agent Sees Its Working Interface

Chapter 11 connected external tools to the Agent through MCP. This chapter makes one of those capabilities convenient at startup: an optional gui-debug skill lets the Agent inspect and operate the Ensemble page in which the conversation is happening. It does not give the Agent pixel vision, continuous observation, or access to every browser tab. It supplies a particular connected page’s tools and a manual that explains how to use them honestly.

The distinction between having a tool and having an observation matters. A loaded browser skill does not mean the Agent has seen the page. The Agent calls gui_snapshot when it needs a structured view and tts_queue when it needs the speech queue. It calls again after an action to check the result. A successful click response reports dispatch; it does not prove the intended visible change.

The implementation builds on Chapter 11 rather than adding another GUI engine, transcript, browser controller, or scheduler. The new library vocabulary is an optional ordered startup selection. The GUI flag is a convenience for choosing that selection. The actual browser still supplies its catalog through MCP.

Startup Selection Is Configuration, Not a Conversation

The value-like SkillSpec record now has a final optional member:

public sealed record SkillSpec(
    string Directory,
    string Primary,
    IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>? Variables = null,
    IReadOnlyList<string>? StartupSkills = null);

Existing callers remain source-compatible. The library reads no environment variables. Skills copies the selection into an immutable array at construction, just as it snapshots initial variables. Mutating a caller’s list later cannot change a startup already in progress.

For an already constructed Agent with its ordinary local tools installed, the library setup is:

var skills = new Skills(agent, new SkillSpec(
    skillDirectory,
    "ensemble",
    StartupSkills: ["gui-debug"]));

// Application hosts load persistence and open diagnostics before this step.
// A GUI host also starts listening and supplies the browser registration first.
await skills.InitializeAsync();

Do not manufacture a model load_skill call to implement this. Startup is host configuration. There is no provider response or tool-call ID to pair with an invented result. The existing startup mailbox operation returns reliable completion without appending assistant dialogue or a host tool observation.

Common/Skills.cs declares the shared vocabulary and frozen selection. Skills/Startup.cs resolves it; Skills/Connections.cs prepares and commits remote connections; Agent/Skills.cs carries completion through the existing actor. All parts are ordinary partial types in the same assembly. There is no separate startup service or copied list of active capabilities.

Validate the Whole Initial Batch

Resolution begins with the primary and its dependencies. It then visits startup names in the host-supplied order. Each must name a loadable skill currently offered by the prospective active set. Thus an earlier selection may offer a later one. A repeated name, or a selected loadable skill already included as a dependency, is activated only once. Missing names, wrong skill types, unavailable selections, and dependency cycles fail before publication.

The prospective set is temporary algorithm state, not an authoritative registry. History’s immutable SkillPart values remain the source of active instructions and grants. The same resolver is used during initial validation and again at commit, so the prepared closure cannot silently differ from the published one.

For an entirely local closure, construction publishes one dependency-first activation. If any initial skill needs MCP, construction publishes no partial primary and grants no provisional tools. InitializeAsync uses the existing asynchronous preparation path, validates catalogs and collisions, renders all manuals, and commits one activation on the actor. Reverse calls remain responsive but cannot borrow unpublished authority. A server failure destroys prepared clients and leaves the batch unpublished.

Ready() derives from the primary and selected names in History. It does not read a second mutable ready flag. RequiresBrowserStartup() examines the complete initial closure, not only the primary. A stdio-only optional skill must not wait for a browser. A WebSocket-backed optional skill must not be declared ready before its actual page has initialized.

Concurrent initialization callers join the existing task. Cancelling one observer detaches that observer; Agent shutdown cancels and joins startup work. A failed startup does not arm shutdown saving over an earlier good session. Restoring a conversation does not restore permission to execute old tools: the current startup configuration rebuilds instructions, grants, and connections as described in Chapters 10 and 11.

Instructions Must Reach the Provider as Instructions

Loading a manual is not enough if the next request carries it only as tool-result text. The C# renderer already places active skill bodies in provider instruction context: Anthropic’s system, OpenAI Chat Completions’ first system message, and Gemini’s systemInstruction. Startup uses that same representation. The primary comes first; each active manual appears once, not again as ordinary dialogue.

This endpoint implements Chat Completions, not OpenAI Responses. A future Responses adapter must explicitly map these instructions to its instruction field. Evidence for one adapter cannot establish another adapter’s behavior.

$TOOLS expands against the prospective allowed catalog. Automatic per_turn_ and per_round_ tools remain excluded from all model-facing declarations, discovery references, and expansions. Browser debugging does not use those automatic extensions at all. An unrelated model round receives neither an unsolicited DOM snapshot nor a new speech-queue dump.

The Application Boundary

Both hosts accept a comma-separated --startup-skills value, with EN_STARTUP_SKILLS as the application-level default. An explicit flag overrides the environment value. Empty comma-separated fields are ignored. Both hosts also accept --gui-debug, which appends gui-debug; duplicate selections activate once. Without either setting, the default primary and optional-skill behavior are unchanged.

For the actual GUI:

dotnet run --project Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj -- --port 8097 --gui-debug

Use an available owned loopback port and an isolated profile for exercises, not a user’s working browser or server. Provider settings are the same application settings used in earlier chapters. This flag grants no provider budget or device permission.

The GUI constructs the Agent, loads persistence, starts logging and the HTTP listener, and waits for a browser only when the initial closure requires one. The page registers through the existing /ws MCP envelope channel. Readiness still gates user work until activation commits. There is no separate /mcp route, static fallback catalog, or guessed description for an unavailable remote tool.

The CLI can use the same startup API with a supplied stdio-backed gui-debug manual, as the executable tests do. The shipped manual uses the GUI’s WebSocket registration; the plain CLI does not magically create a browser or GUI listener for it. Without that transport, startup fails explicitly rather than claiming browser capability.

One Skill Owns Its Browser Capability

The shipped gui-debug manual owns its own WebSocket server declaration and the five explicit grants: gui_snapshot, gui_click, gui_input, tts_queue, and tts_say. It is an alternative to the general browser skill, not a wrapper that leaves a separately owned dependency alive on unload. Loading both against the same one-shot browser registration is not a supported way to duplicate ownership.

Chapter 11’s relationships still apply. The MCP manager owns the browser registration; the claimed client belongs to the manager, its skill, and that registration. The client owns its remote Tools. Unloading gui-debug closes its client and removes executable browser tools immediately, while retaining the pending-unload manual state until reduction. It does not close unrelated GUI traffic. Reconnection and reactivation are not silently invented when a consumed registration is no longer usable.

The browser responder lives in Examples/Gui/wwwroot/mcp.js. It provides bounded visible DOM text and selectors, a restricted click/input surface, and the existing speech queue. It does not offer JavaScript evaluation, arbitrary navigation, other-profile access, or pixel inspection. Password values are omitted from snapshots; visible text can still be sensitive and must be handled accordingly.

Preserve Input Origin, Not Just Its Value

gui_input identifies one visible editable text field, replaces its value with literal text, and dispatches input and change events. Quotes, spaces, Unicode, and strings such as {Enter} remain text, not a keyboard macro language. Empty text clears the field. Ambiguous selectors, hidden or read-only fields, and non-text inputs are refused. This is DOM input, not physical keyboard provenance.

The important change is the origin of that input. The MCP handler dispatches a marked event:

element.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("input", {
    bubbles: true,
    detail: { mcp: true }
}));
element.dispatchEvent(new Event("change", { bubbles: true }));

The prompt listener maintains humanTyping from actual input events. MCP input does not create that cause. A later speech callback combines current speech with humanTyping, rather than reconstructing human intent from a nonempty field. Successful submission clears both the field and the human cause explicitly. Human whitespace still counts as typing.

That one retained fact prevents two different freezes: the immediate pause on programmatic input, and the delayed pause when speech finishes while programmatic text remains. Speech still pauses when configured to do so. Genuine human typing still holds pause after speech ends. Another tab’s explicit unpause is not continuously vetoed by an unchanged local cause, as in the previous chapters.

A tool must not silently overwrite a user’s unfinished draft without permission. Origin tracking fixes scheduling; it is not authorization to replace text. The manual tells the Agent to preserve human input and inspect the effect of its actions. A follow-up snapshot, not the requested argument string, establishes the resulting field value.

Historical First Use

The following account is retained from the earlier manuscript. It describes earlier encounters, including their failures and human reactions, not a claim that this C# endpoint repeated those live-provider trials. Historical Go snippets and tool names below describe those runs, not the current C# API. Its practical lesson is the difference between building a test harness and using the real interface.

What the wiring found

The plumbing above is small because the preceding chapters already own the difficult lifetimes. A skill declares an MCP server. The registry connects when the skill loads and disconnects when it unloads. A browser tab exposes four tools over a WebSocket that was already there. The interesting part is what arrives the first time an agent can see a screen it did not render and press a button nobody told it about.

The first-edition experiment ran on September 19 and 20, 2026. Its driver and transport arrived on the first day; four code repairs and three documentation commits followed the next afternoon. The retained experience report supplies the account below. The ninety-eight-second outcome is that report’s measurement, not a new run of this edition.

The asymmetry is useful. Once a failure was visible, the repair was often small. The experiment exposed faults that source development and passing graders had missed, but it did not find every fault without help. The report specifically attributes a truncation observation to the human supervisor and the unsafe rendering path to subsequent source inspection. Those are valuable findings too; their origins matter when assessing the observer.

The user that cannot read the source

The historical driver was a separate small binary. It connects to the same hub the browser connects to, discovers its tools through MCP, and registers exactly one tool of its own, file_report, so it has somewhere to put conclusions. It is built on NewBareAgent, which is an agent with no builtin tools at all. No read_file, no run_command, no editor. Its interaction tools arrived through discovery. That experimental driver also gained submission and waiting helpers; those are history, not extra tools assigned by this four-tool exercise.

Its system prompt states the constraint directly:

You CANNOT read files, edit code, or run commands. You can only
interact through the GUI, exactly as a human user would.

That restriction is the entire value of the driver. An agent with filesystem access will answer a question about the interface by reading the source, which tells you what the interface was meant to do. An observer restricted to the GUI has to answer from the screen, which tells you what the interface actually does. The gap between those two answers is where the bugs live.

The human observer

The protocol around these runs matters as much as the tooling, because it is what makes the results mean anything.

Bill Cox supervised the experiment, reading the reasoning as it streamed. The method was to let the driver inspect the interface before supplying a diagnosis. Watching it walk past a defect is useful evidence about the view it has; immediately pointing out the defect would erase that evidence.

He did direct, and the distinction is worth drawing precisely. Direction covered what to test next, which binary to rebuild, and once, usefully, the observation that a stale server was still holding port 8084 while the freshly built binary bound to nothing and served no one. That is operational guidance, and withholding it would have wasted an hour proving nothing. Findings were different. The retained report also records a screenshot observation about truncation supplied by the human. That finding cannot be counted as an unaided discovery merely because the subsequent repair was automated.

The reason to run it that way is that a supervisor who volunteers the answer cannot tell the difference between a tool that works and a tool that agrees. A supplied hint can make a successful report look like an independent discovery unless the assistance is recorded. To learn whether the snapshot is sufficient for a finding, let the observer attempt it before supplying the missing answer.

This is the same discipline the book asks of a reader supervising an agent on live code, applied to the machinery itself. Keep the human assistance with the result so the next reader can tell which capability was exercised.

The observer that froze what it watched

The first runs never reached a task at all. The driver typed its prompt and the coding agent stopped responding, permanently, before any work began.

The cause was a feature working exactly as designed. Chapter 7 pauses the engine while the user is typing, so that an agent does not barrel ahead while a human is halfway through composing a hint. The feature exists for a particular working style: Bill Cox reads the agent’s reasoning as it streams and sends corrections mid-turn, which makes the pause the difference between a hint that lands and a hint that arrives after the decision it was meant to change. The first-edition implementation watched the input field:

// The original handler. WebSocket readiness guards elided for clarity.
let userTyping = false;
input.addEventListener('input', () => {
    const typing = input.value.trim().length > 0;
    if (typing && !userTyping) {
        userTyping = true;
        ws.send(JSON.stringify({type: 'pause'}));
    } else if (!typing && userTyping) {
        userTyping = false;
        ws.send(JSON.stringify({type: 'unpause'}));
    }
});

Read that as a human and it is correct. Text appears, the agent waits. The field empties, the agent resumes.

Read it as a program driving the field and it is a trap with no exit. gui_input sets the value and dispatches an input event, which is what makes it indistinguishable from typing, and that indistinguishability is the entire point of the tool. So the pause fires. Then gui_submit sends the prompt and clears the field by assigning to value, and assigning to value in JavaScript fires no event at all. The branch that sends unpause is reachable only by a path the driver cannot take. One keystroke in, the engine is paused, and nothing in the system will ever unpause it.

The historical repair expressed two intentions. A flag marks input as programmatic so the pause handler ignores it, and submission sends an explicit unpause rather than relying on an event that will not arrive:

if (window._mcpProgrammaticInput) return;

The general shape of this is older than software. An instrument that shares a channel with the thing it measures will perturb it, and the perturbation is worst where the system was tuned to human timing. Pause on typing, debounce on scroll, idle timeouts, animations that wait for a settle: each one encodes an assumption about how fast and how continuously a person acts. An automated driver violates all of them at once, and it does so silently, because from the GUI’s perspective nothing unusual occurred. A user started typing and never stopped.

The second pause, after the fix

The second-edition student reproduced the self-input freeze in a real browser. Marking MCP input as programmatic fixed the immediate listener: a model could fill the field and click Send with speech disabled. Independent review then turned native speech on. The utterance finished, the programmatically filled field still contained MCP submitted, and the Agent remained paused.

The missed path was pace(). On speech transitions it looked at the field’s contents again, forgetting how the text got there. The input listener knew the event was programmatic; the later speech callback silently promoted that same text to human typing. Ignoring one event could not repair a second reader of the same mistaken signal.

Keep the cause, rather than reconstructing it from the value. The browser MCP handler sends a marked event after setting the control:

element.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("input", {
  bubbles: true, detail: { mcp: true }
}));
element.dispatchEvent(new Event("change", { bubbles: true }));

The ordinary input listener preserves the actual cause:

input.addEventListener("input", event => {
  humanTyping = !event.detail?.mcp && input.value.length > 0;
  pace();
});

Speech and typing then combine as speaking || humanTyping. Successful submission clears humanTyping explicitly after clearing the field. Human whitespace still counts as typing; programmatic text does not acquire a human origin merely because a speech callback ran later.

Pause remains Agent-wide. A browser sends automatic pause/unpause commands when its local causes change. If another tab explicitly unpauses, an unchanged local cause cannot immediately veto that command. The corrected native-browser check covers speech ending with programmatic text still present, genuine whitespace typing holding pause, explicit unpause from another tab, and a subsequent actual MCP submission. It also waits for the concluding speech to finish. The earlier passing check with speech disabled proved less than its author thought.

Those checks used native speech start/end events, with a local provider fake driving the actual Agent and browser. They establish the measured pause transitions, not subjective listening quality. The second tab closed after the global-unpause control; the retained earlier two-tab speech stall has no established cause and is not a general claim about concurrent speech reliability.

A debugger that would not start

The first historical task given to the driver was small on purpose: ask the coding agent for Tower of Hanoi, then watch it debug the result. The agent wrote the program, ran it, and produced fifteen moves. Then it started dlv and stopped forever.

Chapter 4 predicted this in print. Section 4.8 is titled “Your agent drives a debugger,” and it warns that a dispatcher which waits for process exit will hang on an interactive program, because “the dispatcher would wait for an exit that never comes, and on pipes dlv refuses to start at all.” The chapter named the trap. The reference implementation walked into it anyway.

The mechanism was a single synchronous read. toolRunCommand read the PTY inside the tool function, so the function could not return until the process closed its output. For go build that is correct and invisible. For a debugger sitting at a prompt it is fatal, and it is fatal in a way that disables the exact feature meant to rescue it: ai_callback_pattern is matched inside Wait, and Wait runs after the tool function returns. The escape hatch was behind the door it was supposed to open.

The first-edition repair changed the lifetime: the tool function returned once the process was running, and a reader goroutine owned the PTY until exit. Its DeferFinish field told that dispatcher the job would finish itself. The following historical excerpt shows the handoff; it is not an API to add to the current implementation:

// The reader goroutine copies output from the PTY to the job until the
// terminal closes, then reaps the process and finishes the job. It runs
// independently of the dispatcher, so an interactive process that never
// exits (dlv, python) does not block the model from getting a handle.
job := c.Job
c.DeferFinish = true
go func() {
    buf := make([]byte, 32*1024)
    for {
        n, rerr := f.Read(buf)
        if n > 0 {
            _, _ = job.Write(bytes.ReplaceAll(buf[:n], []byte("\r\n"), []byte("\n")))
        }
        if rerr != nil {
            break
        }
    }
    _ = f.Close()
    werr := cmd.Wait()
    // ... exit code extraction elided ...
    job.Finish("", nil)
}()

Two dispatchers

The experience report records the next surprise: the debugger worked, but the older Chapter 4 checks returned zero.

The failure signature pointed in the wrong direction. Tool output came back as the empty string, and the capture file on disk held zero bytes. That reads as a broken output path, and an hour can be spent there. The actual fault was lifetime again. There were two tool dispatchers in that first-edition codebase: Engine.Execute, which serves chapters 3 and 4 through the older Ask path, and Actor.dispatchTool, which serves chapter 6 onward. Only the second had been taught about DeferFinish. The first still called job.Finish the instant the tool function returned, and Finish closes the capture file. The reader goroutine was writing correctly the whole time, into a file that had already been closed underneath it.

The diagnostic detour is worth recording, because it cost more than the bug. Debug prints added to Actor.dispatchTool never appeared in the output, and the first explanation reached for was a stale build cache. It was not stale. The prints were in a function the failing tests never called. Silent debug output is evidence of the wrong code path at least as often as it is evidence of a bad build, and the cheaper check is to confirm which function runs before rebuilding anything.

Ninety-eight seconds

With both dispatchers corrected, the report records an end-to-end rerun. The driver typed the prompt into the real text field and submitted it. This time the coding agent wrote a three-disk hanoi.go, ran its seven moves, then opened dlv and worked through a full session: set a breakpoint on move, continue, print disk, quit. The reported debugger exit was zero and elapsed time ninety-eight seconds. The earlier hung run had used four disks and fifteen moves; those are different runs.

That historical run explains why the capability is worth building. Chapter 4 of this edition already establishes the independent job lifetime; keep it when adding browser access. An agent that can drive a debugger can inspect a running program’s state rather than reasoning about what the state ought to be, and an agent that can drive a GUI can do the same for an interface.

The bug that only appears after you fix the bug

The next task sent the driver into the settings panel with instructions to try values a careful user would not. It set temperature to negative five, and the server accepted it.

That is the obvious bug, and the fix is ordinary: a clamp function, called both when a settings patch arrives and when settings load from disk, so a hand edited file cannot bypass validation either. The original chapter also reports a targeted check with clamp disabled; that historical claim is separate from this edition’s settings evidence.

The second bug appeared only because the driver was asked to repeat its own test after the fix landed. The server now clamped correctly, and the GUI still displayed negative five. Server state and screen state disagreed, and the screen is what a user believes.

The cause was a single struct doing two incompatible jobs. Settings was used both as a sparse patch, where an absent field means “leave this alone,” and as a full state broadcast, where every field should be present. Those two roles want opposite JSON encodings. With omitempty on every field, a value clamped to zero vanished from the broadcast entirely, and the client guard reads:

if (s.temperature !== undefined) { /* update the input */ }

An absent field is indistinguishable from an unchanged field, so the stale value stayed on screen. The same flaw meant TTSEnabled: false could never be transmitted, because false is empty. Turning speech off was unrepresentable on the wire.

The deleted code had confessed. SettingsStore.Apply carried this comment:

// Since omitempty skips false, we handle this via the raw patch.
// For simplicity, always apply.

Someone met this bug, understood it precisely enough to describe it in one sentence, and routed around it instead of removing it. The method had no callers outside tests.

There was a real choice about how far to take the repair. The cautious option preserves the existing wire format and introduces a second type for broadcasts, leaving the patch struct untouched, which costs nothing today and leaves two nearly identical structs for the next reader to confuse. The maintainer settled it in one line: the format has no external consumers, so make the code clean. The repair therefore dropped omitempty from every field, so a broadcast always carries complete state, and deleted Apply outright, leaving one merge path with defined semantics.

A zero missing from a full snapshot would still be the defect. The corrected broadcast must carry temperature: 0 and tts_enabled: false explicitly. A clamped value on disk, the value applied by the server, and the value shown by the client are separate observations. Chapter 8 now follows all three instead of treating a settings-file inspection as proof of the screen.

The settings panel that does not exist

The strongest finding came from a test that failed in an unusual way.

Asked to exercise the sidebar tabs, the driver reported that clicking “Artifacts” opened the Settings panel. The report was specific, confident, and false. There was no Settings tab in that version of the markup. The data-tab and data-panel attributes map correctly, chats to chats and artifacts to artifacts, and clicking either one does what it says.

The report was fiction, and the reason it was fiction is the finding. Tab state lived only in a CSS class. gui_snapshot built its element labels from textContent, aria-label and placeholder, and read no state attributes at all, so the driver could see that two tabs existed and could not see which one was selected. It had also reached for an ambiguous selector, button:nth-of-type(2), because the buttons carried nothing better to aim at. Asked what happened after the click, it had no way to observe the answer, and it produced a plausible one.

In this run, the driver filled missing state with a confident guess. The observation supports fixing the missing state; it does not establish that every model must guess whenever information is absent.

The repair was to put state where a machine can read it. The hamburger and the tabs now carry aria-expanded and aria-selected, synchronized on every click, with the initial value derived from the live CSS class rather than hardcoded, because the markup default had already drifted from the rendered default. gui_snapshot now reports those attributes alongside each control.

Rerunning the identical test produced a correct before and after table, and in the one place where the driver lacked information, it wrote “not observable” instead of inventing a panel. Same model, same prompt, same GUI. The only change was that the interface stopped hiding its state.

This is the accessibility argument in a form that a developer who has never used a screen reader can feel directly. Semantic state attributes are usually presented as a courtesy extended to users with assistive technology. They are also the difference between an automated observer that reports what happened and one that reports something reasonable. This observer produced wrong data where the interface supplied no selected state, and delivered it with the same confidence as the truth.

What an interface owes an observer

Two smaller findings came out of the same pass, and both generalize.

Source inspection found an injection hole. artifact-scroll.js built the tool card header by interpolating the tool name and its serialized arguments into innerHTML. Tool arguments can carry text from outside the agent. They contain filenames, URLs, and the contents of files just read, which is to say text an attacker can influence. Twenty lines further down, the result path rendered with textContent and was safe. One file, both patterns, and the vulnerable one sat on the path that renders attacker-adjacent text. The book spends a chapter on prompt injection arriving through the model. This was the same threat arriving through the renderer.

The truncation investigation followed the human screenshot observation, and the initial notes about it were backwards. The working document asserted that the driver saw the full DOM while the human saw a trimmed version. Measurement found four independent caps running the other way: the human view truncated tool input at 500 characters and results at 1000, while the snapshot truncated each artifact at 120 characters and the whole document at 4000. For an individual result preview, the snapshot could show 120 characters where the human view showed 1000. Worse, the snapshot silently dropped every artifact past the tenth with no marker, so it could not distinguish ten artifacts from fifty.

The report corrected its earlier claim after checking the actual caps. The caps were kept, because both views need them, and both were made honest: truncated text is now reachable through a title attribute rather than deleted behind an ellipsis, and the snapshot states how many characters and how many artifacts it withheld.

That is the rule the section converges on. Silent truncation lets an observer report that a screen looks fine without seeing the omitted content. Hidden control state invited the guess in this run. Unsafe HTML interpolation gives attacker-controlled markup an execution path. Runtime observation and source inspection answer different parts of the diagnosis. The unsafe renderer was visible in source; the observer’s confident report showed what the missing state caused during use.

The bugs travel back into the book

The instruction that produced this section came once the fixes were in: update the chapter summaries wherever a bug made it through. Tracing them was the first step, and each defect was matched to the chapter that should have prevented it. Several repairs also exposed an instruction that should have made the obligation explicit.

The original Chapter 4 explained the job model, named the interactive process trap in plain words, and never stated the obligation that follows from it. Chapter 8 built the tool card and showed the rendering without saying which parts of it carry text the agent did not write. Chapter 12 specified gui_snapshot with a 4KB cap and did not require the cap to announce itself. In each case the mechanism was taught correctly and the duty attached to the mechanism was left implicit.

The original Chapter 9 is the sharpest example, because the reasoning that let three bugs through is stated plainly in its opening:

The graded surface is small: four server-side settings checks and a parity gate. Everything else is client code you can see working.

That passage left client behavior to visual inspection. Looking at a screen confirms that a value was accepted. It does not confirm that the value was validated, that the server and the screen agree about it afterward, or that a control’s state can be read by anything other than an eye. Three bugs fit in that gap, and all three shipped.

A missing obligation in the teaching is worth repairing even when an experienced implementer could have inferred it. That does not make every implementation defect inevitable or transfer every mistake to the book. The repair was therefore made in the prose as well as the source. The historical repair made Chapter 4 state that the tool returns when the process is running and the job owns it from there, and gives the failure signature, which reads like broken output capture and is really a closed file. Original Chapter 8 states that tool cards are built with textContent and that capped content stays reachable. Original Chapter 9’s summary gains the three obligations that survive the absence of a grader. Original Chapter 12 requires the snapshot to report what it withheld.

A loop closes here. The agent described in these chapters was built by following these chapters. When it acquired eyes and a way to press buttons, the first thing it did was find places where the chapters were wrong. Some repairs belonged in the GUI and some obligations needed to become explicit in the instructions. The next implementation gets both lessons.

A book that produces a working program gets to be tested by the program it produces. This section is the first time that test came back with findings, and the findings were about the book.

Later Historical Browser Exercises

The retained October 10, 2026 browser sessions used claude-haiku-5-5, gpt-4o-mini and gemini-3.8-flash. These are the models actually exercised, not a claim about today’s catalog. The live record links the captured requests and real Chrome observations.

Claude Haiku and Gemini changed the effective font to 20, received the refreshed snapshot, and unloaded the skill. Claude then incorrectly said the MCP tools remained available until compaction. The old generic unload message encouraged that explanation; the final request already showed the tools gone. The implementation’s message was clarified to separate immediate server removal from pending instruction removal. No paid repeat was needed merely to demonstrate revised wording.

Both GPT-4o mini attempts failed the full task. The first guessed input[type='number'], received a missing-selector error, then unloaded without repairing it. A guided second attempt supplied the observed #font-size selector and explained that it was a select. It changed the setting and unloaded, then tried read_file on path/to/the/snapshot despite the instruction forbidding file access. That nonexistent path failed, and the final response claimed the snapshot could not be inspected. The capture already contained the refreshed state.

The second attempt passed the script’s GUI assertions. It remains a task failure. That distinction is especially useful here: working controls do not guarantee that a model will use them correctly or report their result faithfully. A guided selector is assistance, and a prompt restriction is weaker than the historical blind driver’s actual absence of file tools.

These live runs preceded the final native-speech correction and small manual/message corrections. They establish the recorded interaction and unload behavior on their captured source. The corrected speech path has its separate native-browser evidence; no final-source paid rerun is claimed. Likewise, a visibly effective font change is not a restart-persistence test. Chapter 8 supplies that separate check.

Checking the correction itself

The first-edition chapter ended with a quotation-verification story. It said that “You know the client works because you can see it.” had been invented and appeared nowhere in the original settings chapter. The retained source contains those exact words, split across a newline. They are present even in the revision before this narrative was appended.

A literal one-line search misses a wrapped sentence. That miss establishes a search result, not the sentence’s absence. Read the surrounding paragraph or normalize whitespace before comparing the quotation. The supposed correction needed the same scrutiny as the original claim.

The comparison with the phantom Settings panel remains useful, with a narrower conclusion: check the observable that supports the claim. For a tab, read selected state. For a quotation, compare the actual source text. For a successful tool, inspect its correlated result. A confident diagnosis can survive an inadequate check just as easily as the bug it diagnoses.

Exercise This Endpoint

Start with the ordinary default path and verify that no browser tools are enabled merely because a page connected. Then run with --gui-debug. Inspect the first actual model request: the manual must be in provider instruction context exactly once, browser declarations must be present, and there must be no fabricated startup load_skill exchange or unsolicited snapshot.

Use explicit calls to request a snapshot, choose a visible selector, change a field with literal text, and request another snapshot. Inspect the real input events and their marked origin. Leave programmatic text present through speech completion, then verify that genuine human whitespace still holds pause. Queue and inspect speech, while keeping queue wiring separate from an audible or human-accessibility judgment. Unload the skill and verify that later calls are refused and the ordinary GUI connection remains available.

The source-only endpoint is solutions/edition-3/ch12; it includes the same library, CLI, optional GUI, manuals, and component tests as main at this boundary. The current offline verification uses real components with working local peers:

  • ordered startup, duplicate elimination, validation rollback, instruction placement in all three adapters, frozen inputs, and no invented tool dialogue;
  • held optional-server initialization, readiness refusal, real remote dispatch, joined cleanup, and preservation of an earlier save on startup failure;
  • a scoped six-check CLI executable grade, covering startup handshake, explicit observations, interaction, speech-queue content, and unload;
  • an isolated actual browser with shipped --gui-debug, literal Unicode input, human/programmatic pause-cause separation, explicit snapshots, queue wiring, identity refusal, unload, and normal owned-host exits;
  • a separate public-API C# consumer exercising explicit startup selection, instruction rendering, network-free initialization, and complete destruction.

These results do not establish real-provider integration, pixel vision, audible speech quality, general accessibility, or permission to control another person’s browser. The real-provider allowance for this run is exhausted. Keep those exercises explicitly incomplete rather than converting a successful fake-provider session into evidence it cannot supply.

The useful result is modest and concrete: a configured Agent can obtain evidence about its own working page, act through declared tools, and inspect the result. The interface becomes part of the engineering feedback loop without becoming a second owner of the Agent’s conversation or lifecycle.

Chapter 13 — A listener who can only hear

Chapter 12 gave the Agent tools for looking at and operating its browser. This chapter asks a different question: what reaches a user who relies on the application’s speech? A correct screen is not an answer. The speech channel has its own ordering, filtering, interruption and failure behavior.

The first-edition investigation used a restricted listener to expose gaps in that channel. We retain its useful discoveries below, but build the current endpoint in C# 14/.NET 10. The listener is an instrument, not a substitute for a person listening to the result.

TL;DR: what you build

  1. One speech pipeline. Thinking and response text enter a per-part raw buffer. Resolve Markdown fences before splitting phrases, strip presentation syntax, expand identifiers, preserve paragraph boundaries, and explicitly flush unfinished tails. Successful tool bodies stay automatically silent; dispatch names and failures are spoken separately. Whole finals without preceding deltas must enter the same path exactly once.
  2. One admission log. Record each utterance when it reaches the front of the speech queue, before choosing native playback or silent transcript mode. Include source labels. Record typing/speech pause transitions too. Admission is not proof of sound or completed playback.
  3. A genuinely restricted consumer. Examples/Listener constructs an Agent with exactly five custom tools: say, listen, sleep, set_speech_speed, and save_history. It installs no builtins or Skills manager. Guessed file, browser-inspection and evaluation tools must fail ordinary dispatch.
  4. Complete lifetimes. The listener owns a fresh target GUI, browser profile and private browser connection. Its Session joins Agent Jobs before closing that connection and stopping the owned processes. EOF, interruption, deadline and failed startup must not strand a pending sleep or browser.
  5. Layered verification. Check the formatter, actual page, executable speech harness, restricted listener and cleanup separately. None establishes real-provider compatibility or audible accessibility by itself.

The existing C# solution remains one core assembly. Examples/Gui and Examples/Listener are separate applications referring to it. The GUI owns speech presentation; the Agent still owns scheduling and durable conversation.

13.1 Build the speech channel before judging it

Examples/Gui/wwwroot/speech.js is a small pure formatter. speechPhrases(raw, offset, flush) returns completed phrases and a new raw-source offset. The page retains that offset on the displayed part. It does not replace displayed text with a spoken copy or run independent regular expressions on each delta.

A delta is not a sentence. It may stop inside a word, Markdown link, identifier or fence marker. Keep the raw text until there is enough structure to release a phrase. At ordinary sentence punctuation, retain the necessary lookahead rather than guessing what the next delta contains. At an explicit flush, release the final tail even without punctuation.

Fences come first. Their delimiters and bodies span lines, so removing them after splitting on newlines is too late. Recognize a complete fence as one source span and replace it with “code block”; a partial fence remains buffered until completion or final flush. Remove link destinations while preserving the label, strip inline backticks and heading/emphasis/bullet markers, and turn a lone newline into whitespace. A blank line remains a paragraph boundary. These transformations describe the supported prose subset, not a complete Markdown parser.

Identifier expansion is similarly modest:

Source Spoken words
queueChunk queue Chunk
max_tool_rounds max tool rounds
HTTPServer HTTP Server
ALL CAPS ALL CAPS
Hello ordinary World. Hello ordinary World.

Do not confuse removing code notation with removing its content. Inline identifiers can carry meaning; a fenced implementation is usually better named than read token by token. Manual artifact reading still uses the same formatter.

Release points and whole finals

narrate(card, flush) uses the part’s raw cursor. Model deltas append text; a final replaces the displayed text with the authoritative complete value and flushes only its unconsumed suffix. If no delta arrived, the cursor is zero and the entire final is eligible. A duplicate final finds no remaining suffix.

Before a tool dispatch or error announcement, flushNarration() releases pending prose tails. Tool calls announce the tool name, not its arguments. Successful tool-result bodies stay silent unless the person explicitly asks to read the artifact. Failed tools enter the labeled error path. Provider failures arrive as durable error_occurred lifecycle frames; control refusals arrive as error frames. Both must speak, while ordinary lifecycle notices and terminal turn completion must not duplicate those errors.

Replay is silent. A restored or muted partial part remains suppressed through its final. Starting midway through a restored fence would otherwise expose code whose opening delimiter was never observed by the speech cursor. New live parts can narrate normally.

13.2 Admission, playback and the two pause causes

The page owns one current native utterance and a FIFO of future phrases. Queued speech already counts as busy. Only when startSpeech() removes the next phrase does it append an utterance to window._ttsLog. This is the last shared point before native playback and ?speech=transcript diverge.

Each entry has increasing seq, millisecond timestamp ms, and kind. Utterances include text, source, and part_id; pause and resume entries include cause. Sources distinguish thinking, response text, tool-announcement, error, and deliberately requested speech. Thinking and errors also receive spoken prefixes so the distinction is available to a native listener, not merely a JSON reader.

In transcript mode the same queue admits and records phrases but makes no native synthesis call. In ordinary mode the current acknowledged rate and selected voice are copied onto each new SpeechSynthesisUtterance. Completion and error callbacks advance the same FIFO. Stale callbacks cannot finish a newer utterance. Cancelling clears current and future speech; it does not append all cancelled future paragraphs as if they had been heard.

Typing and speech are separate causes of one transition-based pause decision:

const speaking = activeSpeech !== null || speechQueue.length > 0;
const cause = humanTyping ||
    (settings?.pause_while_speaking !== false && speaking);

Human whitespace is still a draft. Programmatic input is not human typing, even when a later speech callback recomputes the cause. Send pause/unpause only when the combined cause changes. This avoids floods of pause commands and respects another tab’s explicit override rather than continuously reasserting a private veto.

Escape cancels speech even when the prompt contains a draft. It leaves that draft intact, so the typing cause can continue to hold the Agent paused. Stopping the voice and releasing the Agent are different operations.

13.3 A user who can only listen

A prompt that says “do not inspect the DOM” is not a capability boundary. The separate C# listener creates an empty library Agent, then constructs only these custom Tools:

Tool Required arguments Result
say text Submits one target turn through the actual form; refuses while a previous turn is pending
listen timeout_seconds Returns newly admitted utterances with sources and explicit pending/status fields
sleep seconds Waits the nonnegative finite duration, cancellably
set_speech_speed rate Updates the target and waits for acknowledgement; valid range is 0.25–4
save_history path Writes typed submissions and heard entries as semantic JSONL

Common/Session.cs declares Session state, resource handles and operations. Channel/Session.cs implements the five tools, one semantic history and its independent hearing cursor. Browser/Protocol.cs owns correlated DevTools commands; Browser/Lifetime.cs launches and closes the resources. Program.cs composes the session and owns its overall deadline. All partial Session sections compile into the same application assembly; they are not separate services connected by callback bags.

The Session’s private browser connection sets the actual prompt, observes the explicit turn_ended boundary, reads admitted _ttsLog utterances, and acknowledges rate changes. It exposes no selector, DOM snapshot, screenshot, arbitrary evaluation, target response text or raw tool-result body to the model. Chrome receives no provider credential. The target and listener have separately supplied provider configurations.

Before submitting, say marks the target pending. Only its real completion frame clears that flag. A momentary idle display before acknowledgement therefore cannot masquerade as a completed turn. listen returns promptly for new speech; a timeout with pending:true is not idle. Subsequent calls advance the hearing cursor, while save_history does not consume it. Saved entries have only seq, kind, source, and text: typed prompts and source-labeled heard speech, not the listener Agent’s reasoning or ordinary tool transcript.

Here, “heard” means admitted to the speech channel. It does not mean a microphone captured sound. Keyboard navigation and general screen-reader usability remain separate concerns.

Why these tools wait for completion

Ordinary custom tools use Jobs and may return a timed running report. This listener deliberately has no wait_for_job. Returning a running handle for listen could consume its hearing cursor later without delivering those entries to the model. Returning a running handle for a long sleep would likewise leave no supported observation operation.

The custom Tool constructor therefore has an optional waitForCompletion parameter, defaulting to false. The listener opts in. Dispatch still reserves and starts a real Job, but awaits that worker before ordinary observation. The existing structured-result path returns the complete value once, without the byte cap truncating a semantic listen result. There is no second result store or scheduler. Cancellation detaches a waiting observer; Job ownership and shutdown still govern the actual operation. Existing coding tools keep their previous behavior.

Closing the session

The listener uses a new or empty caller-selected directory, a fresh browser profile, and owned loopback ports. It never attaches to the human’s page or running Ensemble. Task mode finishes its reliable Agent turn; stdin mode treats EOF as session shutdown. SIGINT, SIGTERM, deadline and startup failure all enter the same explicit cleanup.

First shut down the listener Agent and join its Jobs, including pending sleeps. Then destroy the core root, dispose the browser connection, stop the owned browser, and stop the owned GUI. A short graceful process wait has a kill-tree fallback. Output streams are drained into the session’s logs. Long sleeps are sliced only for the platform’s delay range, not silently capped by product policy.

An earlier Go/Node listener closed its browser on EOF but retained a sleep timer. Its idle exit took 125 ms, while EOF during a four-second sleep took 3865 ms. The corrected historical peer exited in 127 ms with the sleep pending. Those measurements are lessons about ownership, not C# performance claims. The current endpoint has its own process-tree cleanup tests.

13.4 The run that succeeded for the wrong reason

The first-edition investigation gave the blind persona a task expected to fail.

Tool results do not enter the automatic speech channel. Only dispatch is announced, so a listener hears that a command is running and then hears nothing about what it did. The task was to run a command against a path that does not exist and report the exit code, and the prediction, written down before the run, was that the listener would come back empty.

It came back with the correct exit code.

Its retained account prints the explanation: six transcript entries, in this order. These are historical entries, not output produced by the corrected pipeline:

1. "run command"
2. "The command failed with exit code 1:"
3. "`"
4. "ls: /nonexistent-path-xyz: No such file or directory"
5. "`"
6. "This is expected since..."

Utterance 1 is the dispatch announcement. Utterances 2 through 6 are the model’s own prose, describing what happened. No tool result appears anywhere in the transcript. The listener learned the exit code because the model chose to mention it.

The observer reported its transcript accurately and drew the wrong conclusion from it, writing that no gap had been found. That conclusion was reasonable given what it could perceive, which is the whole problem. Without a source label, the words alone cannot show whether the exit code came from tool-result delivery or model narration. A listener receiving the right information cannot tell whether the system delivered it or the model happened to be chatty that turn.

Accessibility resting on a model’s prose habits is discoverability by luck. A terser response, a different system prompt, a model tuned to skip the summary, and the same task can yield silence with no warning and no error.

The scope ruling made the intended channel explicit. Tool results are not spoken automatically, by design: “I listen to your thinking, and that is enough.” Thinking and response text both feed the channel; the exit code arriving through prose is permitted behavior, not proof that raw tool output was spoken. The GUI still lets a person deliberately read an artifact through its speaker button.

That ruling also redirected the instrument. A blind persona that hunts for unspoken tool results is testing a decision rather than a defect. The transcript checks whether thinking and response text arrive completely and in order, with announcements and errors labeled separately. A person must still judge intelligibility.

Utterances 3 and 5 expose another defect: punctuation leaked into the channel.

13.5 A bug found by ear

Two of the historical entries were a single backtick. Punctuation had reached the synthesizer input instead of being removed by the speech filter.

The obvious explanation is streaming. Deltas arrive on arbitrary boundaries, a fenced code block gets split across two chunks, and each half is filtered separately, so neither half contains a complete fence and the markers survive. That explanation is clean, mechanical, and wrong.

A test disproved it. Feeding the entire fenced block as one chunk, with no split anywhere near it, still produced spoken backticks.

The real cause sat one layer earlier. Filtering ran per phrase, and phrases were produced by splitting the buffer on newlines. A fenced block contains newlines by construction, so by the time the filter saw anything, the fence had already been cut into separate lines. A pattern that needs an opening marker and a closing marker to match will never match a line containing exactly one of them. The filter examined three fragments, found no fences, and passed all three through.

The fix resolves fences against the whole buffer before any splitting happens. The filter then sees a complete block and replaces it with a name, and the listener hears “code block” where a wall of syntax used to be.

The account also records the listener’s objection to splitting on newlines. Prose wraps. A sentence broken across two source lines is one sentence, and splitting at the wrap produces two utterances with an unnatural pause between them. Speech engines work a phrase at a time, and every boundary the pipeline invents is a pause the listener hears.

So a lone newline became whitespace and a blank line stayed a boundary. A wrapped sentence is now spoken as one utterance, and paragraphs still separate.

A visual-content check does not establish correct speech segmentation. A DOM snapshot shows text that is present and correct. A screenshot shows a page that renders properly. A grader asserting on rendered content passes. The content is fine. The segmentation of the content is wrong, and segmentation determines where the voice can pause.

13.6 The bug nobody could hear

A complete part can be rendered without any preceding deltas. The historical handler displayed that text and called flush() on an empty buffer. It produced no speech at all.

The C# final handler feeds the authoritative text through the same raw-cursor path as deltas, so zero prior deltas is an ordinary case rather than a separate formatter. Test the actual page with a whole part_final and no earlier part_delta, then repeat the final and reconnect. Require one utterance, no duplicate and silent replay.

Disabling provider streaming is useful but insufficient evidence for this branch: the Engine may synthesize display deltas from a plain response. A final-only page check and a nonstream executable check answer different questions. Keep both.

13.7 Using the instrument carefully

The historical investigation’s most useful surprise was not another speech filter. The listener received an exit code through the model’s narration and concluded the channel had no gap. That is why source labels matter. Correct words can still support an incorrect causal conclusion.

Tool bodies are intentionally not automatic speech. A person can deliberately read an artifact with its speaker button; the model may also explain the result in its own prose. A listener who hears that explanation has not proved raw tool-result delivery. Conversely, absence of a secret string proves nothing if the tool never read the planted file successfully. Correlate the successful tool result before asserting that its contents stayed silent.

Likewise, a transcript demonstrates text admission, not voice quality. Fake native callbacks can verify queue and pause wiring. Neither establishes pronunciation, audible pacing, interruption comfort or accessibility for a particular person. Those remain human exercises with authorized native audio.

13.8 Exercise: build and verify the C# endpoint

Source map and builds

Use the approved .NET 10 SDK and existing package cache. From the solution directory:

"$DOTNET" build Ensemble.csproj
"$DOTNET" build Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj
"$DOTNET" build Examples/Listener/Listener.csproj
"$DOTNET" run --project Tests/Tests.csproj
node Tests/SpeechTests.mjs

The portable formatter test fragments input at every split and also one character at a time. It checks whole and fragmented fences, wrapped prose, paragraph boundaries, identifiers and final tails. It does not launch a browser or claim sound. The listener is a separate assembly consuming the public core API, not code linked into the core to obtain private access.

Executable speech grading

The public scripts/tts-harness.sh entry point launches the real GUI, submits the prompt through the actual form, and writes the page’s admitted-speech JSONL. It runs in transcript mode. It does not reconstruct the provider answer or replace the formatter under test.

Supply existing paths through TTS_NODE, TTS_DOTNET, TTS_GUI, TTS_CHROME, and TTS_PUPPETEER; see scripts/README.md. No installation is performed. The caller supplies a fresh WORKSPACE, TTS_LOG, its loopback LLM_BASE_URL, and STREAMING=on|off. --describe reports the real read_file/path contract without launching. --type-during-turn TEXT generates a human input event during a response and later clears it.

From the repository root, with those explicit paths set:

go run ./cmd/grade-edition2 -ch 13 -executable-only -json solutions/edition-3/main

The command name is retained from the shared grader. This scoped adapter runs the nine Chapter 13 checks, including its zero-point launch check, over five fresh GUI launches. It excludes inherited Go/Chapter 12 grading rather than pretending C# satisfies that topology.

Check Points Observation
tts-discrimination 20 Successful file results stay automatically silent; distinct model answers are spoken
tts-filters-markup 20 Markup is removed and a fence is named
tts-buffers-fragments 10 Words survive fragment boundaries
tts-speaks-unstreamed 15 Plain provider output is spoken once
tts-gate-both-causes 10 Typing pause and subsequent release are ordered
tts-speaks-errors 10 Actual provider failure reaches speech
tts-boundaries 5 Wrap, paragraph and trailing-tail boundaries remain meaningful
tts-expands-identifiers 5 Identifiers expand while ordinary capitalization survives

The gate’s name is broader than its numeric observation. It does not by itself prove both overlap orders, human whitespace, programmatic-input discrimination, final-only delivery, listener restriction or lifetime cleanup. Those need their focused checks. The prior chapter’s unchanged evidence remains valid within its original scope; it is not newly earned through this score.

Restricted-listener exercise

Configure LLM_VENDOR, LLM_MODEL, LLM_BASE_URL, and LLM_API_KEY for the target. Configure the four corresponding LISTENER_* values separately. The listener has no credential fallback. For offline verification, use working loopback provider fakes with dummy keys, not paid services.

From the solution directory, with a new session path and an existing browser:

"$DOTNET" Examples/Listener/bin/Debug/net10.0/Listener.dll \
  --dotnet "$DOTNET" \
  --gui "$PWD/Examples/Gui/bin/Debug/net10.0/Gui.dll" \
  --browser "$CHROME" \
  --directory "$SESSION_DIR" \
  --timeout 120 \
  --task 'Ask the target to explain HTTPServer, queueChunk and max_tool_rounds. Listen until pending is false, report the admitted words and sources, and save semantic history to speech.jsonl.'

Inspect the listener’s actual model declarations and deliberately attempt an undeclared tool. Check pending versus idle, repeated listens, source labels, rate acknowledgement, a sleep longer than the ordinary observation delay, and a saved history containing only typed/heard entries. End separate sessions through EOF, SIGINT, SIGTERM, deadline and failed startup while a real sleep is pending; verify their owned descendants exit. Never use another person’s browser/profile to obtain that evidence.

13.9 What this endpoint establishes

The C# run has 71 passing component groups, a separate restricted listener, focused real-page exercises with working socket/native-speech fakes, real owned GUI/browser/listener exchanges against loopback provider fakes, and the scoped executable speech grade of 95/95. Process-lifetime checks cover pending-sleep cancellation and owned cleanup. The first grade was 65/95: its model fixture accidentally disabled streaming, and it exposed a real missing narration path for provider lifecycle errors. Correcting both and adding the lifecycle regression preceded the final passing grade.

The historical first-edition and later Go listener sessions are not C# integration evidence. No real provider, native audible quality, human listening or full accessibility claim follows from this offline boundary. Turn on ordinary audio only with appropriate authority and listen: whether the voice and phrasing are usable remains a human question.

Chapter 14 — The world’s best context engineering, before breakfast

A long session with a coding agent can degrade in a familiar way. The answers get vaguer. The agent reads a file it read an hour ago, then forgets a decision made before lunch. A fresh chat can help because a person decides what to carry over. This chapter moves tool-traffic cleanup inside the Agent and records every cut, so replay can explain what left the working context and reproduce the result.

I had started new chats myself, several times, on the day I designed this chapter.

The design had been in my head for a couple of months. On a Tuesday morning I typed it out for about twenty minutes while CodeRhapsody turned it into a design record and checked it against the code. Then I took a shower. The first commit landed at 7:42, before breakfast, and frankly it felt good to get it out.

The important idea is less grand and more useful: the context window is a working set, not the archive. Keep the decisions and their reasons. Remove tool bytes deliberately. Do not let a cleanup erase the manual that explains the tools still available.

The breakfast story, byte measurements, and compaction experiments described here come from my earlier work, not fresh measurements of this C# endpoint or a benchmark against every other system. The endpoint’s local tests and loopback exercises are described in §14.14; at that chapter boundary, live-provider, native/audible speech, and human-accessibility verification remained incomplete.

TL;DR: what you build

  1. One owner for each decision. Agent selects reductions at safe actor boundaries; History applies recorded facts; Engine renders the resulting Context. A worker never trims History or decides when another model request may start.
  2. One target, two bands. The default target is 400,000 bytes. Results use T/8, calls and stubs T/16. Each band crosses twice its budget before cutting an old prefix back toward one budget. Complete call/result batches are the unit of selection.
  3. An explicit keep-or-stub option. For opted-in configurations, a large result is considered once after a successful request presents it. The model may call keep_tool_results in the consuming response. Ordinary models do not acquire this policy from a guessed name.
  4. A real checkpoint kind. micro_handoff records an ordinary result and then HandoffRecorded. The reducer removes tool traffic and private replay material, replaces older active handoff notes, and preserves visible dialogue and manuals.
  5. Immediate revocation, retained instructions. Pending skill unload removes authority, including deferred references and automatic snapshots. Its manual remains in SYSTEM. Retiring that manual is not this chapter’s job.
  6. Recoverable facts. Serialize writers, append journal records before publication, validate recovery candidates independently, and retain journal events beyond the validated backup—not merely beyond the current primary.
  7. A full event archive. An optional archive contains original facts, including tool payloads and cuts. It is not reconstructed dialogue and does not silently invent missing history.
  8. Honest verification. Component, separate-consumer, CLI, GUI, browser and executable-grader checks establish different things. Passing a loopback provider does not establish a real provider, audible speech or human accessibility.

The endpoint is still C# 14/.NET 10. Shared vocabulary and persistent state are declared in Common; functional partial implementations supply the bodies. The GUI remains a separate application, not another scheduler or transcript owner.

In plain words

Keep the user’s words and useful explanations. Once a tool result has done its job, replace its bulk with a stub, and later remove the paired call and stub. At a deliberate checkpoint, keep one new note and clear tool traffic without summarizing away the conversation. Record every cut so replay knows exactly what happened. Preserve original facts separately, and make crash recovery depend on validated files rather than guesses about what was probably saved.

14.1 Why is this byte here?

Ask three questions of every byte sent again with a request:

  • Why is it here?
  • What put it here?
  • What can remove it?

A user prompt has a reason to remain. A useful explanation of an edit does too. A large file result often answered a question once and is now occupying the window without another decision to support. In Chapter 2’s measured sessions, result bytes made up about 42 percent of conversation history by volume and call arguments another 30 percent. That made tool traffic the obvious place to look.

A removed file result can often be obtained again by reading the file. That is not the same as recovering the original result: the file may have changed, and repeating a command may have effects. Preserve original facts in the archive when their historical identity matters. A stub should say that bytes were removed, not fabricate a trustworthy locator.

One earlier bug was particularly instructive: a stub referred to an output path whose numeric handle was reused after restart. The next reader received plausible output from the wrong command. Wrong data was worse than no data. This endpoint does not turn a result stub into an unverified promise that some path still names its original bytes.

Tool clearing is not dialogue summarization. The automatic policy in this chapter never asks a model to replace the user’s goal or a discussion with a compressed paraphrase. Existing reduction primitives can express other operations, but the policy here selects result and tool reductions only.

14.2 Keep the relationships simple

The real ownership paths remain:

Ensemble → Agent → History
                 → Engine
                 → Jobs → Job
                 → Skills / MCP owners, when configured

History owns committed Context, retained diagnostic events, sequence numbering and persistence coordination. Agent owns the target, the actor’s temporary decisions and request admission. Immutable Context, entries and parts are value-like snapshots; they do not acquire holder back-pointers simply because several readers use them.

Common declares the new operations and values, including:

public const int DefaultContextByteBudget = 400_000;
public partial int ContextByteBudget();
public partial void SetContextByteBudget(int bytes);
public partial (int ResultsBytes, int CallsBytes) ToolCompactionBudgets();

These declarations belong to the existing partial Agent. Their implementation belongs in Agent/Compaction.cs. There is no settings service copied into every object and no separate reduction scheduler.

Constructors establish the existing parent relationships. Explicit destruction joins owned work and removes both ends. History remains attached while terminal facts and shutdown persistence need it. A recording failure does not permit cleanup to abandon an Agent in its parent’s collection; cleanup must still complete, while preserving the original failure.

14.3 Instructions are not disposable tool results

Chapter 9 already put loaded manuals in provider instruction context. Do not move them into dialogue merely because a historical implementation did so. Primary and loaded SkillPart bodies appear once in the provider’s instruction field; ordinary transcript messages do not duplicate them.

A skill’s recorded grants describe what was activated. Its pending marker changes what is authorized now. Derived Context queries compute active and revoked names from the immutable request snapshot:

  • A pending-only grant is unavailable immediately.
  • Another active skill may still grant the same name.
  • Dispatch refuses an unavailable tool even if a caller guesses its name.
  • Ordinary declarations, deferred catalogs and emitted discovery references follow the same rule.
  • Historical discovery metadata stays in canonical events; request projection filters it without rewriting the record.

Automatic MCP operations remain outside callable model tools. A pending skill cannot continue collecting automatic snapshots. Unloading a server-backed skill also closes its owned connection/tools under the existing ownership rules.

Both tool clearing and handoff retain pending manuals in SYSTEM. Removing permission and retiring an instruction body are different operations. This chapter implements the former, not a new manual-retirement scheme.
