The historical chapter discussed frozen inline declarations. This C# edition uses the Chapter 9 provider declaration mechanism instead. Stable primary instructions and infrequent cuts remain useful, but this endpoint makes no claim to implement that old inline protocol or to have measured a provider’s cache benefit.

14.4 The two-band ladder

Let T be the Agent’s context-byte target. The default is 400,000:

Use Derived amount at the default
Whole-result band, T/8 50,000 bytes
Call-and-stub band, T/16 25,000 bytes
Optional immediate-stub threshold, T/100 4,000 bytes

A positive target has a one-byte minimum for each ladder band. The public setter refuses negative values without mutation; zero disables automatic byte-budget reduction. These are byte measures of serialized tool material, not token counts, model context capacities or a hard cap on the entire conversation. Dialogue and manuals may grow beyond T.

Each immutable entry caches its tool-byte measure. This is a derived value of immutable content, not another mutable accounting authority. Selection examines complete batches, using response-local call/result pairing. Repeated IDs in later completed batches remain legal. An incomplete, orphaned or ambiguous exchange stops safe prefix selection; the algorithm does not invent a result to make progress.

The result band measures eligible batches with whole results. Above twice its budget, select the oldest prefix sufficient to bring the measured band down toward one budget. Record a Redacted event with Redaction.Result and fixed sequence bounds. Applying it replaces result bodies with stubs while preserving their calls and identities. Re-stubbing an existing stub preserves its metadata.

Then consider the call/stub band. It may remove only a stub-only prefix, never jump over a still-whole batch. Above twice that band’s budget, record Redaction.Tool over complete old batches. Calls and results disappear together; surrounding visible text remains.

Why twice the budget? A cut invalidates a region of the request. Cutting larger chunks less often avoids constantly shaving its front. This is hysteresis, not a guarantee about cache hits on an untested provider.

The actor advances its presentation watermark only after a successful response. A new result therefore reaches a successful request before automatic clearing can select it. After restoration, the first request conservatively presents retained results again. Recorded cuts, however, are never reconsidered: raising T later cannot resurrect them.

14.5 Keep or stub, once

Some sessions benefit from more aggressive treatment of a large result after its first use. Configuration(stubsToolResults: true) enables that explicit policy. The hosts expose --stub-tool-results, with EN_STUB_TOOL_RESULTS=1 as their environment alternative. The default is false; no model-name prefix silently enables it.

The concrete keep_tool_results control is installed and granted for this option. It takes no policy arguments. A successful model-dispatched call vetoes the immediate cuts staged for that consuming response. A same-named custom tool is not the control. Invalid arguments, a failed call or an undispatched interrupted call do not count as keeping.

Selection occurs against the Context that was presented, before recording the consuming response. Results larger than T/100 are candidates. The actor holds only temporary proposed cuts while that response’s tool batch completes. Successful keep discards those proposals; otherwise the actor records the cuts after all companion outcomes are durable.

Every completed assistant response has a canonical entry, even an empty response. That entry closes the prior batch’s once-only decision boundary. A later text-only turn or snapshot-only restart must not reconsider a batch that was kept. This uses the existing conversation structure rather than a persistent batch registry.

Keeping is not unlimited retention. The ordinary ladder may still stub or remove an oversized kept batch when its band requires it. Small results, ordinary-model sessions and a zero target retain their defined behavior.

14.6 Explain the work so useful reasons survive

Once a file result disappears, what remains about the edit? Whatever useful explanation the Agent recorded, plus any facts still available in their original sources.

Compare:

read_file config.cs
edit_file config.cs

with:

The port appears to be fixed in config.cs; I'll check it before changing settings.
read_file config.cs
The listener uses a literal port here. I'll move that choice to the existing settings owner.
edit_file config.cs

The second version preserves intent and a reason. It does not need private chain-of-thought or a verbose narration of every keystroke. A concise explanation before an action lets a person supervise it now and helps a future continuation understand it later.

Narration is evidence of what the Agent said, not proof the statement remains true. Record paths, relevant operations, observed outcomes and uncertainties. Re-read a changing source instead of treating an old sentence as a current fact. This is why the chapter keeps words without pretending that words are infallible memory.

14.7 A handoff is a fact, not a destructive summary

The earlier positional compress_context experiment let a model choose messages to replace with a summary. The September 2026 account described repeated loss of most of the conversation, including the goal near its beginning. Later whole-task handoffs started a fresh instance from a document, introducing a second path for durable state. Neither approach is the mechanism to reproduce here.

micro_handoff is smaller and more constrained. The model supplies a nonempty text note through the normal tool protocol. Admission validates it; the ordinary successful result is recorded before the note can take effect. If the response also contains another tool, its outcome must be recorded before the cut. Interruption pairs undispatched tails with their exact-ID refusals first. Independent Jobs are not cancelled merely because their observations no longer belong in context.

The actor then records HandoffRecorded carrying a value-like HandoffPart. History applies that fact by:

  1. Removing tool calls and results from working Context.
  2. Removing opaque reasoning and private replay signatures, including signatures attached to otherwise visible text.
  3. Retaining the visible text, ordinary dialogue, system entries and skill manuals.
  4. Removing older active handoff parts and appending the newest note.

Do not recognize a handoff by a magic prose prefix. The marked part makes replacement precise. Engine converts it to ordinary system text only in the disposable provider projection. Canonical Context and snapshots retain its identity. Original notes and private parts remain in the event archive; clearing a working view does not rewrite history.

The note should say what succeeded, what failed, where the source of truth lives, and what comes next. Failed approaches are often the highest-value bytes because they prevent repetition. Record uncertainty too. A note is a continuation aid, not proof of subjective continuity or a substitute for checking current state.

14.8 Manual clearing follows the same actor boundary

The public control is AgentInput(InputKind.ClearTools). The CLI accepts {"kind":"clear_tools"}; the GUI provides Clear tool traffic. Neither creates a new worker that edits History.

The actor stages one pending flag. After current batch outcomes and any staged result cuts/handoff are recorded, it records a tool-only redaction over the actual committed sequence range. Pause blocks a new model request, not this completed-batch control. An idle paused Agent can therefore clear immediately. A repeated clear with no tool traffic creates no synthetic cut.

For a caller that needs to observe completion:

await agent.PostAsync(new AgentInput(InputKind.ClearTools));
await agent.FlushAsync(cancellationToken);

PostAsync admits the control. FlushAsync observes accepted foreground work; it does not resume a paused turn or wait for all independent Jobs. Manual clear preserves dialogue, pending manuals and the newest handoff. It does not terminate a command simply because that command’s earlier observation is cleared.

14.9 Total reduction is not permissive decoding

A recorded cut contains its decision: event kind, level and exact sequence range. History applies that event. It does not ask today’s Agent policy to select the range again.

Known but inapplicable facts must not stop all later replay. An inverted or out-of-range reduction, or a known event missing the payload needed to apply it, is a safe no-op on Context. History reports a safe diagnostic with sequence, kind and reason, and later valid facts still apply. Sequence advancement includes the skipped durable fact.

That is different from accepting corrupt data. Unknown event kinds, unsupported versions, invalid supplied values, malformed tool identities and broken journal sequences remain errors. Do not implement totality as a blanket catch that hides invariant faults. Separate strict decoding from explicit applicability checks; keep public Reduce pure and put diagnostics on the real History owner.

Snapshot/tail loading stages a complete candidate before publication. A bad candidate cannot leave half a restored conversation live. Replay and incremental append use the same reduction behavior, so a full log and its snapshot produce the same request under the same current runtime configuration.

14.10 The recovery journal, primary and backup

Chapter 10 saved on joined shutdown. A killed process cannot perform that shutdown. Chapter 14 adds a journal to the same History owner, not a second event store or scheduler.

Agent.StartPersistence restores first, activates <save-path>.journal.jsonl, then records current runtime configuration. It runs before accepting input. Direct History.Save remains a snapshot operation; it does not silently enable continuous journaling. Explicitly disabled persistence remains available.

All writers serialize through History’s existing save gate. Append computes its next event and reduced state under a short state lock, writes and flushes the journal and optional diagnostic writer outside that state lock, then publishes committed events/Context/sequence. Readers can still capture the last committed snapshot during slow disk work. Another writer cannot race past it.

If append fails, publish nothing live and poison further append/save attempts. A partially written sequence must not be reused under the pretense that nothing happened. Shutdown may then report the original recording fault, but explicit destruction still joins work and detaches owners.

Recovery validates candidates independently. Prefer a valid primary plus its contiguous journal suffix; otherwise try a valid backup plus its suffix. With neither snapshot present, a journal beginning at sequence one can recover the initial session. Do not turn corrupt candidates into an empty conversation or use a valid primary to conceal an invalid backup-retention assumption.

Only complete newline-terminated journal records count. An incomplete final suffix, even a partial UTF-8 character, may be ignored with a diagnostic. Malformed complete records, duplicate numbers and gaps refuse. Loading does not repair files. Activating a writer after successful recovery rewrites the validated complete prefix before new appends.

Saving follows a careful order:

  1. Capture a consistent snapshot without holding the state lock across disk I/O.
  2. Render and validate the candidate; prepare any requested archive.
  3. Validate the old primary before rotating it into backup. Never overwrite a good backup with corrupt primary bytes.
  4. Replace the primary with the new validated snapshot.
  5. Retain journal records newer than the validated backup. Without a valid backup, retain them all.
  6. Only then trim the live diagnostic tail as configured.

The journal is not trimmed merely to the latest primary boundary: that would destroy the facts a backup needs after primary corruption. No fsync or hardware power-loss guarantee is claimed here. The executable crash exercise tests process kill and recovery, including a torn final suffix.

14.11 A full archive must really be full

An optional ArchivePath is an event-complete JSON-lines log. A dialogue-only reconstruction cannot replay cuts, tool outcomes, skill grants or lifecycle facts, so it is not an adequate substitute.

Before changing snapshots or trimming, merge the existing archive, available journal and retained diagnostic events. Require a contiguous sequence from one through the captured boundary. Overlapping sequence identities must serialize identically; missing earlier facts, conflicting overlaps or future events refuse before snapshot/backup changes. Strict UTF-8 prevents silently changing original bytes through replacement characters.

If no source still contains an early event, enabling an archive later cannot manufacture it from reduced Context. Report the missing history. Keep archive, save, backup, journal and open diagnostic paths distinct. Writing an archive successfully before a later snapshot failure is acceptable; a retry must validate and reuse it safely.

The public History.Load log path can replay this archive. It recovers the reduced working view because the original payloads and the subsequent cuts are both there. Diagnostic retention zero therefore need not mean lost history—provided journaling/archive saving actually preserved it. A snapshot alone remains a different artifact.

14.12 One setting, one authority

The library Agent owns the live byte target. The GUI’s settings snapshot reads it rather than keeping a second mutable copy in presentation preferences. Validate a proposed patch and save it before publishing either preferences or policy. A failed save must leave the old file, live policy and both clients’ acknowledged values unchanged.

The GUI field is context_target_bytes. Its convention is intentionally different from the library setter: zero or a negative value selects the 400,000-byte default, positive values round to thousands, and a rounded zero also selects the default. Large values are bounded safely. A wrong-typed optional field is ignored like the existing preference fields. The control shows acknowledged values, retains a proposed edit while saving, and restores acknowledgement on failure.

The CLI takes --context-budget-bytes N or EN_CONTEXT_BUDGET_BYTES; an explicit flag wins. Here zero disables automatic reduction, and negative values refuse. Document this difference instead of hiding it behind a shared parser with contradictory semantics.

Live reductions also change already-rendered cards. Incremental frames newer than a cursor cannot remove an older tool card. The GUI therefore uses its existing silent replay envelope when a recorded cut crosses the peer’s view. Snapshot Context supplies the transcript; diagnostics cannot resurrect a cleared model dispatch card. The completed-response frontier retires both stored and late streamed partials at ResponseEnded, not only at the end of the entire turn.

A replay is presentation recovery, not another speech event. The newest handoff is readable; refresh and a zero-log restart must project the same reduced transcript without automatically sending a model request.

14.13 Build and exercise the endpoint

From a preserved source endpoint, use an approved .NET 10 SDK:

dotnet build Ensemble.csproj
dotnet run --project Tests/Tests.csproj
dotnet build Cli/Ch04.csproj
dotnet build Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj

The CLI project name remains Ch04.csproj; renaming it is not part of context engineering. Keep credentials, logs, profiles, captures and build products outside source endpoints. Use a fresh owned workspace and local ports, not another person’s running application.

An ordinary interactive CLI launch can opt in explicitly:

dotnet Cli/bin/Debug/net10.0/ch04.dll \
  --context-budget-bytes 400000 --stub-tool-results \
  --save /owned/session/save.json --save-log 0 \
  --archive-log /owned/session/archive.jsonl

Supply provider configuration through the already documented host boundary; do not put credentials in conversation or the archive. For offline replay:

dotnet Cli/bin/Debug/net10.0/ch04.dll dump /owned/session/archive.jsonl
dotnet Cli/bin/Debug/net10.0/ch04.dll render /owned/session/archive.jsonl

These commands inspect recorded facts and render a request; they do not establish provider success. CLI JSON-line user input queues work. If an exercise needs a clear after a particular turn, wait for that turn’s durable completion rather than sending several lines and assuming each blocks.

The executable-scoped grader is invoked from the book repository with -ch 14 -executable-only -gui EXECUTABLE -json. Its executable argument is a launcher for the built C# GUI, not a static-assets directory. The launcher forwards flags; the grader supplies owned paths, dummy credentials and loopback peers. The default Go grading route remains separate.

Its eight checks cover instruction survival, handoff pairing and sibling order, keep/stub behavior, recorded cuts across a changed target, current declarations and actual MCP unload refusal, snapshot versus full-log replay, anchored SIGKILL/backup recovery, and total reduction. Current startup skills are explicit in restart fixtures; saved configuration is not secretly reactivated. Historical inline-tool placement is not credited to this C# path.

Then use the application, not just the report. Observe a full result before a later stub, keep a result, clear while paused, issue two handoffs, refresh, and restart with zero diagnostic retention. Change settings from a second client and deliberately fail an owned settings write. Repeat the cut projection with SSE so a disappearing final cannot leave an old partial tool card. Speech wiring and visual/browser assertions are still not proof of native hearing or accessibility.

14.14 What this endpoint establishes

The final component suite has 89 passing groups. A separate assembly consumer uses public APIs for policy updates, real host-control handoffs, paused clear, full archive replay, zero-log restoration and complete owner detachment. Its seeded historical tool exchanges are replay fixtures, not claims of executed effects. CLI and plain/SSE browser exercises separately use real actor, Job, persistence and host paths with working loopback boundary fakes.

The scoped executable grade passes all eight checks for 100/100. The first attempt scored 70/100 because its adapter assumed restored manuals and a Go event label; correcting the fixture made current startup selection explicit and checked the actual C# encoding. Those earlier failures remain failures, not retroactive successes. The progress record retains the detailed receipts and process exits.

The live-provider check remained blocked by the lack of an approved credential source in the test session. The local results establish the state transitions above, not model quality or the unverified speech and accessibility behavior.

The lesson is not that smaller context proves better memory. It is that every retained byte has a reason, every cut is an inspectable fact, and recovery can reproduce the working state without guessing what the Agent must have meant.

Chapter 15: The Invisible Invoice

Bill reported $2,475 in model spend on the first edition through its recall chapter. He attributed a few hundred dollars to a caching bug that produced correct answers, on time, while quietly losing the discount on repeated input. The answers gave him no reason to look for it.

Every request the agent sends carries a prefix: tool declarations, the system prompt including skill manuals, then retained conversation. Much of that prefix is identical from one turn to the next. A provider cache can make those repeated tokens cheaper to read. Lose the cache and the same useful answer arrives with a different bill.

The bug left no obvious trace in the agent’s behavior. No test failed. No log line turned red. An aggregated invoice is a poor place to discover which turn first lost its prefix. Correct output can conceal a cost defect indefinitely.

This chapter builds the instrument that detects prefix changes, the markers that identify reusable boundaries, and the meter that reports the cost while the operator can still do something about it.

TL;DR

Engine owns an optional CacheLens and its process-local meter. History retains canonical response counts, never a mutable dollar balance. The lens observes actual sends without changing them; an immutable prediction follows each request. Marker selection runs on final provider JSON, after tool-result adjacency. Anthropic support is explicit opt-in; OpenAI uses implicit caching with an optional routing key. Exact response model/tier selects a conservative price. Unknown values remain unknown. GUI projects one coherent Engine snapshot.

In plain words

First ask, “Did we send the same reusable beginning?” Then ask, “Did the provider report reading it from cache?” Finally ask, “Do we know the applicable rate?” Those are three questions, not one. A correct answer to the user’s task answers none of them. Keep the evidence separate so a student can find which assumption failed without rewriting conversation history or guessing a cheaper bill.

Prerequisites and scope

Continue the C# Chapter 14 endpoint in solutions/edition-3/main. Preserve solutions/edition-3/ch14; it is a runnable predecessor, not a directory to edit. Use C# 14 and .NET 10. The CLI, GUI and public examples reference the same core assembly. No new package or caching service is required.

This chapter adds three instruments: an Engine-owned cache lens, explicit Anthropic marker placement, and a process-local usage meter. OpenAI Chat Completions keeps its implicit caching and may carry a documented routing key. Gemini keeps its existing implicit path. A fake can exercise the instruments; it cannot award evidence of a real cache hit, model availability or billing.

§15.1 Correct answers can hide waste

A cache miss can produce a completely correct answer. The tool works, the edit lands, and the test passes. Nothing in that behavior tells the operator whether the provider read a stable prefix from cache. A cost problem can remain invisible until an aggregated invoice arrives, long after the request that caused it.

Build the instruments in an order that makes diagnosis possible:

  1. The lens shows the actual request and a byte-preserving approximation of its provider-ordered prompt. Compare consecutive requests before guessing which content changed.
  2. The markers express supported cache boundaries. A legal marker is not proof that a provider accepted the request or reused its prefix.
  3. The meter shows reported tokens and a conservative price estimate. It must not disguise an unknown price as zero dollars.

The distinction between prediction and observation governs all three. A lens predicts reusable bytes. A response reports tokens served from cache. A price row estimates a charge. None is a substitute for the provider’s invoice.

Do not store dollars in History. Record usage in the existing canonical response facts, while Engine separately accumulates successful sends for this process. Restoring yesterday’s conversation must not silently charge yesterday’s tokens to today’s display.

§15.2 Vocabulary and ownership

Read Common/Cache.cs and Common/Meter.cs before their implementations in Engine. Common declares shared state and callable partial members; the functional files supply their bodies. The compiler combines these parts into one type, not linked wrapper objects.

Object or value Responsibility
Engine HTTP exchange, optional lens ownership, process-local usage rows
CacheLens Consecutive send captures, byte-prefix prediction and diagnostic files
CacheCapture Value-like wire, prompt and options byte arrays
CachePrediction Immutable measurement belonging to one admitted request
UsageIdentity Value-like vendor, actual response model and service tier
MeterSnapshot Coherent immutable latest response, grouped rows and derived totals
TokenPrices Conservative exact-identity price lookup; no mutable balance

A lens constructor receives its real Engine parent and registers both ends. Engine.Lens() reaches the child; CacheLens.Parent() reaches the owner. A second lens cannot silently replace an attached one. Explicit Destroy() detaches both directions, and Engine destruction destroys its lens. There is no global lens registry or copied logger: diagnostics reach the application through the existing parent relationships.

Snapshots and identity records are explicitly value-like. They need no parent back-pointers merely because an Engine returns them. A retained snapshot remains unchanged after another response completes.

The library never reads host environment variables. CLI and GUI composition roots translate their flags into explicit configuration and construct the lens. Engine owns the resulting object’s lifetime.

§15.3 The lens: observe without rewriting

new CacheLens(agent.Engine, directory) attaches private diagnostics. Its Begin operation runs at actual transport admission, not during offline Render, parser tests or restored-history replay. Pre-cancelled sends do not rotate the captures.

The selected directory contains three pairs:

Current Previous Meaning
request.wire.json request.prev.wire.json Exact UTF-8 request bodies, including provider markers
request.body request.prev.body Marker-stripped prompt properties in provider order
request.options.json request.prev.options.json Remaining model/generation/routing properties

request.prediction.json also records the latest sequence and byte comparison. On completion, the existing application logger receives that request’s prediction alongside its reported usage. The wire/body/options files are consecutive-send diagnostics, not a complete per-request archive.

There are no authorization headers in these files. Nevertheless, prompt text, file content and tool arguments can be private. Keep captures outside Git and publication artifacts. Selecting a diagnostic directory is not permission to publish its contents.

Separate the prompt from options

Raw JSON property order is not necessarily the provider’s context order. The C# diagnostic uses these explicit sequences:

  • Anthropic: tools, system, messages.
  • OpenAI Chat Completions: tools, messages, including the system message.
  • Gemini: systemInstruction, tools, contents.

The outer diagnostic envelope is new. Each selected property’s lexical bytes are retained rather than parsed into a DOM and serialized afresh. Options such as model and sampling settings belong in the separate options view, not ahead of the prompt where they would spoil a prefix comparison.

This is a local approximation, not access to a provider’s tokenizer or internal cache key. Compare the raw wire too. A prompt-only view cannot diagnose a changed routing option by itself.

Strip only genuine markers

The moving stable-end marker changes location as history grows. Comparing it as conversation content would report a changed prefix on a healthy request. The comparison therefore strips genuine provider cache_control fields while the actual wire remains untouched.

Do not recursively delete every property named cache_control. A user’s tool argument or JSON schema may legitimately use that name. CacheBytes.cs walks tokens with their structural paths, identifies legal provider marker locations, and copies the untouched byte spans. It handles the adjacent commas without normalizing escaped text, whitespace, key order or number spelling.

The first-edition account describes a useful failure here. Its initial strip matched one compact spelling of a marker, while the actual formatter inserted spaces. Hand-built compact fixtures agreed with the broken implementation. A fixture built by the actual formatter exposed the mistake. Those historical measurements are not results from this C# implementation; the lesson survives: test the artifact the application produces, not a convenient imitation.

Keep each prediction with its request

The lens lock serializes capture rotation, comparison and file writes, not HTTP. More importantly, the predicted fraction travels as an immutable value with the exchange that produced it. A late response cannot consult a shared “latest prediction” and borrow a newer request’s result.

The actor normally serializes its turn decisions, but Engine also has direct callers, and asynchronous completion deserves its own identity. Merely locking one mutable latest value fixes a data race without fixing attribution.

A capture failure is a diagnostic failure, not an inference failure. An unwritable directory or malformed caller-supplied request disables that capture and logs the problem without changing the bytes sent or inventing a cache measurement. The files are a debugging instrument, not a transactional archive; inspect reported capture failures before treating a pair as complete.

§15.4 Mark the final projection

Marker placement belongs in disposable provider JSON. It must not mutate History, skill snapshots, tool definitions or provenance-bearing parts.

The order of work matters:

  1. Render the frozen Context and its allowed declarations.
  2. Complete provider-specific tool-call/result adjacency and turn merging.
  3. Retain the distinction between stable blocks and request-only ephemera.
  4. Choose legal boundaries in that final shape.

Selecting a marker on the last neutral Context entry before rendering can be wrong: the provider adapter may move a result next to its call or merge user turns. Likewise, the final user message can contain both stable text and transient ephemera. Message position alone does not identify a stable block.

Anthropic: explicit opt-in, at most four boundaries

Configuration accepts cacheBreakpoints: true. It is off by default; neither a model-name prefix nor a test fake establishes support. The C# renderer may mark:

  1. The last non-deferred tool declaration, if one exists.
  2. Nonempty SYSTEM instructions.
  3. The surviving marked handoff note, if present.
  4. The last legal stable conversation block before transient ephemera.

Coincident boundaries collapse. Missing content does not require placeholder text merely to use four slots. Empty text, thinking and unknown opaque blocks are not explicit targets. A tool declaration with defer_loading: true must not receive cache_control; if all declarations are deferred, omit that boundary rather than choosing an illegal one.

The Anthropic prompt-caching guide and tool-search guide are the primary references checked for this implementation. Check the current selected model and route before live use. No TTL is sent here: the marker uses the documented default, not a client promise of retention.

The tool boundary remains useful when SYSTEM changes: an earlier tool prefix can still be reusable. The rolling history boundary covers more than the first user message; fixing it at the beginning would leave the growing conversation outside the intended boundary.

Chapter 9’s rule still holds: loaded manuals belong once in SYSTEM. A dynamic activation legitimately changes that instruction prefix. Do not move manuals into dialogue to conceal the change. Pending manuals remain SYSTEM instructions through Chapter 14 cuts, although their pending-only tool authority is revoked.

A handoff changes the working context, so an old suffix may cease to match. The marker describes retained bytes after the recorded reduction; it cannot keep removed tool traffic alive. This chapter implements the surviving handoff boundary, not a future memory-compaction policy.

OpenAI and Gemini: do not copy an analogy onto the wire

This endpoint uses OpenAI Chat Completions, not Responses. It retains implicit caching and optionally supplies prompt_cache_key, documented in the Chat Completions request reference. A routing key is not a breakpoint and is not a credential. Do not put secrets in it. Configuration refuses this option on a different provider.

The earlier manuscript describes experiments with prompt_cache_breakpoint and prompt_cache_options.mode. Those descriptions are historical records, not current API contracts verified for this C# route. This implementation does not emit them or turn off implicit caching by analogy with another provider.

Gemini retains its existing implicit path. No explicit cache object, TTL manager or cache registry is introduced. Its caching guide is a starting point for an authorized live experiment, not proof of a hit here.

Eligibility is separate from stability

Cache minimums belong to a particular model and route, and are measured in tokens. A 6,000-byte fixture does not establish a 1,024-token minimum. A fake can award reads to any prompt size. Zero reads can mean ineligibility, expiry, routing, changed content or another provider decision; do not pick a cause without evidence.

Earlier accounts compared fixed large references with rapidly growing history and got different warm-up behavior. A fixed-reference probe cannot refute a claim about growing history. Similarly, changing content encoding and removing a marker in one probe does not isolate either variable. These are lessons in controlled experiments, not universal cache thresholds or token-block rules.

§15.5 Count first, estimate second

Engine records usage exactly once for each successfully completed send, after its completed response facts have been produced. Plain and streaming requests share final-response decoding. Cumulative streaming updates are not added as separate purchases.

Parsing a fixture, rendering offline, replaying History, failed HTTP and cancelled exchanges do not advance this meter. A provider may charge for a request whose successful usage never reached the client. The GUI explicitly calls this a token-price estimate, not an authoritative account balance.

Four disjoint buckets

Usage retains nullable ordinary input, cache write, cache read and output counts. Missing required usage is unknown. Omitted optional cache buckets may be zero; malformed supplied values must not become reassuring zeroes.

Normalize before pricing:

  • Anthropic input/write/read buckets are disjoint.
  • OpenAI’s prompt total includes cached reads; subtract them to obtain ordinary input. The ordinary Chat Completions pricing fixture has no cache-write bucket.
  • Gemini’s prompt total includes cached reads. Its output accounting includes separately reported thinking without counting that thinking twice.

AllInput() sums the three disjoint input buckets. Unknown operands or overflow produce unknown, not wraparound. Session hit rate is:

session cache-read tokens / session ALL-input tokens

A zero or unknown denominator yields unknown. This differs from the lens’s byte-prefix fraction and from the latest response’s cache-read count.

The actual response identity owns the rate

UsageIdentity retains vendor, actual response model and service tier. Engine groups counts by that identity under one short lock. A later model or tier must not retroactively reprice earlier requests. Meter() captures latest and rows together; MeterSnapshot derives totals, hit rate and estimated dollars.

Prices are intentionally narrow. The implementation verified these standard text-token rows against the primary GPT-4o mini and GPT-4o pages:

Response model or documented snapshot Ordinary input Cached read Output
gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 $0.15 $0.075 $0.60
gpt-4o, gpt-4o-2024-08-06 $2.50 $1.25 $10.00

Amounts are USD per million tokens, with explicit response tier default only. A page can list a deprecated model: a price row is not availability evidence. Missing tier may imply project-level routing, so it is not silently standard. Unknown identity, a different tier, unknown counts or unverified cache-write charges make the estimate unknown. Other providers retain valid counts without invented prices. Update verified pricing deliberately, not by broad model-name matching or aliases invented to make fixtures pass.

The calculation uses decimal arithmetic at view time:

(input × input rate + cached reads × read rate + output × output rate)
/ 1,000,000

The general four-bucket formula also includes cache writes when a verified write rate exists. This table does not supply one; nonzero or unknown writes must not be treated as free. If any contributing session row is unpriced, the whole session estimate stays unknown rather than displaying a partial subtotal as its total cost.

§15.6 A GUI projection, not another meter

The header shows COST, ALL, CACHE and HITRATE:

  • COST: derived estimate for this Engine’s current process.
  • ALL: input total for its latest completed response.
  • CACHE: cache reads for that latest response.
  • HITRATE: the session ratio, including its cold first response.

Server/Meter.cs takes one coherent snapshot. The browser formats acknowledged values; it does not accumulate tokens or own a price table. Both connected clients receive the same projection. Refresh does not create usage. Periodic catch-up repairs missed observations, and a cached serialized frame suppresses identical notifications without becoming an accounting authority.

The published WebSocket shape is:

{
  "type": "usage",
  "agent_id": "root",
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 400000,
    "cache_write_tokens": 0,
    "cache_read_tokens": 600000,
    "output_tokens": 100000,
    "all_input": 1000000,
    "totals": {
      "input_tokens": 400000,
      "cache_write_tokens": 0,
      "cache_read_tokens": 600000,
      "output_tokens": 100000
    }
  },
  "total_cost_usd": 0.165,
  "hit_rate": 0.6
}

That example uses the mini/default price row. The display rounds its estimate to $0.17; the frame retains the more precise value. Unknown is JSON null and visible ?, never silently zero. Expanded details expose session counts and explain the estimate and restart limits without requiring hover alone.

Before any response, latest counts and hit rate are null, session counts are zero, and estimated spend is zero. A new Engine starts this way even after restoring a conversation. An HTTP error does not erase or advance its prior successful meter. Usage notifications are silent to the speech queue.

§15.7 Build, exercise and grade

From solutions/edition-3/main, with the approved SDK and owned offline environment:

dotnet run --project Tests/Tests.csproj
dotnet build Cli/Ch04.csproj
dotnet build Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj
dotnet run --project Examples/Cache/Cache.csproj -- /new/owned/cache-exercise

The separate Cache example uses only public library APIs. It runs two actual Agent turns against an owned loopback provider, checks exact captures and immutable snapshots, changes from a priced tier to an unpriced tier, restores saved conversation into a new empty meter, and destroys both directions of the lens relationship. It does not access a paid provider.

Both hosts accept:

Flag Environment fallback Meaning
--cache-lens DIR EN_CACHE_LENS_DIR Opt-in private capture directory
--cache-breakpoints EN_CACHE_BREAKPOINTS=1 Explicit Anthropic marker support
--prompt-cache-key KEY EN_PROMPT_CACHE_KEY OpenAI routing key

Explicit value flags override environment values. These are host configuration, not saved browser preferences. Missing values and a routing key on the wrong provider refuse startup. No flag establishes that a selected model accepts the request.

From the repository root, use the existing Go grader’s narrow C# adapter:

grade-edition2 -ch 15 -executable-only -json \
  -gui /absolute/path/to/built/Gui \
  -cache-prices .15,0,.075,.6 solutions/edition-3/main

Use the actual built GUI apphost, with its runtime dependencies and .NET root available, or an equivalent launcher. Unlike early chapters, -gui here names an executable, not static assets. The adapter creates owned workspaces, sends real /ws prompts, waits for completed turns, and joins SIGTERM shutdown. The original Go route and its historical defaults remain unchanged. In this C# invocation supply the shown exact mini/default fixture rates; the original defaults are not the C# pricing contract. The adapter uses the C# fixed lens filenames, not the Go route’s -cache-current/-cache-prior paths.

Check Points C# executable scope
cache-lens-exists 15 Current/prior full wire equal the actual sent bodies
prefix-is-stable 20 Unchanged tools and SYSTEM across a growing conversation
request-has-breakpoints 15 Legal Anthropic tool/SYSTEM/advancing stable-history markers
cost-is-computed-not-stored 15 Count-only events, independently priced OpenAI fixture, unknown model/tier
usage-is-session-scoped 10 Prior dialogue restored while new latest counts stay unknown and totals zero
cache-read-rate 10 Disjoint cold/warm fixture counts produce the expected session ratio
all-vendors-report-usage 15 Actual adapter requests and normalized final counts for all three providers

The marker session and priced session are deliberately separate. An unpriced Anthropic fixture must not acquire a fictional tariff merely because the historical grader combined those tests.

The marker grade has no handoff or ephemera. Focused component tests separately cover final adjacency, deferred declarations, empty instructions, retained handoffs and transient tails. Out-of-order completions, malformed/unknown usage, streaming, capture failures and ownership also need their own real-component checks. A numeric grade is not an architectural review.

Personally use the application

Run the GUI from a fresh owned workspace on a free loopback port, not a working user’s port or browser profile. Supply provider values as in earlier chapters; keep real credentials out of commands, source files and captures. For example, when an authorized Anthropic route has already been configured:

dotnet /absolute/path/to/Gui.dll --port 18085 \
  --cache-lens ./private-cache --cache-breakpoints

For an OpenAI route, omit --cache-breakpoints; optionally use --prompt-cache-key chapter15-owned-demo. For a fake, configure its loopback base URL and dummy key instead. Choose the actual model explicitly; the older manuscript’s model labels are not recommendations or availability checks.

Send two short questions with a genuinely stable reference between them. Wait for each completed turn. Inspect the header and expanded totals, then compare request.body against request.prev.body and the raw bodies. Check the provider’s usage rather than concluding that a plausible answer means a cache hit. With a real provider, first verify its current eligibility rules and use a small bounded authorized exercise.

Refresh and open a second owned tab: both must show the same meter without another request. Stop the owned host gracefully with Ctrl-C, then restart it in the same workspace. Conversation should return, but current-process latest usage and hit rate should be unknown and cost zero. No inference is required to restore the display. Do not use EOF as the GUI’s shutdown contract.

What this endpoint establishes

The preserved C# boundary has 99 passing component groups, a scoped executable 100/100, a separate public consumer, CLI flag/capture exercises, and owned GUI exercises using plain and SSE responses. Browser checks cover two clients, refresh, restart isolation, unknown pricing/counts, failed HTTP, speech silence and a 360-pixel-wide layout. DOM/geometry evidence is not pixel assessment or a human accessibility audit.

Live API testing was authorized, but no approved credential source was available in the test session. Thus no C# live-provider cache grant, billing, current model availability, native speech or human-accessibility result is claimed. Historical cache counts and dollar tables from previous implementations cannot fill that gap. Correct fake replies establish the client contract; only an authorized real exchange can establish what the real provider did.

The enduring lesson is not “the cache works.” It is that useful engineering keeps the wire, prediction, reported counts, estimated cost and evidence limits separate enough to diagnose when one of them is wrong.

Chapter 16: Leaving Anthropic for OpenAI

This chapter is about freedom. It is also about choosing how you pay.

I built this codebook on Anthropic’s models. Eighteen chapters of tools, steering and context management. Then Anthropic shipped Opus 5.5 with restrictions on changing the context behind retained thinking. My agent depends on removing stale context. I am not giving that up to use a newer model.

Protecting private reasoning matters. So does letting the person building an agent control what it sees. The migration tests whether the vendor seam can preserve that choice.

So we are voting with our feet. In this chapter the agent authenticates through your existing ChatGPT subscription. No separate API-key signup for that route. The subscription has its own permissions and limits; it is another funding source, not a promise of unlimited inference or a measured tenfold saving.

TL;DR — Specification Brief

Add OpenAI Responses and an explicit ChatGPT-plan funding mode without giving Agents copies of account credentials. One Credentials object belongs to the Ensemble root. An Engine reaches it through its Agent and asks for a fresh bearer immediately before sending. API-key billing remains a separate choice; a failed plan request never becomes an API charge.

Common declares the vocabulary and ownership. Auth implements protected storage, PKCE login, signed identity validation, renewal, discovery and sign-out. Engine implements Responses projection and streaming. CLI and GUI provide human account controls; neither is another credential store. History records ordinary conversation and compatible opaque replay data, not OAuth secrets.

The preserved reference endpoint has a scoped 70-point transport grade; signed local issuer tests separately exercise the credential owner. In the October 29, 2026 joint session, Bill completed real CLI login with Ensemble’s own registration. Account-specific model discovery and three plan-funded Responses calls succeeded through current main. Renewal, sign-out, GUI login and billing reconciliation were not exercised live. The cache result was zero reported reuse; see Chapter 23. These observations supplement, rather than expand, the earlier executable grade.

The coding brief

Extend the previous chapter’s C# solution; do not replace its actor, Jobs, History, meter or speech queue. Read the current primary protocol references in this chapter before attempting a live integration. Their changing service details are separate from the following ownership and safety contracts.

Ownership and authentication

  • Declare Credentials and immutable public account values in Common. Construct the store with its strong Ensemble parent; parent add/remove operations update both ends. Destroying the root joins Agents before destroying shared credentials. Destroy cancels and joins auth operations and detaches; it does not log out.
  • Use only an explicitly selected private directory. Never import another tool’s account, inspect its credential files, or place OAuth state in History, skills, logs, ordinary configuration or browser snapshots.
  • Implement authorization-code PKCE with random state, nonce and verifier, exact callback validation, and signed identity validation. A returned client ID is a registration, not proof of the user’s identity. Save it before consuming the one-use code; only a verified ID token can bind the subject.
  • Share one protected, versioned file and cross-process lock. Reread under the lock; serialize refresh through durable replacement. Refuse damaged data rather than interpreting it as an empty store. Keep accounts and registrations separate.
  • Renew near expiry and allow one same-funding-source recovery after inference HTTP 401. Reuse a newer durable grant if another owner already rotated it. Bound transient refresh retries; never automatically replay an uncertain authorization-code exchange. Clear local tokens on terminal grant rejection.
  • Distinguish local logout from remote sign-out. Clear locally before attempting revocation; report whether the provider confirmed it. Preserve registration and saved plan selection either way.

Transport, policy and presentation

  • Make Surface.Responses and BillingMode explicit immutable Configuration choices. Plan mode requires OpenAI Responses, streaming and an account label, with no API key. Keep existing provider/surface defaults for other callers.
  • Project tools, instructions and results from the existing vocabulary. Preserve exact call identity and compatible opaque reasoning; request encrypted reasoning for stateless replay. Unsupported media must refuse, not vanish.
  • Parse JSON and SSE. Require response.completed; failed/incomplete terminal events, unfinished fallback items and EOF without success cannot run tools. A nonempty terminal output wins. An empty one uses only completed streamed items.
  • Preserve real arrival order for tool explanation. The exact supported gpt-6-astra capability row requires ordinary visible text before tools; a reasoning summary is not an explanation. Refuse tool-first calls with paired results before effects, even if later terminal text is reordered ahead of them.
  • Keep reasoning effort and summary policy per Agent. The supported row defaults to medium/auto; efforts are low, medium, high, xhigh, max. Explicit off omits summary requests. Do not infer capabilities or prices from a name.
  • Display returned summaries separately, stream them incrementally, and admit final-only suffixes once to the existing speech queue. Replay is silent. Browser projection must never expose encrypted reasoning. Expected plan-authorization refusal records one durable error for narration, not duplicate turn-end speech.
  • Discover visible plan models through the credential owner, retaining server order. A catalog entry establishes neither renderer support nor price. CLI model flags/environment bypass discovery; the GUI catalog is read-only, not a picker.
  • Announce model and funding source before inference. Successful login atomically saves the future plan choice; explicit launch overrides do not rewrite it. Never change a running Agent’s model/account/billing after account management.
  • Keep plan token counts, but do not apply API-dollar estimates to them. Use only supported cache fields: this endpoint supports an optional OpenAI prompt_cache_key, not the historical explicit-cache extensions discussed in earlier development records. Preserve Anthropic/Gemini behavior.

Test real owners, files, sockets, processes and host lifecycles with working boundary fakes. Keep local component evidence, executable evidence, live provider proof and audible/human-accessibility evaluation distinct.

The idea in plain words

An encrypted reasoning block looks safe to store or share because its owner cannot read it. But the provider’s model can. If another model accepts the same block, the encryption has not established who may ask for its contents. That distinction made a seemingly opaque artifact a source of leaked secrets.

In August 2026, researchers demonstrated the consequence. They replayed a frontier model’s encrypted reasoning into a cheaper model behind a jailbreak prompt, and the decoder treated the replayed block as its own prior thinking and decoded it. From 6,708 public agent trajectories, they extracted 315,320 reasoning blocks. The genuine user sessions contained 62 distinct API keys, 33 passwords, 24 access tokens and 7 private keys; 64 of the 704 recovered artifacts were absent from visible chat history. These are the researchers’ findings, not an invitation to test recovered credentials. The original account’s $720 figure describes the paper’s estimated cost for a separate 10,000-trace example, not the measured cost of this extraction. (Panfilov et al., August 2026, §§3.1 and 4.1.)

Binding a reasoning artifact to its authorized context is one way to close that gap. OpenAI’s September 30 report says it strengthened protections across users, workspaces, organizations and model families, closed a replay pathway, and added output checks. That report establishes the mitigation it describes; it does not disclose enough implementation detail to call it exactly the paper’s proposed cryptographic design. (OpenAI’s incident report.)

Anthropic’s preserved-thinking policy creates a different integration constraint. The Opus 5.5 launch applied it to that model and Fable 5.1 for API accounts created on or after August 31, 2026. The current documentation, checked October 11, ties retained thinking to the prefix against which it was produced. Changing earlier messages or tool results can invalidate later thinking. It also documents server-side editing and client-side compaction that discards stale thinking, so “no compaction at all” would be the wrong criticism. The conflict is with keeping those artifacts while independently editing the earlier context. (Launch policy, preserved-thinking rules.)

Several chapters depend on owning that editing policy: Chapter 2’s ephemera, the changing GUI and speech views in Chapters 12–13, the cuts in Chapter 14, the later memory in Chapter 21, and Chapter 22’s recorded recall attachments, which survive until a checkpoint. They do not all have the same lifetime. They do share the ability to stop sending material without asking a provider to make the cut. Beyond this codebook, any agent that needs to see its current state ephemerally is affected by such a constraint: a family assistant tracking a conversation, a virtual tabletop tracking game state, an accessibility tool streaming its reasoning to a developer who cannot see the screen.

Protecting hidden reasoning is a legitimate requirement. So is choosing a service compatible with the context policy the agent already implements. This exercise takes the latter route instead of designing a new policy around preserved thinking. Current Anthropic examples elsewhere in this edition stay on supported older models such as Sonnet 5; a newer catalog entry is not proof that the existing ephemeral-context behavior works with it.

This chapter migrates the agent to OpenAI. The vendor seam built in Chapter 2 and tested in Chapter 15 against three providers now faces the migration that motivated the first-edition account. The investment in the agent depends on the answer: if the seam works as designed, this is a refactor. If it was aspirational, this is a rewrite.

It is a refactor.

The credential seam

There is no AuthProvider interface, copied service bag or host-held bearer cache. The concrete path is:

Engine → Agent → Ensemble → Credentials

Common/Auth.cs, AuthProtocol.cs and AuthLogin.cs declare the shared types, persistent fields and partial operations. Their implementations live in Auth in the same assembly. For example, the public declarations include:

public partial Credentials(Ensemble parent, string directory);
public partial Task<string?> SelectedPlanAccountAsync(
    CancellationToken cancellation = default);
public partial Task<string> GetBearerTokenAsync(
    string label, CancellationToken cancellation = default);
public partial void Destroy();

These are declarations from the partial owner, not a separate interface to inject into Engines. new Credentials(app, directory) registers with the real parent. Ensemble.RemoveCredentials clears the reverse link itself. Public AuthAccount and PlanModel records are explicitly value-like snapshots; they contain no access, refresh or ID tokens and need no holder back-pointers.

Engine.SendAsync renders without credentials, then resolves the selected bearer through the parent path immediately before HTTP. Token acquisition failure has a fixed safe error. An actual plan HTTP 401 permits exactly one retry of the same request bytes. The internal rejected-bearer operation compares that exact bearer under the file lock, so a delayed 401 cannot unnecessarily rotate a newer grant. API-key requests never enter this path. Other statuses and interrupted successful streams do not trigger an inference retry.

The Engine still owns wire exchange and its process meter; the actor still owns durable admission, tool effects and History. A successful retry yields one completed response and one meter update, not two conversational turns.

One protected store, not copied account state

The C# implementation uses credentials.json beside credentials.lock in the explicit directory. It requires private Unix permissions and refuses unsupported storage-policy platforms. Version 2 stores a nullable selected_plan_account, installation identity, and account registrations/grants. Version 1 remains readable as having no saved selection. A read does not silently migrate the file.

The decoder validates the entire candidate, including unique labels, registration identity, dates, token completeness and selected-label membership. A damaged file is an error, not a successful empty login. The local operation gate coordinates one owner; the file lock coordinates processes. Each writer rereads the file under that lock, writes a private temporary file, then replaces the primary before publishing success. This is atomic replacement, not a hardware power-loss/fsync guarantee.

The file is the authoritative credential and selection state. The owner retains only an active login attempt and lifecycle resources, not a second token cache. Refresh, registration updates and logout preserve the selected label; successful login changes it in the same write as the validated grant. Matching email strings do not authorize registration sharing.

Credentials are private, but they are not hidden from the person operating the application. The user controls the store and may clear it. Ordinary snapshots and saved Agent configuration deliberately omit it.

OAuth from first principles

A distributed local application cannot hide a shared client secret. A web server can keep one on its backend, but a binary running on the user’s machine can be decompiled, inspected, and copied. Authorization Code with PKCE solves this: instead of proving you possess a long-lived secret, you prove that the app finishing the flow is the same app that started it.

The mechanism is a verifier and a challenge. Before redirecting the user to the authorization server, the agent generates 32 random bytes, base64url-encodes them without padding as the verifier, and hashes that verifier string with SHA-256. The base64url-encoded digest goes in the authorization request; the verifier goes in the token exchange. The server checks the same transformation. An attacker who intercepts the code still needs the verifier, which is sent only in the token exchange.

The agent binds a TCP socket to 127.0.0.1 on any available port, with the path /auth/callback. The host must be the literal 127.0.0.1; the OpenAI documentation says “Do not substitute with localhost.” The path must be exactly /auth/callback; their documentation says “/callback does not match /auth/callback.” Only the port may vary. For the duration of login, the host becomes a small callback server. A tool-calling application that reads files and runs processes now also listens on a socket and serves the browser callback.

The authorization request includes several things that matter beyond PKCE. A state parameter prevents cross-site request forgery: the agent generates a random value, sends it in the request, and rejects any callback that returns a different one. A nonce prevents replay: it is embedded in the returned ID token and validated on receipt. A stable ext_agent_host_id identifies the installation. An RFC 8707 resource parameter (https://api.openai.com/v1) appears on the authorization request and is repeated at code exchange.

On first registration, the client_id is the bootstrap value dynamic_agent_client. The authorization callback returns an issued client_id alongside the authorization code and state. Persist the issued ID before exchanging the code. All subsequent requests for that registration use it. A returning callback may omit the ID; if it supplies a different one, reject it.

The course flow uses this callback-based registration rather than a separate RFC 7591 registration request. The bootstrap dynamic_agent_client is never valid for token exchange. Send agent_name_hint=Ensemble on first registration and omit it when reauthorizing. The requested scopes include identity, offline access, resource.invoke and chatgpt.tokens.use.direct. These small fields are part of the protocol, not labels to improvise. (Registration and sign-in.)

The C# library returns the private authorization URL; it does not launch a browser. CLI auth login binds an owned listener first, prints the URL in the dedicated local command, and waits with bounded cancellation and cleanup. The GUI uses a user-opened separate sign-in window. The URL never enters the main DOM, WebSocket transcript, or model context: it may contain an ID-token hint. A blocked popup fails before login starts.

An unsolicited wrong-state callback does not consume the active attempt. A matched denial or failed exchange does. Callback pages contain no codes, state, URL, or account information. The listener may therefore serve more than one request before the valid callback finishes the attempt; it is not a one-request server. Hosts ask the owner whether the attempt remains pending instead of copying its mutable state.

Persist the issued client ID before exchanging the one-use code. Failed exchange leaves a pending registration with no subject or tokens, ready for a later login. Only the signed, validated identity binds the subject. Do not automatically retry an uncertain code exchange. A changed registration from another process invalidates the pending attempt. There is no implemented /complete headless redirect; use the documented local loopback flow rather than inventing one.

Identity is not permission

A successful login proves who the user is. It does not prove the user has granted plan usage. Two separate checks are required, and both must pass before inference.

The token exchange returns three tokens: an access token for API calls, a refresh token for renewal, and an ID token for identity. The ID token is a signed JWT. Validating it requires fetching OpenAI’s published JWKS (JSON Web Key Set), verifying the signature against those keys, and then checking the identity claims: issuer exactly matches the trusted https://auth.openai.com URL, audience matches the issued client_id, the token has not expired, and the nonce matches the one sent in the authorization request. The sub claim is the stable account identity. Keep the issued client ID with it: the same email, or the same person in another workspace registration, is not a reason to merge token sets. A returning verified identity must match the account being renewed before replacing its credentials.

The second check is the granted scope. The token response includes a list of scopes the user authorized. Among them, chatgpt.tokens.use.direct means plan-usage inference is permitted. Without it, identity may be saved, but plan inference remains disabled. Refuse that request rather than quietly trying an API key. Login and permission to spend are separate results.

The discovery document inspected during the original implementation listed scopes_supported as openid, profile, email, and offline_access. It did not advertise the plan-usage scope. The missing catalog entry did not make the scope optional. A developer implementing against the discovery document alone will build a login that works and an agent that cannot infer. Inspect the token response itself for the granted scopes. The current sign-in contract likewise makes that grant a separate inference gate.

The C# validator is deliberately narrow RS256, using .NET RSA/SHA-256 rather than a general JWT framework. It rejects ambiguous JSON/key selection and checks audience, authorized party, timestamps, nonce and subject continuity; a supplied access-token hash must also match. A decoded JWT is not a verified identity. The tests sign genuine local RSA tokens and exercise refusals, but do not prove that a real account can complete this flow.

Tokens that expire

The access token is valid for about one hour. The refresh token is valid for about thirty days. Those are the documented lifetimes on October 11, not constants to substitute for the returned expiry. The agent tracks the expiry and refreshes proactively: when the current time passes five minutes before expires_at, the agent sends a refresh request before the next inference call.

Refresh-token rotation is a security feature that punishes mistakes. Each refresh response returns a new access token and a new refresh token. The old refresh token is dead the instant the server issues the replacement. If two threads both see an expired access token and both attempt to refresh, the first one succeeds and the second one submits a dead token. The server treats that as a potential replay attack and may invalidate both tokens.

The fix is mechanical: serialize credential updates. The C# owner serializes local operations across its shared store; two processes using that file also coordinate through its file lock. The owner locks and reloads the store before deciding whether to refresh. A second request uses the replacement already saved by the first instead of rotating the old token again. Save both new tokens atomically before using either of them. If the process crashes between receiving the tokens and persisting them, the old refresh token is already dead and the new one is lost. Atomic persistence means writing a temporary file and renaming it, or using a transaction. Writing two fields in sequence can leave an unusable mixed profile. Atomic replacement prevents that partial local state; it cannot recover a new token lost between server-side rotation and local persistence. (Token lifetimes, refresh and storage.)

Six refresh errors are terminal: invalid_grant, invalid_refresh_token, token_expired, refresh_token_expired, refresh_token_invalidated, and refresh_token_reused. Any of these means the credential is unusable. Keep the issued client_id and host ID, discard the tokens, and re-authenticate from scratch. The user signs in again, but the agent remembers who it is.

Network errors and HTTP 5xx are transient. The C# refresh path makes at most three attempts with bounded exponential backoff. The critical distinction: a terminal error is the server saying the credential is dead. A transient exchange failure does not establish that: a reachable server can return a temporary error too. Retain the stored credentials. A 401 on inference alone does not establish revoked refresh credentials; this implementation attempts renewal once through the same funding source, and clears tokens only after a terminal refresh rejection. (Error recovery.)

After an inference HTTP 401, Engine asks Credentials about the exact rejected bearer. Under the existing lock, the owner reuses a newer valid grant if another process already rotated it, or refreshes the rejected token. Engine retries the same request body once. A second 401 ends the exchange. API-key requests, quota errors, and failed or interrupted streams do not enter this recovery path. Only the successful completed response contributes to the Engine meter.

LogoutAsync clears local tokens and retains registration, host identity and saved plan selection. SignOutAsync clears locally before attempting remote revocation, then reports whether revocation was confirmed. A network failure cannot undo local logout. Destroying Credentials is different again: cancel and join operations, dispose HTTP resources and detach from Ensemble, without logging the account out.

The Responses API

Chat Completions, Responses and funding are separate choices. Existing OpenAI callers keep Chat Completions unless they select Responses or an explicitly Responses-only model row. API-key mode can use Responses too. Plan mode validates OpenAI + Responses + streaming + nonempty account, rejects an API key, and uses a redirect-disabled client with HTTPS endpoints except literal loopback HTTP tests.

The exact gpt-6-astra row is explicit capability data, not a model-name pattern. It selects Responses, streaming, application reasoning defaults medium/auto, and ordinary explanation before tools. It does not establish account availability, media support or an API price. --reasoning-effort and --reasoning-summary override their OPENAI_REASONING_* environment values; each Agent freezes its own Configuration. Unsupported explicit values refuse before HTTP. off omits the summary request. Other models do not inherit these settings by guesswork.

References: model documentation and reasoning guide.

Projection uses the existing vocabulary

Engine/Responses.cs projects text, tool calls, tool results and compatible opaque items from Context. Shared final rendering combines primary and skill instructions once; it does not create a second manual store. Human text is a user message, ordinary assistant text is an assistant message, and system-like input uses the developer role. The top-level instructions field is also supported; the current plan limitations allow instructions or developer messages, contrary to an older grader’s blanket prohibition.

For plan tools, the final projection uses a named namespace:

{
  "model": "gpt-6-astra",
  "instructions": "Explain tool actions before calling them.",
  "input": [
    {"type": "message", "role": "user", "content": [
      {"type": "input_text", "text": "Inspect the requested file."}
    ]}
  ],
  "tools": [{
    "type": "namespace",
    "name": "ensemble",
    "description": "Ensemble tools",
    "tools": [{
      "type": "function",
      "name": "read_file",
      "description": "Read text from a file",
      "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"path": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["path"]
      }
    }]
  }],
  "include": ["reasoning.encrypted_content"],
  "reasoning": {"effort": "medium", "summary": "auto"},
  "store": false,
  "stream": true
}

This illustrates the shape, not the complete installed tool catalog. A returned function call retains its native item and call ID. A function_call_output uses that same call ID; the actor’s ordinary result becomes its output text. Compatible opaque reasoning replays with exact surface/model provenance. It is neither assistant prose nor a tool result. A billing switch adjusts the disposable tool namespace rather than mutating History. Blob/media projection currently refuses explicitly; documented provider media support does not make our renderer support it.

Streaming progress is not execution authority

The SSE reader tracks output indices, completed items, displayed text and stable part IDs in request-local assembly state. Deltas can update the page immediately. Only a successful response.completed can finalize a response. When its output is nonempty it is authoritative; when empty, only completed item-done values may supply the fallback. Added skeletons and unfinished argument deltas are not facts. Failed/incomplete terminal events and missing terminal success refuse tools.

Explanation policy uses actual SSE arrival order, not reordered terminal output. A completed visible message can explain a subsequent tool even without deltas; a summary cannot. Tool-first responses get paired refusals through the normal actor, with no ToolStarted or effect. A later model request can consume those refusals normally.

The GUI projects summary_text to distinct collapsed Reasoning summary cards. Encrypted reasoning remains only in canonical compatible replay data. The existing per-part speech cursor admits incremental text and final-only suffixes once; reconnect/replay is silent. These are public summaries, not a private reasoning trace and not a promise that the provider always returns a summary.

Keep usage and price separate

Responses usage maps cached input into the existing disjoint count buckets. Missing or malformed required counts remain unknown; an omitted optional cache count is zero. The Engine meter distinguishes billing mode, so plan usage never receives an API-dollar estimate. Unknown models/tiers keep valid counts without invented rates. Historical preview price tables are not production pricing authority.

The supported optional OpenAI cache-routing field is prompt_cache_key. Historical cache_control, prompt_cache_retain and prompt_cache_min_tokens experiments are not implemented as Responses guarantees. The executable exercise checks configured API routing and default plan omission; it does not infer a provider prohibition or live cache hit from that difference.

The stream that had already finished its tool call

In the historical implementation, after removing an unsupported cache option, the subscription request reached the model and still failed. The body contained SSE, but the parser selected its whole-JSON branch. Fixing that decision exposed the second assumption: a completed read_file item had already arrived in response.output_item.done, while the terminal response.completed carried an empty output array.

The parser needs both parts of the protocol. Detect the stream without waiting to buffer its entire body, retain completed items by output index, and use them when terminal output is empty. A nonempty terminal output remains authoritative. In either case, terminal success must arrive before those items become conversation facts or executable tool calls. Usage may remain unknown; it is not an execution gate. The fact that a tool’s arguments have streamed is no permission to execute a response that subsequently fails.

That captured stream made both defects reproducible without another model call. In the C# run, a headerless loopback stream separately exposed the same dispatch assumption; the scoped executable grade verifies the correction without another provider call. A parser test that always repeats every completed item in the terminal array cannot expose the second defect. The real route had done less repetition than the fake, which was enough to lose a perfectly good tool call.

Reasoning summaries

Reasoning summaries are model-generated descriptions of private thinking, streamed separately from the assistant’s visible answer. They are not the private trace itself. Earlier adapters already distinguished displayable thinking from opaque replay material; Responses needs the same distinction. Preserve encrypted reasoning for compatible replay without reading or speaking its ciphertext.

Bill has no macular vision and reads code at about 80 words per minute. He listens to model output at about five times speaking rate. A reasoning summary that arrives as a single paragraph after the answer has lost its chance to help him intervene. The value is in the delta: hearing the model think one phrase at a time while the answer is still forming, and sending a hint to redirect the model before it finishes the wrong approach. This is the accessibility payoff for the entire migration.

The first-edition coder treated the reasoning-summary gate as a research question before any code was written. Live measurement against gpt-6.1-sol with reasoning.summary: "detailed" and effort set to high produced 314 summary deltas across 3 parts. The auto setting produced 186 deltas. The concise setting produced 4. Summaries stream, they produce enough content for real-time listening, and the variation across settings is large enough to warrant a configuration knob.

The first probe returned zero summary deltas and looked like a capability gap. The prompt was trivial and generated 18 reasoning tokens. The coder suspected there had been too little reasoning to summarize. A single sample nearly produced a “this does not work” report. Measure with a prompt that makes the model think.

That October 2 report is evidence of those probes, not a promise about every response. In the later student run, the API-key session produced 90 public-summary deltas. The subscription session requested detailed and used 165 reasoning tokens on its final response, yet returned no public summary at all. More reasoning is not a guarantee of a summary. Completion and shutdown must not depend on hearing one.

The observer receives summary events through the existing observation interface. Summary deltas have a distinct kind in that existing path, separate from assistant-text deltas. They are delivered incrementally, kept separate from the assistant’s visible text, and preserved when a tool call is adjacent. A response that interleaves reasoning, tool calls, and assistant text must emit every event in stream order. The existing part identities keep the streams associated with their finals. The GUI can feed summary phrases to the speech queue while the response continues, without merging them into the answer or speaking the encrypted item that accompanies them.

The selected C# row supports auto and explicit off, not the historical detailed/concise choices above. A final may include text beyond its delivered deltas: admit that suffix once through the existing per-part speech cursor. Replay remains silent. Local transcript tests prove queue admission, not hearing. Reasoning summaries do not satisfy the selected model’s ordinary pre-tool explanation requirement; that is Ensemble admission policy, not a provider promise.

Funding selection and account controls

Funding is consent, not fallback order

The implementation has two funding modes: api and chatgpt. It deliberately has no “try plan, then spend API credits” mode. An expired grant, denied permission, quota refusal, server error or network failure does not change the chosen payer. A plan HTTP 401 can renew and retry once against the same source; that is not payment fallback.

Only an explicitly supplied --credentials-dir / EN_CREDENTIALS_DIR is consulted. Successful login saves the selected plan label atomically with the grant. On a later launch, absent billing selection uses that saved choice; absent account selection uses its label. Plan launches default to OpenAI Responses only when those choices were not explicitly supplied. An incompatible explicit choice refuses. An explicit --billing api or EN_BILLING=api overrides the launch without rewriting the saved plan choice. Flags override their environment settings.

Logout leaves plan selected. A signed-out next launch therefore refuses before inference instead of discovering an ambient API key and charging it. A damaged selection file also refuses. Identity-only login saves the choice too, but does not grant inference permission. A running GUI Agent never changes its immutable funding, model or account after account-management operations.

Before inference, CLI stderr and the GUI’s visible funding banner identify the model and API metering or selected plan label. The GUI uses its existing usage frame, so reconnect shows the same running configuration. This description is not a token, provider instruction or new accounting store.

Human commands, not model tools

From the C# endpoint directory, the standalone commands are:

dotnet run --project Cli/Ch04.csproj -- --credentials-dir /private/path/auth auth status
dotnet run --project Cli/Ch04.csproj -- --credentials-dir /private/path/auth --account work auth models
dotnet run --project Cli/Ch04.csproj -- --credentials-dir /private/path/auth --account work auth login
