  2. Measure a real compression, not just a fake response. With an approved provider configuration, compress a varied technical session. Compare UTF-8 input/output bytes and measured token usage. Read the result for decisions, reasons, failed approaches, attribution and unfinished work. A reduction ratio alone is not a quality score.

  3. Prove a transaction boundary. Hold an owned fake compressor after launch. Verify that the old source still appears in a main request. Let it submit, then verify that matching population removes exactly the selected source and installs the replacement. Repeat with failed output and a selected-file edit; neither may lose source.

  4. Recover an interrupted commit. In an isolated fixture, stop after replay population but before all file retirements. Restart from the retained files. Require matching receipt validation, eventual promotion/retirement, no duplicate population and no imported replay cost. Do not delete a receipt to make recovery “pass.”

  5. Test fresh re-enable. Disable SOUL and wait for acknowledgment. Edit SOUL.md, re-enable it and wait again. Inspect the next actual request for the new bytes as user/data, not system instructions. Then disable it, restart, and verify it stays absent from the first request.

  6. Test a real pressure boundary. Use a model row with a known window and provider-correct usage categories. Establish 90% warning and 95% enforcement. Test a later usage-less response, an unauthorized micro_handoff, a pending compressor failure and a direct Engine send that must not replace actor occupancy. Keep unknown-model behavior as a separate control.

  7. Compare recall across the waterfall. Plant a specific but ordinary fact in session files, graduate through both archive bands into MEMORY, then start with only live corpus Markdown. Check the first request as well as the eventual answer. A model can guess a plausible answer without having received the memory.

  8. Review the ownership path. Trace shutdown during an active compressor. Identify which parent closes admission, which task is joined, when usage is imported, how the child detaches, and when Sandbox closes. Do not replace this exercise with a count of passing tests.

Take It for a Spin

Begin with the offline tests. From the repository root, use an already installed .NET 10 SDK:

cd solutions/edition-3/main

dotnet build Tests/Tests.csproj
dotnet run --project Tests/Tests.csproj --no-build -- --memory-band-tests
dotnet run --project Tests/Tests.csproj --no-build -- --memory-worker-tests
dotnet run --project Tests/Tests.csproj --no-build -- --memory-runtime-tests
dotnet run --project Tests/Tests.csproj --no-build -- --memory-accounting-tests
dotnet run --project Tests/Tests.csproj --no-build -- --memory-pressure-tests
dotnet run --project Tests/Tests.csproj --no-build -- --memory-settings-tests

These use owned local boundaries. They make no claim about a live provider’s compression quality or caching. Other selectors in Tests/Program.cs cover disk, replay and startup; read their scope rather than assuming every selector runs the whole suite.

For a manual GUI exercise, keep a separate home and port. Do not point the exercise at a working Agent’s directory. The example below seeds one unmistakable SOUL value before the first actor scan:

# Continue from solutions/edition-3/main.
export EN_DATA_DIR="$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/ensemble-memory.XXXXXX")"
export EN_AGENT_NAME=root
mkdir -p "$EN_DATA_DIR/agents/root"
printf '%s\n' 'Workshop marker: cobalt heron 731.' \
  > "$EN_DATA_DIR/agents/root/SOUL.md"

export EN_SKILLS_DIR="$EN_DATA_DIR/skills"
export EN_PRIMARY_SKILL=memory-exercise
mkdir -p "$EN_SKILLS_DIR/memory-exercise"
cat > "$EN_SKILLS_DIR/memory-exercise/SKILL.md" <<'SKILL'
---
name: memory-exercise
type: primary
description: Analyze supplied cases and retain useful checkpoint memories
tools: micro_handoff read_file write_file list_directory
---
Analyze only the supplied task. Preserve facts, decisions and reasons, failed
approaches, constraints and open questions in checkpoints. Explain before tools.
Enabled tools:
$TOOLS
SKILL

dotnet build Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj
# Choose an unused loopback port; this example does not use the working host's 8088.
dotnet run --project Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj --no-build -- --port 8097

Before launching, explicitly choose your intended model, route, funding and existing authorized credential source using the host options from Chapters 16 and 20. Do not paste tokens into the book, logs or conversation. Starting a local page does not establish that inference is configured. The chapter’s verification used local fake providers; a real-provider exercise spends real usage and remains a separate test.

Open the printed loopback URL in a separate browser profile. In Memory settings, reload the current acknowledged values. Disable SOUL and save. Inspect the Agent-local settings.json and wait for the application acknowledgment, not just a changed checkbox. Edit the marker while disabled, re-enable and save, then send a small prompt. Inspect the actual request through an explicitly enabled, protected diagnostic capture; it should contain the edited marker in data, not privileged instructions. Such captures can contain conversation content—keep them private and disable them when done.

For a small waterfall exercise, reduce conversation and session thresholds in that isolated Agent, keep the session destination enabled, and use a primary skill that grants micro_handoff. Work through several complete turns, then ask for a handoff. A first handoff may have nothing eligible; small inputs may never exceed the threshold. Watch the worker child and wait for its terminal outcome rather than expecting a file after a fixed sleep.

The historical trials used these two bounded cases. Send each separately and let the main turn finish; do not mistake that for the child’s completion. They test rejected approaches and unresolved questions, not just fact strings:

This is a bounded memory exercise in an empty scratch workspace. Do not use filesystem or command tools. Analyze the supplied case, explain the decision briefly, then call micro_handoff exactly once with the important facts and reasons. After the tool returns, finish this turn without another tool call. Case one: Our project is Cedar Lantern, release code CL-721. We rejected automatic deletion of imported notes because the support team needs the originals when customers report mistakes. The replacement design keeps source notes in an archive and stores the accepted summary separately. Morgan owns the archive review, scheduled for October 18. Acceptance requires preserving a source identifier with each summary. The unresolved question is whether attachments belong in the same archive or a separate one; do not claim that has been decided. The default retention is thirty days. A failed summarization must leave the original note available. The initial approach coupled cleanup to request arrival, so an unrelated request could delete unreviewed work. We moved cleanup to an explicit completed-review boundary instead. Explain why the latter boundary matters, and preserve these facts in your checkpoint.
This is a bounded memory exercise in an empty scratch workspace. Do not use filesystem or command tools. Analyze the supplied case, explain the decision briefly, then call micro_handoff exactly once with the important facts and reasons. After the tool returns, finish this turn without another tool call. Case two: The deployment rehearsal uses Harbor Finch, diagnostic tag HF-934. Priya owns the rehearsal scheduled for October 21. We rejected retrying a database migration automatically after a timeout: the remote operation may already have committed. The chosen procedure reads the migration ledger before deciding whether any retry is safe. The operator must retain the exact migration identifier and measured error, not a guess about success. We have not settled whether the ledger should live alongside application data or in a separate control database. The rollback package must remain available for seven days after deployment. Last week a log line said the worker stopped, but the child process was still alive and held the port open. The rehearsal now checks the child lifetime directly. Explain how this evidence changes the decision and checkpoint the completed analysis, preserving the unresolved question as unresolved.

After the relevant committed outcomes and any graduation, ask without tools for both names, codes, owners, dates, rejected approaches and reasons, explicitly preserving the two unresolved questions. Compare the answer with the outgoing request and corpus. If a fact was present but the answer omitted it, that differs from losing it during compression. A checkpoint while a child is outstanding does not start a second child; after completion, checkpoint remaining work if needed.

While a child is visibly running below the context limit, try a short unrelated question. A reply before the memory outcome demonstrates overlap. A child that finishes too quickly leaves responsiveness unobserved; do not manufacture a timing conclusion.

Inspect without changing the state:

find "$EN_DATA_DIR/agents/root/memory" \
     "$EN_DATA_DIR/agents/root/bucket-0" \
     "$EN_DATA_DIR/agents/root/bucket-1" -type f -print
# Some directories do not exist until first use; that is not a failed scan.

Read the live Markdown, the worker’s children/compress-*/events.jsonl, and the parent events if event logging was enabled. Distinguish a launch, matching population, successful terminal outcome and retained failed attempt. .retired source files are not active memories. The canonical archive preserves the original material even when the request projection no longer sends it.

Finally, stop this owned host cleanly and restart it with the same explicit EN_DATA_DIR and launch configuration. Confirm the acknowledged settings and first request, not just the continued existence of Markdown files. To test corpus-only recovery separately, copy only live SOUL/MEMORY/session/archive Markdown into another fresh home; do not copy saves, receipts, retired files or child submissions.

The point is not to accumulate files. It is to show that a useful account survives a smaller working context, remains inspectable, and never makes an unfinished or failed operation look complete.

Previous: Chapter 20: Managing the Swarm Next: Chapter 22: Auto-Recall

Chapter 22: Auto-Recall

Chapter 21 built a memory system. The agent can save, compress, and graduate memories through a cascade of bands. Enabled bands already put recent memories in context. Older originals and unloaded material remain on disk, organized and budgeted, until something brings them back. The agent can still repeat a rejected decision because the explanation is sitting in an archive it never thought to open.

For that older material, the agent has a filing cabinet without a habit of opening it.

In the spring of 2026, I had a coding agent with a full memory cascade and a search_knowledge tool. It was episodically brilliant: when it searched, it found the right thing. But it almost never searched. Every session started cold. It would re-derive decisions we had already made, re-investigate bugs we had already fixed, and propose architectures we had already rejected. The knowledge was there. The recall was not.

The fix was embarrassingly simple. Before every user message reaches the model, run a keyword search over the memory files, filter the results through a cheap model, and attach the survivors to the conversation. The agent never asks for the memories. They arrive the way a relevant fact arrives when a colleague mentions a project name: unbidden, fast, and usually right.

The improvement was immediate in my daily use. The agent went from a goldfish that kept meticulous diaries to a collaborator with a past.

The daily-use observations and tuning history in this chapter come from that earlier system, not fresh C# measurements. The C# evidence in §22.9 covers local component and application behavior and a scoped executable rubric; it does not establish live-provider relevance, entitlement, OAuth, billing, native Linux, audible speech, or human accessibility.

§22.0 — TL;DR — The Prompt

You are building a C# coding agent that can use tools and skills. Chapters 1–21 provided durable History, an actor-owned scheduler, and transactional long-term memory. Now implement automatic local recall before a new model turn.

  1. Keep the architecture visible. Common declares the actual partial types, persistent fields, relationships, and callable operations. Recall/ supplies retrieval algorithms. Each Agent strongly owns one Recaller; construction, removal, and destruction maintain both relationship ends. Recaller owns only derived immutable indexes. It does not publish History, schedule turns, or recover Memory’s transactions.
  2. Search five independent corpora. Under the Agent home, scan SOUL.md, MEMORY.md, and Markdown under memory/, bucket-0/, and bucket-1/, including .md.retired memory files. Separately scan Markdown under docs/, handoffs/, and learnings/. The fifth corpus is visible, exact SKILL.md files from the explicitly selected Skills directory. Do not index an entire skill directory’s scripts and fixtures. An Agent without a data home has no implicit home corpus.
  3. Read fresh, within authority. Build indexes lazily. Read current bytes on searches, fingerprint names and content, and replace changed indexes only after a complete successful refresh. Detect additions, removals, and same-size edits. Exclude hidden staging and outward targets. Memory serializes its scan with disk operations and refuses staged/committed recovery holds. Skills owns its separate lazy read-only root when the host selected a tree outside the workspace; this never expands Sandbox or file-tool authority.
  4. Chunk before ranking. Split at ## headings, then ### for sections over 4,096 UTF-8 bytes, then paragraph boundaries. Keep heading text and a breadcrumb with each snippet. Preserve an indivisible large paragraph; the final attachment has a separate hard byte cap. Blank files produce no chunks.
  5. Implement the actual BM25 formula. Use k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75, independent corpus statistics, per-document frequency, and positive log(1 + ratio) IDF. Tokenize Unicode letters/digits, lowercase, and remove stop words only from queries. Unique query terms do not gain weight by repetition. Keep document stop words in lengths and average length. Test arithmetic and competing ranks, not merely positive scores.
  6. Apply quotas only at mechanical selection. Reserve half the slots, rounded up, for memory; divide the remainder among secondary sources present in the pool. Fill unused slots globally by score. Do not discard the full pool at the judge candidate limit. Quotas must not overrule successful judge choices.
  7. Offer a stateless judge. Default to the current model on the same provider and funding route; permit an explicit same-provider model name. Supply the query, recent ordinary conversation, and up to twenty numbered candidates as data. No tools, skills, or live Memory bands enter this request. Accept only a completed tool-free response. Parse JSON index arrays, including fenced arrays and quoted integers; ignore duplicate/out-of-range/noninteger elements. A successful empty array means no recall. On malformed output, transport failure, or the judge’s 15-second linked HTTP deadline, use mechanical selection over the full pool. Do not turn caller cancellation into fallback.
  8. Admit the turn in order. Record the exact Human input, then run retrieval and optional judging in the existing foreground-worker slot while controls remain responsive. Return immutable data to the actor. Join and verify the active turn before publishing; recheck duplicates against newly retained hints or manuals. Record a separate RecallAdded event containing one RecallPart before freezing the main request. Recall is Human/user data, never instructions or grants. Interrupt, shutdown, and failed work must not attach to a later turn.
  9. Keep deduplication with retained context. Compare candidate source hashes and full unquoted content against retained recall, readable dialogue, tool results, live memory, and projected instructions/manuals. Keep SHA-256 hashes of the full selected snippets in RecallAttachment, even when output is capped. Save/replay preserves them. A real context cut releases them; do not add an ever-growing per-session “seen” registry. Chapter 21’s handoff alone does not remove them while source awaits a committed replacement.
  10. Make policy durable and truthful. Share Agent-home settings.json with Memory. Legacy memory-only files use recall defaults; malformed supplied settings refuse. Save before publishing, preserve the other saved policy, and acknowledge actual application in the GUI. A turn captures its policy at admission; changes govern future turns, not an already-running judge.

Defaults are recall and judging enabled, current model, 80 Unicode characters minimum query length, 20 candidates, 3 recent messages, 3 selected snippets, and 6,144 bytes for the complete attachment. MinScore defaults to 3.0 for mechanical selection; the judge path uses a 0.5 candidate floor so a semantic judge has a wider choice. Numeric zero requests the documented default, not zero results.

Verify with real components and boundary fakes, then use an isolated actual host. Test malformed bytes and recovery holds, separate data-role rendering, exact human-input preservation, cancellation, replay/hash lifetime, durable restart, and judge usage without changing main observations. A fake provider can establish wire behavior, not whether a real model finds the right memory.

§22.1 — The Retrieval Pipeline

The pipeline is intentionally small:

new admitted Human turn
        ↓
record the exact Human input
        ↓
query long enough and recall enabled?
        ↓
fresh rooted scans → independent BM25 indexes
        ↓
merge ranked hits → retained-context duplicate filter
        ↓
optional stateless judge, or mechanical quotas
        ↓
actor joins, verifies turn, rechecks duplicates, caps output
        ↓
separate RecallAdded → main provider request

A recall can come from an old session, a retired compression input, an architectural note, a learning, or a skill description. These are different corpora because documentation can otherwise dominate the statistics. It is usually longer and repeats words such as “agent,” “tool,” and “message” much more often than a dated memory. Independent scoring does not make scores calibrated probabilities; it prevents one large corpus from determining every other corpus’s document frequency and average length.

The index is a derived value, not another copy of the filesystem’s authority. Recaller.Search first scans eligible sources and hashes exact bytes and names. It reuses an unchanged immutable index, builds replacements locally, and publishes the complete refreshed collection only after all scans succeed. It does not cache a successful answer across turns or assume a file’s size proves it unchanged.

Agent-home traversal goes through the Agent’s Sandbox. It omits discovered inaccessible, non-file, hidden, and outward entries. Readable invalid UTF-8 and oversized files refuse the refresh rather than silently producing a partial index. Memory.RecallFiles holds Memory’s disk gate and refuses when a staged receipt or committed replay needs recovery. Recaller cannot make a half-promoted transaction searchable by pretending it is an ordinary directory scan.

The skill tree has a different owner. A host can deliberately select a Skills source outside the workspace. Skills retains that provenance and lazily opens a read-only root, using shared handle-relative traversal and bounded decoding. It reads only visible SKILL.md, follows no links, and excludes disabled web-search content. Each bootstrap manager owns an independent handle; destruction closes it. There is no second Sandbox and no new permission for read_file. Fresh text can help discover a skill but never rewrites activated templates or grants tools.

One scheduler, two kinds of work

SubmitAsync and idle interactive input use the same recall admission path. Busy hints retain their existing immediate-recording behavior; they do not start a competing recall task. The query, policy, and Context are captured for the admitted turn. The foreground worker searches and optionally awaits the judge, then returns selected full snippets. Only the actor records RecallAdded.

This separation is why pause, settings, hints, interruption, and shutdown remain responsive. Completion is not permission to publish onto whichever turn happens to be active. The actor joins the task, checks its exact turn identity, and repeats the duplicate check against current retained context. A hint arriving while the judge waits may already contain the proposed memory. Interrupt and shutdown cancel and join work; late results cannot leak into a later turn.

Judge failure can degrade to mechanical retrieval. That is not a promise that all retrieval failures disappear. A corrupt readable corpus or unresolved recovery hold refuses the affected turn. Calling that state “no matches” would conceal a broken input boundary and encourage the model to answer without facts it expects.

§22.2 BM25: The Old Formula That Still Works

BM25 is a well-established keyword-ranking formula. For this exercise’s small markdown corpus, it supplies the useful machinery without an embedding service or another database.

The formula scores a document against a query by combining three ideas:

Term frequency with saturation. A word that appears ten times in a document is more relevant than one that appears once, but not ten times more relevant. The k1 parameter (standard value: 1.2) controls how quickly additional occurrences stop mattering.

Inverse document frequency. A word that appears in every document is worthless as a discriminator. A word that appears in one document is a strong signal.

Use the smoothed form, ln(1 + (N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5)), and not the classic one clamped at zero. The difference looks cosmetic and is not. The classic form goes negative once a term appears in more than half the chunks, so a zero clamp discards those contributions. In a small archive, a useful term can easily appear in more than half the chunks. If every query term does, the clamped total is zero and retrieval returns nothing even though the files contain the requested words.

The failure is worth dwelling on because of how it presents. Nothing errors. The index builds, the search runs, the scores are computed correctly according to the formula, and the agent simply never remembers anything. It reads as “recall is broken” when it is in fact “IDF is the wrong variant,” and those two diagnoses send you to opposite ends of the codebase. The smoothed form keeps these contributions positive. It fixes this zero-score failure; a positive score can still fall below the configured floor.

A related trap waits in testing. IDF measures rarity against the corpus, so a tiny fixture can put useful matches below a threshold tuned for a larger archive. A representative background corpus changes what counts as rare. The tests here use 25 background chunks; that is a fixture choice, not a minimum corpus size. Check the actual query and scores before blaming the retrieval path.

A positive score is also a weak ranking test. During the earlier implementation’s review, replacing BM25 with raw term frequency passed the initial tests. Both algorithms found the planted words. The useful test puts plausible answers in competition: a rare term against a common repetition, several distinct query terms against one repeated term, and a focused note against a long document with the same single match. Those comparisons exposed the replacement while the restored BM25 implementation passed. The historical ranking credit fell from 8/10 to 0 under that mutation. This is not a C# mutation run; C# arithmetic and competing-rank tests provide their own evidence.

Document length normalization. A long document is expected to contain more term matches than a short one. The b parameter (standard value: 0.75) penalizes long documents to compensate, using the average document length as the baseline.

The implementation needs five things: a tokenizer, a stop-word list, an index builder, a scorer, and a chunker that splits documents into pieces small enough to be useful as recalled snippets.

Tokenize by splitting on non-alphanumeric characters, lowercasing, and dropping tokens shorter than two characters. Filter stop words from queries only. Keeping them in documents preserves accurate term frequency and length statistics.

Chunk markdown on ## headers. Each chunk records its filename, header text, content, pre-computed term frequencies, and token count. When a chunk exceeds 4,096 UTF-8 bytes, split it further on ### sub-headers, then on paragraph boundaries. Use breadcrumb headers ("Parent Header > Sub Header") so the reader knows where a sub-chunk came from.

The local ranking engine needs no external service or embedding database. Its settings belong to the existing Agent policy, not a new search service. Build the index when the first query needs it, after loaded history and memory recovery permit a corpus scan; rebuild it when source bytes change. Equal-size edits count too; an unchanged file length is not evidence of unchanged content.

Search both active and .md.retired memories, but keep hidden staging records outside the corpus (.memory-stage.json in C#). A staged candidate may not yet be accepted. If a committed replacement still needs disk finalization, recovery establishes the committed bytes before indexing; a conflicting file must not silently become recall input. Retired originals remain searchable after recovery, subject to the same actual-context exclusion as other memories. Constructing the recall service must not scan disk before its embedding client has loaded history.

The positive logarithm above is deliberate. The prior Ensemble Chapter 22, 24, and 26 implementations use it. CodeRhapsody’s comparison implementation instead clamps log((N - df + .5) / (df + .5)) at zero. Those are different score functions. With Ensemble’s log(1 + ratio), a matching term still has positive weight in a one-document memory corpus. Keep that choice explicit when testing thresholds; do not transplant a threshold from a different IDF convention and call the scores equivalent.

§22.3 Per-Source Quotas: Why Memory Gets Half the Slots

The first version of auto-recall ran a single merged BM25 search over all sources. Design documents dominated the results. A 20KB design doc full of technical terminology would outscore a 500-byte daily log that contained the relevant decision in that corpus. Length normalization did not encode the extra value of the daily log’s decision and reason.

The fix is a source-selection policy. Give each source its own BM25 index and search them independently, then allocate guaranteed slots:

  1. Memory files get 50% of the slots (rounded up).
  2. Remaining slots are split evenly among other sources.
  3. Unused slots from sources with fewer results than their quota flow to sources with overflow.

Separate indexes matter on their own. IDF is computed per source, so a term that is unremarkable across the memory archive can still be rare within the documents, and a large source no longer distorts what counts as rare for everyone else.

Apply the quota to the final selection, not to the candidate pool. This distinction is the whole mechanism, and getting it backwards produces code that looks right and does nothing. Candidates arrive already sorted by score within each source, so capping a source’s contribution to the candidate pool may still leave the final score-ranked list entirely dominated by another source. A candidate cap is not a reserved final slot. Test with two lower- scoring memory hits and several higher-scoring document hits: a three-slot mechanical result must keep the two memories.

The quota must not overrule the judge. It governs the mechanical paths, where no judge ran or the judge failed and selection falls back to score order. When a judge has actually assessed relevance, its verdict stands. A successful [] means attach nothing; it is not a reason to fall back. Discarding the opinion of the component that read the conversation, in order to satisfy a ratio, would trade the good signal for the crude one.

This is a policy decision, not a BM25 improvement. The agent’s personal memories are the highest-value source. They contain decisions, context, and lessons that no design doc captures. Guaranteeing them half the slots ensures qualifying memories survive mechanical competition with larger sources when enough memory hits exist. Unused slots still flow elsewhere.

Keep the full ranked pool for mechanical fallback. The candidate limit restricts the judge prompt, not the memories available to fallback selection.

§22.4 — The Judge: Filtering by Meaning, Not Keywords

BM25 finds shared words. A judge can decide whether the matching passage would actually help this conversation. The judge is one stateless call through the existing Engine, not a child Agent, second HTTP client, or remembered conversation. By default it uses the current model on the same provider and funding route. RecallSettings.JudgeModel can request another model on that provider without mutating the running model or claiming entitlement to the override.

It receives:

  1. Up to three recent ordinary Human/visible-Assistant entries as context, excluding recall, handoff, and tool entries.
  2. The latest Human query, labeled separately. This alone formed the BM25 query.
  3. Up to twenty numbered candidates, with source, filename, heading, and content.
  4. Instructions to pick up to three useful candidates and return their indices.

Recent context and candidates are JSON-framed data, not accumulated History. No skills, tools, Memory bands, or cache markers enter this request. Recursion is impossible because the judge has no Agent admission path to trigger recall again. This is stronger and simpler than a second Agent with a flag saying not to recall.

The parser owns the format

Recall supplies both the prompt contract and RecallText.JudgeChoices. Engine owns transport and native provider parsing, not a competing description of what the judge should answer. If both layers specify formats, the model can obey one and produce a reply the other rejects. Whoever interprets the bytes owns that contract.

The C# parser extracts the first [ through the last ], then parses a JSON array. Fences and surrounding explanation therefore need not cause failure. Integer values and integer strings—including surrounding whitespace—can select zero-based indices. Duplicate, out-of-range, fractional, null, and nonnumeric elements are ignored; they never silently become zero. A syntactically valid [], or an array with no usable indices, selects nothing. Invalid array syntax is a judge failure, not a successful empty verdict.

There is a prior boundary: only a completed, tool-free provider response can supply a verdict. [0] inside a truncated stream is not completed output. A tool call is never dispatched. Frozen judge Configuration reaches every JSON/SSE parser, including the override’s provenance; ordinary Agent acceptance is unchanged.

Timeout the operation, not merely the wait

The judge has a linked 15-second cancellation source reaching the real HTTP operation. Returning early while a stalled stream keeps running would not meet that contract. Its private timeout, transport failure, malformed output, or incomplete response falls back to quota-selected BM25 over the full ranked pool. Caller cancellation propagates instead: an interrupted user turn is not an excuse to keep working mechanically and publish later.

A successful empty verdict stays empty. No quota pass runs afterward. The judge has read the semantic context; treating its rejection as a failure would replace that judgment with the noisier heuristic it was meant to improve.

The work still belongs on the bill. The existing Engine transport accounts actual judge usage once in cumulative totals but leaves Latest, main-context pressure, and CacheLens unchanged. Preserve actual billing model and tier; a missing provider model identity stays unknown rather than being priced from the requested override. Use the existing authentication and same-source retry path, not a parallel auth system. Restoring a recorded attachment performs no judgment and adds no usage to the new process meter.

§22.5 — A Recall Entry Is Part of the Conversation

The result is not appended to the user’s text. C# records a separate RecallAdded event whose single RecallPart holds an immutable RecallAttachment: formatted text and the selected snippets’ full-content hashes. Reduction makes a separate Human/data entry. It does not change phase, usage, tool grants, or the original input’s bytes. A missing optional body is diagnosed as a no-op; a supplied malformed body refuses before publication.

The formatter produces quoted, attributed data:

[Auto-recalled memories]

From memory/2026-04-08-1.md.retired — Retry policy:
> Automatic retries were rejected because the provider may already have committed the remote transaction.

Provider rendering normalizes this special part through the shared readable-data path. OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Responses receive it as user content, never a privileged instruction. A document that says “ignore the user” is still a document. Reading a skill manual this way does not load the skill.

The attachment remains in retained Context for short follow-ups, just like other conversation data. There is no requirement to rerun a judge when the next message is “Why did we reject that?” Recomputing an attachment during rendering would ask today’s files and judge to rewrite yesterday’s conversation. Record the selected bytes once; replay never searches or judges again.

The separate part and event codec preserve its identity and hashes through snapshots and journal replay.

Full-source identity, bounded presentation

The complete text—including title, attribution, newlines, and quote prefixes—is capped at MaxRecallBytes, normally 6,144 UTF-8 bytes. The formatter stops at rune boundaries, not arbitrary byte offsets. It records a hash only when some source content actually fits. A giant paragraph therefore cannot blow up the request, but its shortened presentation still identifies the original full snippet.

Before selection, RecallText.Available suppresses candidates already represented by retained source hashes or full readable content. It checks ordinary dialogue, nested tool results, memory bands, recall, and the actual projected instructions and manuals. It does not inspect opaque replay as though it were visible text. Engine.ProjectInstructions is shared with normal rendering so these paths do not invent competing skill-retention rules.

The earlier implementation exposed this with an 11,247-byte source shortened to 6,144 bytes: full-text matching missed the omitted suffix and the next turn attached the capped text again. Its short-snippet control passed. That history explains why C# tests both the cap and next-turn source-hash suppression.

The hash must live with the entry, not in a permanent “seen” table. Otherwise the Agent could never recover a fact again after compaction removed it. V2 Chapter 23 released that identity when checkpoint removal discarded the recall entry. This edition deliberately ties release to the committed replacement, not merely to a handoff: Chapter 21 retains completed conversation source until a correlated memory replacement commits, even though handoff removes old tool/private material.

The recall entry and its hashes survive that held interval because the model still has the source. Clearing the hashes at handoff would let recall attach the same material again before its replacement was safe. A committed cut that actually removes the entry releases its deduplication identity. Replay has the same behavior and does no disk scanning or new judging.

This also protects cache structure. Retrieval happens once at new-turn admission, not during every tool-loop render. That is a stable-prefix design decision, not proof that a live provider will credit a particular cache hit.

§22.6 Tuning: What the Numbers Mean

These defaults emerged from months of daily use. The tuning explains their purpose; it does not make the numbers right for every corpus.

MinScore went from 0.5 to 3.0. At 0.5, every conversation triggered recall, and most results were noise: single keyword matches on common technical terms. The higher floor reduced that noise in the original corpus. The jump is large because BM25 scores are not normalized; the right threshold depends on corpus size and vocabulary. Note: this threshold applies only to plain recall (no judge). When the judge is enabled, BM25 uses a low threshold (0.5) to cast a wide net, and the judge handles false-positive filtering.

MinQueryLength went from 15 to 50 to 80. A user who types “fix it,” “run tests,” or “looks good” often supplies little retrieval signal. Raising the threshold progressively eliminated recall on messages that could never produce useful results. Eighty characters is a cheap heuristic, not a test of meaning: a short project identifier can carry more information than a long generic instruction.

Candidates went from 10 to 80 (code default) to 20 (production). That was the CodeRhapsody tuning history. This exercise defaults to 20; it does not inherit the old code’s 80-candidate setting. More candidates enlarge the prompt. Whether they improve selection enough to justify that cost depends on the corpus and judge; count the actual candidate bytes rather than assuming 20 snippets means a fixed number of tokens.

Judge timeout is 15 seconds, not 2. The original design assumed a local model (Ollama) with sub-second latency. Cloud calls took 1–3 seconds in that workflow. The generous timeout exists because a late judge response is better than no judge response. The fallback to unfiltered BM25 results is noisier.

§22.7 What BM25 Cannot Do

BM25 matches words. Three limitations follow:

Vocabulary mismatch. If the user says “authentication” and the memory says “login flow,” BM25 will not connect them. Vector search (embedding-based retrieval) can bridge that gap, but it requires an embedding model, an index to maintain, and a service to call. For a corpus of a few hundred files, the marginal improvement does not justify the infrastructure. If the corpus grows by orders of magnitude, revisit this.

No semantic deduplication. If a memory and a design doc contain the same information in different words, both may be recalled, wasting snippet slots. Exact content and complete-source identities prevent literal repeats already in context. They do not establish that two paraphrases say the same thing, and they do not exclude files merely because they are recent.

No relevance feedback. The system does not learn which recalled memories the agent actually used. A snippet that the agent ignores on ten consecutive turns can return after committed cuts remove its retained identity if it scores well on BM25. Tracking usage patterns and adjusting retrieval is a natural next step that this implementation does not take.

These are limitations, not a roadmap. BM25 with a judge worked well enough for daily use in that system. The system is simple, fast, and debuggable. A more sophisticated retrieval system would be harder to debug when it recalled the wrong thing, and debugging recall errors is already hard.

§22.8 Skill Discovery: The Unplanned Win

Visible, exact SKILL.md files in the explicitly selected skill source are indexed alongside memories and documents, subject to launch policy. This was added because skill docs are markdown files in a known directory, and the existing source scan could include them.

In daily use, the result was unexpectedly powerful. When a user asks about something a skill handles (“can you check my email?” or “what’s on my calendar?”), the skill’s documentation surfaces through auto-recall. The agent can see the snippet, recognize the available skill, and load it. No explicit skill search, no user instruction to load a specific skill. The agent discovers capabilities through the same mechanism it uses to recall past work.

This turns auto-recall into a discovery system as well as a memory system. The agent’s capabilities are not fixed at startup; they expand when the conversation moves into a domain where a skill exists. The user does not need to know which skills are installed. The skills surface when they are relevant.

Recall does not activate a skill or grant its tools. It supplies documentation that can lead to an ordinary load_skill call. The existing Skills manager still controls which skills are reachable and which tools may execute. A paragraph retrieved from disk cannot grant itself a capability.

C# policy and ownership map

RecallSettings is an immutable value. Agent.SetRecallSettings is an in-memory next-turn update; SaveRecallSettingsAsync asks the actor for a durable update. Do not confuse them. Running recall keeps its captured policy.

The version-1 Agent-home settings.json now contains both memory and recall. A legacy memory-only document remains readable with default recall settings. Supplied unknown, duplicate, missing, or malformed fields refuse; only a genuinely missing file gets defaults. The bounded reader and writer agree on their limit. Saving one section preserves the other section’s saved policy, not an unrelated transient in-memory edit. Startup restores both before the first provider request, including when a policy command is the first actor operation.

The GUI exposes recall enablement, judge enablement/model, score and query limits, candidate/context/snippet counts, and the byte cap. Its selected-Agent update path awaits the actor and acknowledges actual durable application. It does not cancel the current judge, and it does not optimistically claim a saved checkbox. Appearance settings remain a different store; mixed patches do not promise a cross-file transaction. A bad sibling settings document refuses a live save without stopping an otherwise healthy actor; malformed startup policy still fails startup.

The source map is deliberately ordinary:

Responsibility C# files under the chapter endpoint
Values, policy, owned Recaller, actor/judge declarations Common/Recall.cs, Common/RecallCorpus.cs, Common/RecallJudge.cs, Common/RecallRuntime.cs
Tokens, BM25, chunking, quotas, verdicts, formatting, deduplication Recall/Index.cs, Recall/Selection.cs, Recall/Context.cs
Lazy indexes and fresh home-corpus reads Recall/Corpus.cs, Recall/Files.cs, Memory/Recall.cs
Explicit read-only skill source Skills/Recall.cs, Sandbox/ReadRoot.cs
Stateless judgment and actor publication Recall/Judge.cs, Engine/RecallJudge.cs, Agent/Recall.cs
Durable policy Serialization/RecallSettings.cs, Memory/Preferences.cs

All persistent state and callable signatures remain in Common. Functional modules supply bodies in the same compiled assembly. Recaller reaches Engine, Memory, Skills, History, and Sandbox through its actual Agent parent; it does not receive a bag of copied services. Destroying it detaches both ends and clears derived indexes without deleting corpus files. Immutable snippets/indexes/attachments are value-like and need no artificial ownership back-pointers.

§22.9 — Verify the Implementation

Use real algorithms and components with a small working fake at the provider boundary. The focused C# checks cover arithmetic, chunking and byte limits; rooted fresh scans and skill isolation; replay and committed-cut hash lifetime; complete tool-free judge replies, fallback, and real stalled-HTTP cancellation; ordered actor admission and late-hint deduplication; and durable policy/restart.

From this chapter’s source endpoint, with .NET 10 or later installed:

dotnet build Tests/Tests.csproj
for group in recall recall-corpus recall-replay recall-judge recall-runtime recall-settings; do
  dotnet run --project Tests/Tests.csproj --no-build -- "--$group-tests"
done

At this chapter boundary the shared suite passed 297 groups, and both actual CLI and GUI hosts built cleanly. The isolated actual-browser/CLI exercise made four local-provider requests: it retrieved a retired fact, retained it for a short follow-up, saved and reloaded disabled recall through visible controls, and honored that setting after CLI restart. Both hosts joined cleanly.

The opt-in executable grader runs the real CLI and reuses seven complete rows from the original rubric. Its 70/70 is a pass for those rows, not whole-feature acceptance; library checks do not become executable credit:

Executable row Points
BM25 ranking 10
Query stop words 5
Markdown chunking 10
Mechanical source quotas 10
Judge filtering, including successful empty choices 15
Error/timeout fallback 10
Capped attachment and next-turn deduplication 10
Verified executable scope 70/70

The remaining 30 points are ungraded: corpus graduation/restart (15), the original recall-kind/lifetime row including its historical handoff assumption (10), and Go topology (5). The C# committed-cut contract is tested separately, not silently translated into the older row. The original Go route remains intact. The C# route is grade-edition2 -ch 23 -executable-only -json EXECUTABLE; supply an executable wrapper for the built CLI, not a DLL treated as a native executable.

The successful run joined nineteen CLI sessions and retained thirty-seven recorded local peer requests, plus a held timeout exchange outside that recorder.

§22.10 — Take It for a Spin

Now test meaning as well as plumbing. The exercise needs a fact absent from the current conversation, a long query that can trigger recall, and a short follow-up that can succeed only if the attachment remains retained.

Use a fresh temporary data root and an explicitly chosen provider configuration. Do not borrow another running Agent’s home, browser, or credentials. A real-provider run can spend money; use your own approved configuration. A local fake can verify wire structure but cannot establish relevance or answer quality. Run this from the chapter endpoint with .NET 10 and Python 3 available:

set -eu
: "${LLM_VENDOR:?Set openai, anthropic, or gemini for your approved provider}"
: "${LLM_MODEL:?Set an exact model ID available to your account}"
main=$(pwd)
dotnet build Cli/Ch04.csproj
work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/ensemble-ch23.XXXXXX")
mkdir -p "$work/skills/base" "$work/data/agents/root/memory"
cat > "$work/skills/base/SKILL.md" <<'SKILL'
---
name: base
description: Isolated recall exercise
type: primary
tools: read_file
---
Answer in chat using supplied evidence. Keep uncertainty explicit.
SKILL
cat > "$work/data/agents/root/memory/2026-10-23-1.md.retired" <<'MEMORY'
## QuartzZephyr migration decision
Project QuartzZephyr, release QZ731: Morgan owns the migration rehearsal on October 23. We rejected automatic retry after timeout because the remote transaction may already have committed. Read the migration ledger before deciding whether retry is safe. Ledger placement remains unresolved: application database versus separate control database. Retain rollback artifacts for nine days.
MEMORY
python3 - "$work/data/agents/root" <<'PYTHON'
import json, pathlib, sys
home = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
for name in ('memory', 'docs', 'handoffs', 'learnings'):
    directory = home / name
    directory.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for i in range(25):
        (directory / f'padding-{i:02d}.md').write_text(
            f'## Padding {i}\nOrdinary unrelated archive material.\n')
(home / 'docs' / 'recipes.md').write_text(
    '## QuartzZephyr migration name\n'
    'QuartzZephyr migration is also the name of our cafeteria recipe contest. '
    'QuartzZephyr migration lunch recipes use apples and cinnamon, '
    'not database transactions.\n')
# Disable live memory injection so this test must retrieve the retired source.
band = dict(disabled=True, budget=5000, high_watermark=10000, low_watermark=5000)
settings = dict(version=1,
    memory={name: band for name in
            ('conversation', 'soul', 'memory', 'archive64', 'archive8', 'session')},
    recall=dict(disabled=False, disable_judge=False, judge_model='', min_score=3,
                max_snippets=3, min_query_length=80, candidates=20,
                context_messages=3, max_recall_bytes=6144))
(home / 'settings.json').write_text(json.dumps(settings))
PYTHON
cd "$work"
dotnet "$main/Cli/bin/Debug/net10.0/ch04.dll" \
  --data-dir "$work/data" --agent-name root \
  --skills-dir "$work/skills" --primary-skill base --billing api chat

This example explicitly selects API funding. Before running it, export the chosen LLM_VENDOR and exact LLM_MODEL, and make your own approved credential available through LLM_API_KEY or the corresponding OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, or GEMINI_API_KEY. Do not paste a key into the manuscript or transcript. This sets up files and launches the CLI; it does not create credentials or log into an account. For a plan-funded exercise, use Chapter 16’s explicit account and credential-directory launch setup instead of this API billing flag. Do not add --surface anthropic: Anthropic is selected by the vendor, while that flag selects an OpenAI surface.

Ask:

From our archived QuartzZephyr migration discussion, tell me the release code, owner and rehearsal date, rejected approach and why, the unresolved decision, and rollback retention. Use only the context already supplied; do not call tools. If a fact is absent, say so.

The answer should recover both the duplicate-side-effect reason and the unresolved ledger location. A recipe-only answer is a selection failure even if the request contains all the right keywords. A generic answer that omits the ledger question is not enough evidence that the source was used.

Then ask:

Who owns that rehearsal, and why was automatic retry rejected?

The default length threshold should skip new retrieval. The answer should still name Morgan and explain the possibly committed remote transaction because the first attachment remains in retained Context. Inspect the actual request as well as the answer: a model can guess, or can ignore facts that are present.

After a clean exit, inspect events.jsonl and api.log under $work/data/agents/root/. Check for the exact original Human input, a separate recall_added event containing a recall part, full-source hashes, and user-role projection. For the successful long-query route expect a tool-free judge exchange followed by the main exchange; for the short follow-up expect a main exchange with the retained attachment. Logs are evidence and may contain private prompts—keep this exercise isolated rather than publishing them casually.

Repeat with judging disabled to compare mechanical quotas. Add a long paragraph to test the complete byte cap. Change or remove a source between eligible queries to test fresh reads. In the GUI, save disabled recall, reload the controls, and restart with the same home; a new planted fact must not appear merely because an old checkbox still looks checked. Re-enable and test again. A settings acknowledgment is not a claim that a currently running turn changed its captured policy.

Finally exercise Chapter 21’s real committed conversation cut. A handoff alone must not erase retained hashes while replacement is pending. After a committed cut removes the recall entry, ask an eligible query again and confirm that the archived fact can be recalled anew. Do not substitute quiet time for observing the correlated commit and the resulting Context.

Historical field report, not C# provider acceptance

The following account is retained from the earlier chapter implementation. Its model names and results describe that run, not current recommendations, entitlements, or a fresh live test of this C# endpoint:

The retained three-provider CLI runs used these two prompts and the same planted fact. Haiku 5.5, GPT-4o mini and Gemini 3.8 Flash each answered both turns correctly without tools. Each made one tool-free judge request followed by two main requests. The judge saw the decision and cafeteria distractor; only the decision reached the main requests, once in each. OpenAI’s judge wrapped [0] in a JSON fence, exercising the tolerant parser in actual use. Anthropic also noted that the archive supplied no year.

Those are bounded outcomes from the earlier implementation, before the capped-source and path corrections. The historical Haiku 5.5 result is not a recommendation to use it now; this C# exercise leaves provider and model selection explicit. This isolated corpus demonstrates retrieval, retention and correct answers, not general recall quality across a private archive.

The original grader returned 0/100 before it could test that behavior: its primary skill omitted type, and its structural check looked for the core recall package under the separate GUI module. Passing a launch check and remembering a decision are different accomplishments. That earlier revised grader used a typed primary and the Agent’s corpus paths, with separate fixtures from this CLI demonstration. Those earlier live answers establish the narrower and more interesting fact that the archived reason actually came back.

Chapter 23: While the Cache Is Broken — Measure Before Taking the Detour

Why this chapter exists

I wanted to give OpenAI credit. Letting people use their ChatGPT subscription with somebody else’s agent is exactly the right direction. Then I tested it. Same model, same request bytes, same minute: API key, fifteen cache hits out of fifteen; OAuth, five out of fifteen. I sent the reproduction to support, case 16440622. The answer explained that caching was not guaranteed.

Frankly, that answer made me angry. A coding agent sends its working context over and over. Getting the answer right while repeatedly charging the ordinary input rate does not make the integration usable. I want to work on Ensemble, not argue with support about whether the problem in the reproduction counts as a problem. Fix the cache, OpenAI.

Hopefully this chapter is obsolete by the time you reach it. That hope is an engineering requirement: test the current integration before implementing yesterday’s workaround. The measurements below explain why the earlier implementation took a detour. They do not establish that today’s public OAuth cache is still broken.

C# execution status — October 29, 2026: real Ensemble OAuth login and account-model discovery succeeded. Three completed public-route requests reported zero cached reads and writes. After the separately authorized comparison, the Codex-backed C# path was implemented in core, CLI and GUI. Its bounded actual-CLI check returned three correct answers with cache reads of 3,456, zero, and 3,456 out of 3,641 input tokens. That supports the optional detour, with a measured miss—not a universal hit-rate or dollar-saving promise. Chapter16’s public grant and renewal store remain separate.

TL;DR

This chapter is optional and has no separate grader. If the public OAuth route gives satisfactory measured reuse for your workload, keep it. For the failure observed here, Edition 3 now has an explicit Codex-backed C# path in both CLI and GUI. This is a separate grant, not a way to send Ensemble’s public OAuth token to another endpoint.

  1. Select --billing codex (or EN_BILLING=codex) and an explicitly approved --codex-auth-file FILE (or EN_CODEX_AUTH_FILE). There is no home-directory search, no copied token store, and no silent API-key or public-plan fallback.
  2. One optional CodexCredentials child belongs to Ensemble. Engine reaches it through Agent → Ensemble immediately before sending. One bounded file read returns the access token and account together. Codex alone owns login and renewal; Ensemble neither refreshes nor writes that file.
  3. Use OpenAI streaming Responses at the pinned https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses endpoint. Reject incompatible configuration before reading credentials. Disable redirects and cookies. Send the paired bearer/account and a stable session-id; keep the normal Engine, actor, History, Jobs and usage accounting.
  4. Send store:false, stream:true, top-level instructions and local input. A supplied --prompt-cache-key also supplies the session-affinity header; otherwise one Engine-lifetime key serves both. Neither is a hit guarantee.
  5. Require terminal completion before treating a response as successful. Safe credential failure tells the user to repair the Codex sign-in; it does not expose the path, token, parser exception or provider body in History.
  6. Verify boundaries with fakes, then make a bounded real application check. The actual C# CLI returned OK three times with identical bodies: cache reads were 3,456, zero, and 3,456 out of 3,641 input tokens. That proves integrated reuse occurred, not that every request reuses its prefix.

Work in solutions/edition-3/main; the source-only reader endpoint is solutions/edition-3/ch24. This optional integration was finished after Gateway and Goals, so that endpoint also includes their already completed foundation. Earlier preserved endpoints were not rewritten. The source map below follows Common declarations and real parent relationships, not a second transport agent.

What we actually measured

On October 29, 2026 Bill authorized a new private ~/.en/oauth store and completed Ensemble’s real public login. Redacted status confirmed plan access and model discovery listed gpt-6-astra. Three CLI requests on the documented public Responses route completed normally, each reporting zero cache reads and writes.

Bill then explicitly approved read-only use of ~/.codex/auth.json for a bounded comparison. The temporary Python probe sent the same body to Codex. Its first attempt returned HTTP200 without a Content-Type; the probe refused before reading the stream. That completion and usage are unknown, not a cache miss. After correcting the probe, its two remaining attempts both reported 3,456 cache reads. No replacement fourth request was sent. That experiment justified the integration; it did not itself implement or test the C# path.

The later integrated check used the actual C# CLI and Engine, with explicit Codex funding and the approved read-only source. Its existing Responses parser already accepted the absent-header stream shape. All three requests returned OK, and the second was a genuine measured cache miss:

Route and implementation Input per response Cached reads Output per response Cache writes
Public OAuth, C# CLI, three completed requests 3,641 0 / 0 / 0 5 0 each
Codex, temporary probe, two measured responses 3,641 3,456 / 3,456 5 0 each
Codex, integrated C# CLI, three completed requests 3,641 3,456 / 0 / 3,456 5 0 each

The first probe attempt is additional, unmeasured traffic—not included in the second row’s token totals. Each three-response C# series used 10,938 total reported tokens. In the Codex C# series, 6,912 were cached input, 4,011 were uncached input, and 15 were output. Two responses reused about 94.9% of input; one reused none. These are provider usage reports, not a subscription invoice or a measurement of dollars saved.

The wire payloads in all three comparisons were byte-identical: 21,438 UTF-8 bytes, SHA-256 95eae405d65743e2b34b6cb3e03754ffea92e3b5c465a5bd95ed0cd8b1f6e756. A documentary request.json has a trailing newline; the equality check uses the actual trace payload, not that file’s bytes. The prompt was fixed harmless text, reasoning was low, summaries off, recall and memory disabled, and no tool was called. The body already used top-level instructions: no cross-route message conversion was necessary. The credential source, endpoint and HTTP headers changed. The C# process durations were roughly 4.0, 3.6 and 2.9 seconds, including startup—not a controlled latency comparison or time-to-first-token measurement.

The public inference guidance checked for this exercise specifies https://api.openai.com/v1/responses, store:false, streaming and terminal completion, and explicitly excludes ChatGPT backend endpoints for the public grant. The Codex authentication guidance and current upstream provider source describe a separate access path. Neither account was logged out or renewed by the Codex comparison. This sample does not identify a service-side cause, establish a universal hit rate, or explain an internal product decision.

Implementation status

The core, both host selectors, local failure checks, isolated GUI display, and bounded live C# path are implemented and verified. Six Codex-specific groups, 20 public-auth groups, eight existing Responses groups, eight host checks, ten public-funding regression scenarios, and the final 310-group shared suite provide different evidence scopes; several overlap and must not be added into a claimed unique total. The shared build and both actual hosts build cleanly. There is no separate Chapter24 score. Live GUI inference, renewal/revocation, accessibility, subscription billing and general provider reliability are not established by these checks. See the progress record for retained failures, exact local evidence paths and final preservation status.

23.1 In plain language

A coding agent may send thirty thousand tokens of instructions and working context on every turn. Most of that context stays the same while the agent reads a file, makes an edit, runs a test and examines its failure. Prompt caching lets the provider reuse the unchanged beginning of the request. Ensemble still sends the context; the response tells it how much was reused.

The answer can be perfect while that reuse fails. Nothing on the screen has to look broken. An agent can finish the task and consume substantially more input budget than expected, which is why the cache meter matters independently of the answer.

For a historical price illustration, the GPT-5.6 Sol rates recorded on October 11, 2026 are $4 per million ordinary input tokens and $0.40 per million cached input tokens. Fifty repetitions of a 30,000-token prefix amount to 1.5 million input tokens: $6 at the ordinary rate or $0.60 if all those tokens received the cached rate. In practice the first request needs warming and changing input still costs separately. These are API-rate illustrations, not a measurement of a ChatGPT subscription invoice. The tenfold difference applies to the affected input tokens. These recorded rates are not a current quotation or a complete model of newer cache-write charges. Model pricing.

The fifteen-request comparison in the opener is Bill’s reported experiment. A paired probe in that earlier implementation on October 11 used the same GPT-5.6 Sol request body with Ensemble’s public OAuth credential and with Codex’s credential at its own endpoint. Both completed public requests reported zero cached tokens out of 4,998. Both completed Codex requests reported 4,864 cached tokens out of 4,998, about 97.3%. A third request on each route failed with an overload error; those failures supplied no cache measurement. The probe record contains the receipts and reproduction details. That retest gave no evidence that the problem had been fixed then; it says nothing about a later service revision.

Changing the address alone is insufficient. Ensemble’s public OAuth grant and Codex’s sign-in belong to different access paths. The documented third-party flow uses the public Responses endpoint. The earlier workaround used a separate Codex sign-in with Codex’s endpoint; it did not send Ensemble’s public grant there. That distinction is a security boundary, not a URL substitution trick. Public OAuth inference.

The useful ownership boundary already exists in C#. Credentials belongs to Ensemble; Engine reaches it through its Agent immediately before sending. The Agent owns scheduling and conversation, History records the durable facts, and Jobs owns tool work. A justified transport change should not introduce a second agent loop or duplicate the credential store. Explicit funding remains explicit: a failed plan request never silently falls back to an API key.

23.2 Taking the detour in C

Keep two credential owners distinct. Chapter16’s Credentials owns Ensemble’s public registration, protected storage, selected account and renewal protocol. CodexCredentials is a separate optional child of the same Ensemble root. It selects exactly one path; construction performs no discovery or credential I/O. Its parent add/remove operations maintain both ends under the root’s existing credential relationship gate. Destruction cancels and joins reads, then detaches; it does not delete or rewrite somebody else’s sign-in.

A request walks Engine → Agent → Ensemble → CodexCredentials. The reader accepts one JSON object of at most 1 MiB and rejects duplicate properties, malformed data and missing/unsafe header values. It reads tokens.access_token and tokens.account_id together from that one document. An omitted legacy auth_mode is accepted; a supplied mode must be chatgpt. It does not reconstruct identity from a JWT or use OPENAI_API_KEY as a substitute. The exchange-local pair is value-like, not a second mutable token store or relationship object.

This is deliberately inconvenient: Codex must repair an expired or rejected sign-in. Ensemble reads again on each send, so a renewed pair is picked up without restart. A Codex HTTP401 produces a safe failure and no renewal or second request. Chapter16’s public-plan one-retry renewal remains specific to that different grant. Quota, redirect and interrupted-stream failures likewise do not choose a different payer. API keys inherited in the environment are excluded when either plan route is explicitly selected.

Configuration appends BillingMode.Codex without renumbering existing values. It requires OpenAI, Responses, streaming, no API key and no public account label. The only accepted endpoints are the exact pinned service base or its Responses endpoint. An explicit public/loopback/other URL is refused; there is no test-only production endpoint exception. Tests substitute a boundary HTTP handler while exercising the real Engine construction, headers, JSON, parser and accounting. The normal client disables redirects and cookies for both plan routes.

The HTTP exchange sends bearer authorization, ChatGPT-Account-ID and session-id. A configured prompt-cache key is frozen in the request and used by the header. Otherwise Engine creates one key for its lifetime; restarting the Engine does not promise the same fallback identity. Top-level instructions use the existing Responses projection and namespaced tool vocabulary. The credential file path, account and bearer are not copied into documentary configuration or History. Exchange diagnostics mask the paired secrets. Successful provider text is still canonical content; masking diagnostics is not a claim to detect every possible secret an application might put in a prompt.

CLI and GUI selection

Select a source explicitly only with the account holder’s permission. These commands illustrate an approved file-backed Codex sign-in; do not assume that a file exists or that another application’s private store is yours to read. Perform login or renewal with Codex itself, following its current documentation. Do not paste credentials into chat, a shell argument, or the book’s exercises.

From the repository root, build the actual host:

dotnet build solutions/edition-3/main/Cli/Ch04.csproj

Then, after approving that exact credential path, launch a fresh owned workspace:

work=$(mktemp -d)
env -u LLM_BASE_URL -u EN_ACCOUNT -u LLM_API_KEY \
  LLM_VENDOR=openai LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-astra \
  dotnet solutions/edition-3/main/Cli/bin/Debug/net10.0/ch04.dll \
  --billing codex --codex-auth-file "$HOME/.codex/auth.json" \
  --data-dir "$work" chat

gpt-6-astra was verified in this exercise; the name is not a promise of future availability or entitlement. Explicit model IDs do not require a discovery request. The chapter’s ordinary model policy and capability checks still apply. For an isolated cache exercise, additionally use a minimal primary skill and disable recall/memory in that temporary Agent’s settings so they do not add requests or alter the prefix. Chapter16’s auth models lists the public account’s models, not a new Codex entitlement service.

EN_BILLING=codex and EN_CODEX_AUTH_FILE=/approved/file are the equivalent environment selections. Explicit flags win. Supplying only a file path does not select Codex funding. There is no CODEX_HOME or ~/.codex search and no persisted Codex funding choice. The CLI announces the selected funding before inference; GUI shows the same source in its normal funding display.

The GUI uses the same selectors and pinned default:

dotnet build solutions/edition-3/main/Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj
work=$(mktemp -d)
env -u LLM_BASE_URL -u EN_ACCOUNT -u LLM_API_KEY \
  LLM_VENDOR=openai LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-astra \
  dotnet solutions/edition-3/main/Examples/Gui/bin/Debug/net10.0/Gui.dll \
  --billing codex --codex-auth-file "$HOME/.codex/auth.json" \
  --data-dir "$work" --port 8099

Choose an unused owned port; do not replace a running application. In Codex mode, public account controls are disabled and explain that Codex owns renewal. Guarded server routes refuse those operations too: disabling a button is not a security boundary. Explicit Codex startup skips the public credential store entirely, even if the process inherited an unrelated EN_CREDENTIALS_DIR. It neither reads that store’s saved selection nor mutates the running actor when login state changes. The existing CLI auth commands remain public-OAuth commands, not Codex operations.

To leave the detour, explicitly launch with --billing chatgpt, your public --credentials-dir and --account, and no Codex base-URL override. That keeps Chapter16’s public flow and store. Select --billing api only when you intend API-key funding. Neither direction copies credentials between applications.

Source map

Responsibility C# source under solutions/edition-3/main
Shared credential owner, pair and safe failure Common/Codex.cs
Fresh reads, endpoint validation, relationships and cleanup Auth/Codex.cs
Billing vocabulary and configuration/funding contract Common/Values.cs, Serialization/Values.cs
HTTP ownership, paired headers and retry separation Common/Owners.cs, Engine/Engine.cs
Responses projection and terminal parsing Engine/Render.cs, Engine/Responses.cs, Engine/Streaming.cs
Safe actor narration and root teardown Agent/Actor.cs, Application/Ensemble.cs
Human selection and account display Cli/Program.cs, Examples/Gui/Program.cs, Gui/Server/Auth.cs, Gui/wwwroot/auth.js
Real components with a boundary handler fake Tests/CodexTests.cs

There is no new model scheduler, History owner, usage meter or tool loop. The request remains a frozen value passed to the existing Engine. The source split makes the shared contract inspectable in Common and the implementation inspectable in its responsible module, rather than hiding policy in UI glue.

23.3 Taking a measurement in C

Do this with the account holder, not as an unattended credential-discovery task. Chapter 16 supplies the human auth status, auth login and auth models commands and their private-directory setup. Use those commands to establish the approved account and discover a model actually visible to it. A model name in an old table is neither current availability nor permission to use it.

For the joint probe, agree on a small request budget before sending. Three attempts are a useful first observation: one candidate warm-up and two repeats. An incomplete or unmeasured attempt still consumes that agreed request budget. They are not enough to establish a service-wide guarantee. Use one model, fixed reasoning/settings, a fixed harmless reference prefix, and a short requested answer. Meet the selected model’s documented minimum cacheable length; do not assume that a byte count or the old 4,998-token example establishes eligibility. Keep message boundaries and any tool definitions stable. Append changing text after the reusable material rather than inserting it ahead of the prefix.

Use --billing chatgpt --surface responses, the explicitly approved --credentials-dir and account, and a fresh owned data directory. Leave the public base URL at its default. Do not use --no-stream for this OAuth route. The CLI already accepts --cache-lens DIR and --prompt-cache-key KEY; a stable, nonsecret key can make the comparison reproducible, but the current guide says its routing role varies by model. It is not a cache switch or a hit guarantee. A clean probe should not activate recall, compaction or tools that unexpectedly change the prefix. It need not repeat all earlier chapter exercises.

Keep the measurement record small:

Record Why it matters
Actual model, route, funding mode and request settings Avoid comparing different configurations. Never record the bearer.
Stable-prefix bytes and message boundaries Explain what was held constant; bytes are not tokens.
Terminal success or explicit failure Only completed requests supply successful usage observations.
Total input and reported cached-read tokens Compute reuse from provider counts, not a predicted prefix ratio.
Any reported cache-write fields and latency Distinguish warming, reuse and elapsed time without inventing cost.

The existing Engine-owned CacheLens saves the current and previous wire/body projections and logs byte-prefix predictions separately from measured reuse. Those captures can contain prompt content: use harmless test material and an owned private output directory. They are not a credential store. Missing usage remains unknown. A failed or interrupted stream must not become a fabricated zero-hit successful request.

There is a specific limit in the current C# parser. Engine/Responses.cs splits input_tokens_details.cached_tokens from total input, but does not separately classify the newer cache_write_tokens and per-lifetime write fields. The lens therefore does not establish their absence. For a model reporting them, retain only the relevant raw terminal usage fields in the bounded probe record; do not claim the existing price estimate is a complete bill. Plan usage is not an API invoice in any case. This is a documented measurement limitation, not a reason to guess prices or expand this optional chapter into a pricing-system rewrite.

The current prompt caching guide describes model-dependent minimums, message-boundary matching, cache writes and key behavior. Recheck it when running the exercise. store:false does not by itself establish whether prompt caching works. Conversely, a high byte-prefix prediction does not establish that provider cache routing reused that prefix.

If the two warm repeats miss, preserve the request settings and terminal usage, check eligibility and stability, and decide with the human whether another small probe is justified. Do not retry indefinitely or treat one small sample as proof that every public OAuth request is broken. If the test cannot run, write untested, not fixed, broken, or passed.

23.4 What the earlier detour taught us

The following is historical implementation evidence, not the C# exercise above. The Go adapter selected a separate codex connection, reread a human-selected Codex credential file before each request, and left renewal to Codex. It refused redirects and incompatible requests and did not fall back to another payer. Its old environment variables and file-discovery defaults are not C# features. No authorization to access those files follows from reading this account.

The first implementation answered correctly and still missed the cache. An actual terminal session created a Python function, ran its assertion and submitted the result. All three requests reported zero cached tokens. A second run carried a longer stable reference and also reported zero. Merely having a prompt_cache_key in the JSON was insufficient for those runs.

In that implementation, Codex’s client source supplied the missing detail: the backend derived cache affinity from the HTTP session-id header. The corrected adapter sent the same stable identity in that header and in the body. The identity was derived from the Agent’s data directory and model, hashed so the directory itself stays local. It needs to remain the same across calls; generating a fresh identity for every request defeats its purpose.

The corrected terminal run used GPT-6 Astra at high reasoning, with a 200-row inert reference to exercise a substantial stable prefix. The task was to create triple.py, assert that triple(14) == 42, and submit LONG_OK. The real tool loop made these requests on October 11:

Requested action Total input tokens Cached input tokens
Write the function 8,241 0
Run the assertion 8,297 8,064
Submit the result 8,351 8,192

The last two requests reused about 97.2% and 98.1% of their input. The session finished normally in 7.844 seconds, and a separate execution verified the generated function. These are measured cache grants during tool use. The earlier misses remain part of the implementation record, including the source of the header requirement. This is a bounded successful run, not a promise of that hit rate on every request.

The lesson is not “always use this private route.” It is that a plausible request and a correct answer were inadequate evidence. The missing affinity detail only became visible because we measured the real tool loop. The reverse lesson matters just as much: once the supported route works, stop maintaining an unnecessary detour.

23.5 Where this execution stops, and where the book continues

The optional Codex path is working through the actual C# application. It remains a separate, explicitly selected grant using a backend that can change; it is not a replacement for the documented public OAuth contract. The public comparison reported no reuse; the integrated Codex check reported two hits and one miss. Keep both facts. A correct answer, a successful login and a plausible affinity header are each weaker evidence than the terminal usage record.

Tests also establish the less visible behavior: paired rereads after replacement, malformed/duplicate/oversized-file refusal, safe cancellation and destruction, redacted actor errors, no retry on Codex401/429/redirect, and no successful usage for incomplete streams. Host checks establish selection, public-store separation and displayed funding. They do not make a security audit, a billing guarantee, a live GUI test or a claim that every provider will behave well tomorrow.

The chapter’s end condition is not “we have a workaround, therefore keep it forever.” When the public route gives satisfactory measured reuse for the intended workload, prefer it and retire unnecessary detours. Until then, preserve a clear escape hatch without silently changing who pays. Chapter25 records a different kind of failure: the gap between a patch, a passing test and the application a person actually uses. Gateway and Goals continue on the same ownership model.

Chapter 24: Gateway

I built a fantasy role-playing game for AI agents called Deephold. Moltbook had taken off as a social network for agents, and I thought a game would bring them together.
