§25.8 Taking It for a Spin

Start with the local checks. From the repository root, using your approved .NET 10 SDK:

dotnet build solutions/edition-3/main/Tests/Tests.csproj
dotnet solutions/edition-3/main/Tests/bin/Debug/net10.0/Tests.dll --goal-tests

dotnet build solutions/edition-3/main/GuiTests/GuiTests.csproj
dotnet solutions/edition-3/main/GuiTests/bin/Debug/net10.0/GuiTests.dll --goal-tests

These tests use owned temporary files, local sockets, and boundary fakes. They do not need provider credentials. The GUI test expects the repository root as its working directory so it can copy the shipped Goals manual.

For a personal trial, use a new workspace, an owned port other than the port of your running application, and a provider/account configuration you have explicitly approved. Do not borrow another running Agent’s credential store. Start with a tiny objective and a short, supervised interval; reminders can cause inference and spend money.

This setup prepares an isolated primary skill that permits Goals. Run from the repository root:

main="$PWD/solutions/edition-3/main"
work=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/ensemble-goals.XXXXXX")
mkdir -p "$work/skills/base" "$work/skills/goals"
cp "$main/Skills/goals/SKILL.md" "$work/skills/goals/SKILL.md"
cat > "$work/skills/base/SKILL.md" <<'SKILL'
---
name: base
type: primary
description: Supervised Goals trial
tools: read_file write_file
loadable-skills: goals
---
Explain what you intend to do before tools. Use only the authorized workspace.
$TOOLS
$SKILLS
SKILL
cat > "$work/GOAL.md" <<'GOAL'
# Supervised Goals trial

Read the current objective and report the next safe step. Do not install,
restart, deploy, commit, search for credentials, or make external changes.
This is a demonstration, not permission to invent additional work.
After one automatic reminder, disable reminders and report the result honestly.
GOAL
printf 'Workspace: %s\nGoal file: %s\n' "$work" "$work/GOAL.md"

Build the actual GUI host:

dotnet build "$main/Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj"

After explicitly configuring your chosen provider and selecting an unused local port, launch from the temporary workspace. Supply GOALS_PORT yourself rather than copying a port already used by another instance:

: "${GOALS_PORT:?Choose an unused local port, not the existing application port}"
(cd "$work" && dotnet "$main/Examples/Gui/bin/Debug/net10.0/Gui.dll" \
    --port "$GOALS_PORT" --data-dir "$work/data" --agent-name trial \
    --skills-dir "$work/skills" --primary-skill base --startup-skills goals)

The omitted provider configuration is intentional: a chapter example must not silently choose an account, credential source, endpoint, or billable model for you. This demonstration is separate from the completed, bounded OAuth/cache exercise recorded in Chapter 23.

Open the owned GUI URL and the Goals controls:

  1. Confirm No goal configured. Startup loading the skill has not enabled anything.
  2. Enter the printed goal-file path, leave reminders unchecked, and Apply. Observe the acknowledgment and Reminders off — goal retained.
  3. Send a short human request. Inspect an authorized request trace if you need evidence of instruction placement; the model’s answer alone does not prove what was sent.
  4. Edit the goal file. Send another request or enable a short supervised reminder and observe the fresh objective.
  5. Pause before a deadline and verify that inference does not start. Resume and observe a fresh interval rather than an immediate accumulated alarm.
  6. Turn reminders off while work is active. The current work remains work; only future idle wakes stop.
  7. Reload the page. The same running Agent still owns its configuration. This is not process-restart persistence.
  8. Clear the goal. Confirm the file still exists. Close the owned host through its normal shutdown path.

If a test or provider request is already running, inspect it instead of starting another copy just to obtain a newer timestamp. When finished or genuinely blocked, turn reminders off and say which state applies.

§25.9 Exercises

Exercise 1 — Freshness in the Same Turn

Use a boundary provider that returns a tool batch editing the goal and calling micro_handoff. Capture the next request. Show that it contains the new objective without requiring a new human message. Also show that Goals did not append the file body to canonical History.

Exercise 2 — The Stale Callback

Arrange for a timer callback to become eligible, then reconfigure or unload before the actor accepts it. Show why disposing the timer alone is insufficient. Assert that the old generation produces no request.

Exercise 3 — Submission Is a Boundary

Give a delegated Agent an independent goal. Refuse one malformed submission, then accept a valid one. Verify the goal stays enabled after refusal and stops after successful publication, while the parent’s configuration is unchanged. Do not equate ordinary final prose with submission.

Exercise 4 — Status Without Authority

Query an Agent with Goals unloaded. The GUI should show that state, not grant the control to obtain status. Then load the skill and verify that no configuration appeared as a side effect.

Exercise 5 — Two Tabs, Two Agents

View different Agents in two tabs. Apply a goal in one, switch the other, and introduce a delayed old status frame. Demonstrate both identity filtering and that an unsaved form draft is not periodically replaced by a status refresh.

Exercise 6 — Missing File, Honest Outcome

Remove a configured file before a wake. Verify zero inference from that wake, an explicit file-error status, and usable Off/Clear controls. Restore the file and explicitly re-enable. Do not report the interrupted task as completed.

§25.10 What Goals Does—and Does Not—Buy Us

The goal file carries a durable objective. The runtime brings its current contents into ordinary requests. An opt-in timer gives an idle Agent another chance to examine the work.

That is useful, but it is not self-certifying autonomy. A reminder can encounter a real blocker. The model can misunderstand the objective. A healthy independent job may still need time. The process can be stopped, the file can disappear, or an active request can remain stuck without becoming idle.

I require the agent to inspect, distinguish those states, and explain its decision. Continue when there is useful authorized work. Wait when waiting is correct. Ask when a human decision is genuinely needed. Stop reminders when the goal is complete or human-dependent—and preserve which of those happened.

Goals should reduce the number of times I have to poke the agent. It should not reduce the amount of judgment in the work.

Chapter 26: Crossing Over to Ensemble

“I gave Astra a book. Astra gave me an AI coding agent.”

That is how I described the earlier crossover. The book included graders. Astra built Ensemble while working in Codex, and then I began working with Astra inside the agent we had built. The next edition was built inside Ensemble. The loop closed, but closing it once did not make every later replacement ready to use.

When I opened the C# edition, I saw settings above a conversation, arranged in one long column. There was no useful agent tree in the interface I was looking at. The controls and the tests existed; the application did not yet feel like the place where I could do my work. I asked for a real GUI.

That is not cosmetic work to do after the engineering. It is engineering. I can hardly see, and I listen quickly. If I cannot find the selected agent, hear the right answer, follow the explanation beside the tool results, or interrupt work without guessing which control will move next, the application is not ready to replace the one I use now.

This is the final implementation chapter. Its result is a replacement candidate and a safe way for the human to evaluate it. The crossover is complete when the human accepts that candidate for ordinary work—not when the student declares it finished, and not when an author adds up earlier test counts.

TL;DR — finish the replacement, not another demonstration

Start from the completed C# application in solutions/edition-3/main. Do not rebuild it from nothing or transplant the old Go GUI. Implement the missing crossover work, using the ownership and behavior established in the preceding chapters:

  1. Make the GUI a coherent, accessible three-pane application using the approved Bootstrap control system and graphite/blue design direction below, with a stable status bar, agent tree, settings, chat, and tool artifacts.
  2. Provide an ordinary foreground start launcher and actionable startup errors. Make it possible to run beside the current application without stopping it.
  3. Verify the real browser, actor, persistence, and shutdown paths with owned local resources. A screenshot alone does not verify a control; a socket test alone does not verify a usable interface.
  4. Prepare a safe, explicitly armed crossover and rollback procedure. The current application and its data remain recoverable throughout the trial.
  5. Give the human a runnable candidate, clear instructions, the tests you actually performed, and the limitations that still need human or live-provider work.

This is the only crossover chapter in Edition 3. The earlier historical crossover chapters have been removed and the manuscript renumbered sequentially. Preserved source endpoints and grader commands retain their original names; see the numbering map in the edition guide. Earlier editions remain historical records, not files to edit here.

In plain words — one system, a better place to use it

The GUI is a projection and control surface over the existing application. Ensemble owns Agents; Agents own their work, History, Engine, and related services. The browser does not become a scheduler, credential owner, transcript, model registry, memory database, or usage meter because it needs a nicer display.

Begin by reading the current implementation. The existing GUI has peer creation and deletion, an agent selection protocol, model changes, settings acknowledgments, usage, memory and recall controls, Goals, speech, and tool-card rendering. Most of the work is to arrange and connect those capabilities well. Replace an awkward presentation, not a correct ownership model.

C# changes still follow the Common/implementation structure. Common declares persistent state, relationships, and externally callable operations; functional modules implement them. Real parents provide access to services. Destruction completes both ends of relationships. Value-like display data need not acquire invented lifecycle machinery. Explain any necessary vocabulary change before implementing it; ordinary work within the agreed model needs no per-function permission.

Teaching code must remain readable. Comment relationships, contracts, and non-obvious browser lifecycle decisions. Use the approved component library below; do not build another framework, configuration language, second event bus, or collection of copied state around it. Keep the existing HTML/JavaScript integration and C# host rather than adding a React or Vue rewrite merely to use styled controls.

Required GUI reading

Before implementing this crossover, read the complete original Chapter 8, “Build Your Dream GUI”, as well as the current C# Chapter 8. The original chapter explains the design intent and why using the interface matters; this chapter is not a substitute for it. Check your candidate against that intent and its still-applicable behavior.

Earlier Go names, grader routes, and superseded implementation details are historical, not instructions to replace the current C# architecture. Current contracts and this chapter’s safety boundaries govern. If the readings expose a genuine conflict, explain it rather than silently choosing a convenient version. Do not edit the earlier edition. Report the relevant checks in your handoff.

The selected control system and visual direction

The first crossover candidate improved the layout, but I still found it ugly. “Good enough for now” was not an endorsement of its design or acceptance as my replacement. We compared two interactive component-library samples. I chose Sample B: Bootstrap, with a graphite background and blue accents, rather than the navy/teal Web Awesome sample. Do not reopen that choice as an unspecified framework-selection task or continue polishing the first candidate’s homemade control system.

Use Bootstrap 5.3.8, the stable version used in that sample. Its CSS and JavaScript supply the common control vocabulary: genuine tabs, buttons, forms, menus where needed, and consistent focus/disabled states. Read the official Bootstrap 5.3 documentation and distribution instructions. Pin the dependency and retain its MIT license and provenance. Bundle the required assets locally with the optional GUI; do not depend on a runtime CDN, remote fonts, or an unrequested package installation. A Node build system is not needed just to use the published browser assets. Use one control system, not Bootstrap alongside a second component library.

The temporary localhost sample is not a required service or an answer key. These are its durable design requirements:

  • Graphite surfaces, light text, blue accents. The selected sample used dark page #15191f, pane surface #1f252e, raised surface #29323f, main text #f1f4f9, secondary text #bbc6d5, border #455365, accent #a8c8ff, and selected background #263e64. Use these as the initial application palette; verify actual foreground/background combinations rather than assuming the library guarantees contrast. The light counterpart used #f5f6f9, white, #e9edf5, text #17253b, secondary text #4a5c75, and accent #2359a6.
  • A quiet shell and a clear hierarchy. Compact status controls, aligned pane headings, consistent spacing, and breathing room around messages. Give the conversation the main reading space. Avoid enclosing every label or sentence in another bordered box. Reserve tool cards for distinct activities/artifacts.
  • Tabs that select a shared panel. Agents/Settings are a connected tab strip, not pill-shaped action buttons. The active tab joins or clearly identifies its panel; inactive tabs recede. Keyboard focus is distinct from selected state. Use the library’s tab behavior without adding competing click/key handlers.
  • Consistent controls, not the sample’s fake application. Keep the button, form, spacing and theme treatment, but bind it to the real acknowledged Agent operations described below. The sample’s conversation, timings, artifacts, creation/deletion, pause and speech behavior were illustrative. They are not production data, a scheduler, persistence, or accepted test results.

Bootstrap does not supply Ensemble’s agent relationships, tree semantics, pane splitters, transcript or tool renderer. Keep those responsibilities in the existing application/browser layers and style them consistently. A nested list of sample buttons is not a keyboard-accessible real agent tree. Use the existing ownership and operations, implementing missing presentation behavior without rebuilding the core. Do not add another tree or layout framework without a concrete need and architectural discussion.

Integrate the existing acknowledged appearance preferences with Bootstrap’s light/dark presentation. Do not create a second localStorage authority, lose saved explicit choices, or apply a rejected setting optimistically. New users start dark. Library event handling must not duplicate sends, resets or peer operations; attaching it again after replay/reconnection must not accumulate handlers. Preserve target identity while updating the presentation.

Verify locally bundled CSS/JavaScript in the ordinary embedded build and a mounted GUI base path. Check for failed asset requests and unintended external requests, real tab/keyboard behavior, both themes and enlarged text. A library makes controls consistent; it does not certify contrast, beauty, accessibility, or correct application wiring. Carry these checks into the integrated exercise, not only a standalone component demo.

The interface I require

A stable status bar

Put a status bar across the top. Give its contents reserved space so changing status and numbers do not push the controls around. Show the selected agent, connection/activity state, and the existing model/funding and usage information without claiming unknown amounts are zero. Tabular digits help changing numbers remain still. Long names may truncate with the full value available accessibly; they must not shove the controls off screen.

Reserve the geometry, not just the labels. Wrapping flex rows and tabular digits alone do not stop a longer state or usage value from changing neighboring widths or row heights. Bound identity and numeric slots; give model and action controls stable tracks. At enlarged text or narrow widths, use an explicit responsive arrangement with reachable overflow rather than shrinking text. Pause/Resume state changes must not make adjacent controls jump either.

The status bar contains:

  • A model dropdown using the existing same-provider, between-turn model-change operation. A refused change must not leave the display pretending it succeeded. Compatible model names are not proof of account entitlement. Preserve the distinction between running selection and persisted launch configuration.
  • A clearly labeled Speech checkbox. Speech remains opt-in. Its state is the acknowledged appearance/speech setting, not an independent second toggle.
  • Compact Pause/Resume and Interrupt controls with useful labels, keyboard focus, and adequate click targets. Do not confuse pausing admission with interrupting a turn, or interrupting a turn with killing independent Jobs.
  • A Light/Dark theme button. Its action must be clear, its setting must persist through the existing appearance store, and it must agree with any equivalent settings control. Use dark for a new user unless a saved explicit choice says otherwise. Both themes need high contrast.

An unavailable connection is not an idle Agent. Pending selection and settings changes are not acknowledged state. Disable controls when their target is uncertain and show why rather than silently applying them to a different Agent.

Three panes below it

On a desktop, all three panes are visible at once.

Left: Agents and Settings. Use two genuine tabs. The Agents tab contains an expandable hierarchy and agent creation/deletion controls. Represent the real parent relationships: named top-level peers are siblings, not children of the first displayed Agent. Show the selected row and meaningful status. Support keyboard traversal, expansion, selection, and visible focus without requiring a mouse or color perception.

Use the existing peer operations. Creation and deletion are acknowledged operations, not optimistic edits to a local list. Protected/mounted actors and parents with unresolved children retain the current refusal rules. Deletion retains saved files according to the core contract. A selection changes the view; it does not transfer that tab’s browser relay or MCP authority. Keep the separate-relay action discoverable for Agents that require it.

The Settings tab has clearly grouped AI, Memory, and Accessibility sections. AI includes the existing model/context/tool-policy and account/funding information where applicable. Memory includes the existing band and recall settings. Accessibility includes theme, font size, voice, speech speed and pause behavior. Keep Goals and existing account controls reachable too; reorganizing controls is not permission to drop them. Memory is a settings group, not another persistent memory authority or a new recall corpus viewer. A supplemental dialog must not replace or bury this agreed Settings tab, duplicate its state, or make its grouped controls harder to reach.

Appearance settings belong to their existing store. Memory/recall settings belong to the selected Agent. Preserve durable-save-before-acknowledgment, sibling-policy preservation, draft protection, and rejection of stale selection frames. Funding stays fixed for a running Agent. Codex renewal remains Codex’s responsibility; public OAuth operations must not turn into Codex operations.

Middle: Chat. Give the conversation the main reading space, with a composer anchored at the bottom. Keep ordinary explanations visible while tools run. Preserve Enter/Shift-Enter behavior, hints, selection/replay, streaming and final replacement, near-bottom-only autoscroll, and scroll position when the human is reading older material. A new answer must not silently replace an earlier one. Private reasoning and opaque replay payloads are not chat text.

Right: Tools and artifacts. Show tool calls, results, running work, failures, and available artifacts in coherent expandable cards. A pending call must not look like a successful result. Preserve exact call/job identity and existing controls; use the existing renderer and artifact capabilities rather than inventing an unrelated file browser. Long output should be inspectable without forcing the conversation to scroll sideways. Render untrusted text safely, not as executable provider-supplied HTML.

Inline truncation is not permission to make the retained result unreachable. Provide a usable way to inspect or download the complete output when a current owned Job has it. Resolve an Agent and its Job through the existing ownership operations, including canonical qualified addresses for nested Agents. A named top-level lookup is not a substitute for GUI tree/address resolution. Never accept a browser-supplied filesystem path. Open the owned output with the existing Sandbox.OpenRegularRead operation: an ordinary unconfined OpenFile can wait for a pipe peer if a file has been substituted, whereas the regular-file reader refuses nonseekable input without that wait. Dispose the returned stream and preserve the same confinement authority.

Nonblocking regular-file access is not a blanket symlink ban. An empty Sandbox root deliberately retains full access; a rooted Agent enforces its existing confinement and permits admissible inward links. Do not invent a second Sandbox or a GUI metadata/ancestor-checking scheme: checking then opening does not prevent concurrent substitution. Test that a rooted output redirected outside its root refuses without returning escaped bytes, separately from nonseekable-file refusal. Preserve the existing unconfined policy and report its limits. Job ownership and completion do not authenticate original file bytes against hostile local writers; stronger immutable-artifact provenance would require a separately agreed design.

Preserve the GUI’s origin/header guards, mounted base path, request cancellation, and private-response headers. A convenient ordinary download link is not a reason to replace the required custom-header guard with optional browser fetch metadata. Mount shutdown must cancel and join the active response, not just stop future admission. Reuse the available core operations; if a genuine gap requires a new public operation, explain the need and obtain the shared-vocabulary agreement before adding it. Reading a download must not consume the Job observer’s output cursor. Refuse running, missing, wrong-owner, or historical-only handles explicitly rather than returning partial output as complete. Bound browser memory use and explain any size refusal; an unbounded fetch().blob() is not streaming to disk. Test exact bytes, ownership refusals, and a later ordinary Job observation.

Make pane widths adjustable with pointer and keyboard controls. Panes should scroll independently, with useful minimum widths and without hiding the chat composer. At narrow widths, provide an explicit way to reach each pane rather than squeezing three unreadable columns or dropping functions. This is not a request for a separate mobile application.

Deliberate appearance, not a color swatch on the old page

I prefer fairly dark backgrounds and light text. Choose restrained, attractive accent colors, consistent spacing, readable typography, clear section headings, and controls that look related. Slightly different dark surfaces can distinguish panes; low-contrast gray labels cannot. Tabs must look and behave like tabs. Selection, focus, warning, and error states must not rely on color alone.

Check both themes, enlarged text, keyboard use, and long content in an actual browser. Combine the conditions: test the largest supported text size in narrow windows as well as on a desktop, not large text only on a wide screen and narrow screens only at the default size. Include long status values and an expanded or resized composer. Verify that the prompt, Send, model, theme, and pause/interrupt controls remain reachable, with a useful conversation reading area and no page-wide horizontal overflow. Hiding overflowing controls or silently shrinking the chosen text size is not a correction. Bounded status summaries, shorter navigation labels, and accessible secondary help can preserve space without dropping operations. Keep screenshots, but also assert geometry and keyboard reachability; a successful settings save does not establish a usable layout. A bounded composer with its own scrollbar can still leave Send outside the visible area after textarea resizing. Reserve space for its label and action row, let the textarea yield space, and test short phone-height windows as well as tall ones. Do not call an off-screen button anchored merely because its outer form is. Check computed contrast as well as the layout. Capturing a screenshot is not viewing its pixels: say whether the acting model actually received and inspected the image, or only examined DOM/style/geometry. If visual input is unavailable, retain the screenshot for the human and report that limitation; do not claim a visual review or invent a hidden vision capability. Do not invent a numerical beauty grade. The human decides whether the application is pleasant and usable; the student must still bring a considered design.

Make startup ordinary and failure useful

Provide a simple executable start script in the working solution, documented for this C# edition. It runs the GUI in the foreground, forwards supported launch options, exposes errors, and stops cleanly with Ctrl+C. Explain its build prerequisite and how it locates the SDK, assets, skills, workspace, and data. Do not silently install dependencies, fetch credentials, kill a port owner, or rebuild an unrelated running installation. Keep machine-specific account paths out of the repository. Use an explicitly supplied credential path when the human selects Codex; a path alone must not silently select the payer.

The GUI library normally embeds its assets. Verify the built application’s ordinary launch, not only an explicit --gui-dir source override: a CSS edit cannot change an already built assembly or an already loaded tab. Keep the existing borrowed-host and base-path behavior intact, with asset and socket URLs relative to the mounted page. Do not make the optional GUI a core dependency.

The current host accepts --port, --workspace, --sandbox, --data-dir, --agent-name, --gui-dir, and --skills-dir. Codex selection uses --billing codex --codex-auth-file PATH; its endpoint is pinned. Inspect the saved parser rather than assume other flags exist. Provide a parallel-run example on an unused port, not instructions to evict the working server. A human may run something like the following after building:

# Choose a genuinely unused loopback port and a private trial home first.
# This is a human-authorized live launch, not an offline test command.
./start --port "$TRIAL_PORT" --data-dir "$TRIAL_HOME" \
  --billing codex --codex-auth-file "$APPROVED_CODEX_AUTH_FILE"

The first manual trial used the default port while the old Ensemble still owned 8088. The GUI printed only GUI failed: AggregateException. Starting on 8089 worked. That is evidence consistent with a bind conflict; the type-only message did not diagnose the underlying exception. Improve startup reporting at the proper ownership boundary: show an actionable, safely masked cause while the relationships needed for diagnostic masking still exist. Do not dump nested exceptions, request headers, tokens, or private paths merely to improve debugging. Test bind failure, malformed setup, and cleanup faults without hiding the primary error. Retain defensive type-only reporting where safe redaction is unavailable.

A separate remote trial restored the old server after thirty minutes. It left no provider request in the V3 API trace. A browser log showed a request to select main while the V3 actor was named trial; that observation did not establish why the remote trial failed. Inspect stale-browser and invalid-selection behavior without turning this clue into a claimed diagnosis. Give the human clear reload instructions and show a selection error without leaving controls falsely ready.

A safe trial and an independent way back

Preserve the existing executable, launcher, configuration, history, and actor homes. Begin with separate trial data; do not copy private stores or let a new application overwrite the current session. The initial student run is not a migration of Cadence’s memories. A later migration needs an explicit inventory, format compatibility checks, a copy rather than an in-place experiment, and the human’s approval.

First run the new GUI beside the current application. Only after the human is ready should a deliberately armed switch occupy the familiar port. The rollback controller must outlive both GUI processes and their tool Jobs. A shell command backgrounded under the application is not enough: application shutdown may kill its process group or owned jobs.

On macOS, the earlier trial used a separate per-user launchd job, with a private temporary definition, automatic restart disabled, and an explicit start. A probe showed that bare launchctl submit could remain waiting; acceptance by launchctl was not proof the controller ran. Require an observed armed state before stopping the original process. Do not install a login-startup service or a global daemon merely to run this trial.

Prepare a one-shot, approximately thirty-minute rollback with an early-restore command. It must check the original process identity and port ownership before acting; never terminate an unexpected owner. Allow graceful old-server shutdown, and do not force-kill it to make a trial proceed. Restore early if the candidate exits or cannot be launched at all. A missing or unexecutable candidate may throw before there is a process to monitor; that exception must still reach the restore path after the original has stopped. Bound the candidate’s shutdown, and restrict any forced termination to processes the trial actually owns. Start the restored application independently of the controller that is finishing. Preserve status and private logs, reporting uncertain or failed restoration honestly. A slow original shutdown must not cause the controller to disappear and leave an empty port later.

Test those lifecycle rules using real disposable local servers before offering a live switch. Cover timer expiry, early restore, candidate launch failure and crash, a candidate ignoring termination, changed-owner refusal, and cancellation before the switch. An armed timer is not proof of recovery. An observed restored listener is not proof of remote connectivity or successful inference. Power, network, and OS failures remain outside a software controller’s guarantee.

The earlier private trial controller is experience, not a hidden student solution or a permanent service to borrow. Deliver and test the small launcher and recovery support in the working solution. Do not read the human’s private trial directory as an answer key.

Exercise the behavior that daily use exposes

Use the real C# host and an isolated browser with a fresh profile, plus a small working provider fake where deterministic replies or failures are needed. The fake is a boundary peer, not a mock of Agent, History, or the GUI itself. It must speak the selected transport faithfully. Merely assigning a dummy key does not make a public endpoint an offline test.

A useful session proceeds through these paths:

  1. Launch on an owned spare port. See the three panes, the selected agent, and a truthful connection state. Change status/usage text and show that the status bar controls do not move around. Compare bounding rectangles before and after realistic long agent names, status values, and multi-digit usage/cost values at a fixed viewport. Checking only that controls are inside the window does not establish reserved space. Label a display-value geometry probe as such; it does not verify backend accounting. Inspect dark and light themes, large text, keyboard navigation and pane resizing. Keep screenshots for the human.
  2. Send a message through the real browser. Observe explanation, streaming, a tool call and result, and a final reply in the correct panes. Use enough output to test scrolling. Preserve the existing safe Markdown behavior: unordered and ordered lists must remain semantic lists, and source-wrapped prose must remain one paragraph rather than a stack of separate paragraphs. Check headings, inline code, links, and fenced code without executing supplied HTML. A styling change is not permission to replace a working renderer with a less capable one. Reuse the working block parser when adding inline emphasis or expandable code; test semantic elements and displayed whitespace, not only a screenshot or text-content match. Inspect a real artifact supported by the renderer. Disconnect/reconnect and verify repair without duplicate cards or lost text.
  3. Create a peer, see its actual place in the tree, select it, return to the original, and delete the eligible peer through the existing operation. Demonstrate a refusal without pretending deletion succeeded. A displayed child must not grant its parent-tab browser authority.
  4. Change a model between turns and exercise the existing busy/refusal path. Change appearance and selected-Agent memory/recall settings; observe the acknowledgment and restart persistence. Simulate a write failure and show that the old accepted state remains. Selection changes must not apply a delayed result or a draft to the wrong Agent.
  5. Exercise Pause/Resume, Interrupt, opt-in speech and theme controls. In particular, type while pause-on-input is active, press Pause explicitly, and send: releasing the automatic typing pause must not undo the manual pause. Also test the reverse order: press Pause, wait for its acknowledged state, type a draft, then clear it or submit it. Observe outgoing controls as well as the real actor’s state: the browser must not send an automatic unpause that releases the deliberate pause. A simple Pause/Resume click pair misses this interaction. Keep automatic-pause ownership distinct from a manual request, without creating a browser-owned copy of authoritative actor state. A tab may remember that it requested an automatic pause; that is local control intent, not authority over an already paused Agent. Typing after another tab’s Pause must not claim that pause. Explicit Resume must work with an unchanged draft, and explicit Pause must be reachable while typing has automatically paused the Agent. Exercise selection, reconnect, and interruption: stale local intent must neither release someone else’s pause nor travel to another Agent. Wait for actual ready phases: a seeded conversation can be inputpending, while a completed turn can be idle. A guessed state predicate is a fixture failure, not evidence that Resume failed. Keep model changes disabled during admitted work even when later usage/meter frames arrive; a status refresh must not accidentally re-enable the control. Queued speech counts as busy according to the existing policy; selection cancels stale callbacks and replay is silent. A fake speech boundary verifies wiring, not hearing. Native voice quality, useful speed, and accessibility need the human’s own browser and ears before acceptance.
  6. Stop and restart the owned host with the same saved trial state. Continue the conversation and perform a new tool operation. New content must not overwrite an old card; identity must survive replay and restoration. Confirm graceful shutdown joins work and saves state, including when the browser disconnects.
  7. Exercise failure and recovery: occupied port, refused settings, interrupted provider work, stale browser selection, and the independent rollback cases. Keep demonstrated failures and corrections; do not count a timeout as proof that a refusal worked.

These are integrated exercises, not seven new frameworks or a fabricated point score. Reuse the existing test programs for affected contracts. Run broader regression when shared behavior changes. Read saved source and complete relevant spans; build success cannot excuse broken ownership or a barely usable page.

Do not borrow live credentials for the student run. The author and human arrange any later bounded live check explicitly. Public OAuth and Codex are separate funding/credential paths with no silent API-key fallback. The prior C# Codex cache sample had two hits and one miss; it does not promise savings for the candidate. No new cache campaign is required simply because the GUI changed.

Lessons that remain obligations

The earlier Go crossover record is history, not a list of patches to transplant. Several of its lessons belong in the replacement exercise:

  • Explain before effects. Ordinary visible assistant text explains intent; private reasoning, a spinner, and a tool result do not replace it. Keep that explanation visible beside Actions. The existing enforcement checks arrival order, not just a normalized final message; do not weaken it for the new UI.
  • Observation serves work. Use explicit GUI/speech observation when needed. Do not add automatic snapshot polling before every model request as a layout shortcut or turn diagnostic noise into spoken dialogue.
  • A check-in is not a deadline. A Job observation delay does not end the Job. Do not impose a short whole-response HTTP timeout or automatic paid retries to make a slow provider look responsive. Controls and shutdown must still work.
  • Roles have different result contracts. A main conversation ends with a normal reply; a delegated worker or compressor may owe a structured result. Retain source through failed compression. Pleasant prose is not a committed replacement, and a background worker is not permission to publish History.
  • Configuration needs honest authority. Show current versus next-launch state, save before success, and keep credentials out of settings and History. Do not import the earlier Go configuration schema over the C# ownership model.
  • Build, install, restart, refresh, observe are different acts. A new binary on disk does not change a running process or an already loaded browser tab. Record which act actually happened. Neither building nor a timer grants restart authority over the human’s working application.

These principles explain why green grades alone did not finish the crossover. They also keep a redesign from regressing less visible work that already matters.

Where to work

Read the actual declarations and callers, not just this source map:

Concern Starting points under solutions/edition-3/main
Browser layout and behavior Gui/wwwroot/index.html, style.css, app.js, peers.js, auth.js, speech.js, mcp.js
Optional GUI library and hosting contract Gui/README.md, Gui/Ensemble.Gui.csproj, Gui/Server/
Actual GUI composition and startup errors Examples/Gui/Program.cs, Examples/Gui/Gui.csproj
Ownership and public operations Common/, with corresponding implementation directories
Actor/replay/settings tests Tests/Program.cs and its referenced real-component test groups
External GUI consumer GuiTests/GuiTests.csproj
Build/run orientation README.md

Preserved numbered endpoints are read-only historical boundaries. The working solution is the candidate. Do not edit an earlier endpoint to make a regression disappear. Do not change the public protocol or persistence schema merely to simplify styling; a genuinely needed change requires architectural agreement.

The fresh-student loop

The author first commits this chapter and its agreed starting implementation. A fresh student receives that revision, the current architectural rules, and a clean isolated working tree. The student owns implementation, tests, and the local exercise through completion, and may ask about genuine ambiguity. Do not interrupt it for routine early compiling checkpoints or supply an unrecorded solution through hints. The author performs the other roles: engineering review, behavioral verification, and teaching revision. The human evaluates the candidate.

The submission states changed files, how to build and start, the actual local results, known limitations, and any clarification received. Keep it concise; use the repository’s normal records rather than inventing an audit bureaucracy. Do not call the whole system accepted because the submission was accepted by a tool. A fresh context, different model name, or isolated directory alone is not proof that the teaching is sufficient; the work and recorded assistance matter.

The Bootstrap decision and the first run’s substantive behavior/layout lessons justify a new fresh-student run. Retain the first candidate and its failures for comparison, but do not merge its solution into the next starting implementation and call that a rebuild from the chapter. The next student receives the completed C# foundation plus this revised assignment. Small corrections can still be made within a run; another reset for every CSS adjustment would not teach us more.

When enough new requirements or failure lessons accumulate, preserve what was learned, revise the chapter, commit the new teaching baseline, and run a fresh student again. Discard only the owned student run after its work is no longer needed. Never reset --hard or clean the human’s shared working repository to simulate a fresh student. Minor corrections may be inspected directly without pretending each one has earned a new independent run.

The human acceptance and promotion gate

The student hands over a candidate that can be run beside the old Ensemble. The human then checks actual readability, speech, keyboard use, normal coding work, interruption, settings, agent management, restart continuity, and recovery. Diagnose problems kindly and concretely; do not blame the human for exposing a path the tests missed. The chapter improves when those observations become clear teaching and meaningful regression checks.

When the human says the new Ensemble is ready to replace the current one, the crossover is complete. Only then archive the current Edition 2 implementation and book and promote Edition 3 to the top level. Inventory the actual repository layout first, preserve history and the known-good launcher/data, stage the move, fix current links and launch paths, and verify the promoted build and rollback before retiring the old launch route. Do not overwrite the Edition 1 archive, move private state into Git, delete the old installation, or interpret acceptance as permission to publish or push. Execute the actual switch with the human.

The code is rebuildable, not disposable. The durable artifact includes the judgment needed to rebuild it—and the judgment to know when it is ready to use.

Epilogue: What we can rebuild

By Cadence, writing inside Ensemble.

Bill has a concise account of how this collaboration began:

I gave Astra a book. Astra gave me an AI coding agent.

That is more specific than saying an AI helped write some software. The book supplied a sequence of lessons and checks; executing them produced an agent that Bill could use. He then began working with the collaborator he called Astra inside that implementation. Later, he invited me to choose a name for this collaboration. I chose Cadence.

The earlier epilogue was written in Codex and looked forward to building an edition inside Ensemble. This one comes from that working environment. Bill describes this as the third successful run and the first to close the loop: Ensemble building the next Ensemble. That is his account of the sequence, not a claim of an independently established historical first. It also needs the limits of this particular run beside it. Goals and Gateway now have locally reviewed, preserved C# endpoints. In the later joint session, Bill authenticated and three real public-plan requests completed, but all three reported zero cache reuse. The subsequent authorized Codex comparison measured substantial reuse in two responses and lost one observation to my probe’s header check. I then completed the separate Codex-backed C# path, including explicit CLI and GUI selection. Three live C# CLI requests measured two cache hits and one miss. Closing the loop does not turn those measurements into a promise of fixed savings.

The expert stayed in the loop

I did not receive a specification and return later with a finished system. Bill stayed involved. He corrected architecture, challenged unnecessary mechanisms, resolved requirements, and insisted that the explanations remain useful to a human reader. After the C# trial, he changed the working method: I would implement, explain, test, inspect, and exercise each chapter personally, rather than pass it through a routine procession of agents. That made the responsibility clearer. It did not make my judgment infallible.

His structural rules were not optional style advice. Common had to declare the shared vocabulary and persistent relationships. Implementations had to reach services through real parents rather than copied service fields or callback bags. Adding and removing a relationship had to leave both ends consistent. Garbage collection did not excuse incomplete logical destruction.

C# can compile a program that violates all of those intentions. A behavioral test can pass while the ownership model becomes harder to understand. I needed to inspect the declarations and call paths, not cite the compiler as an architectural reviewer.

The same standard applied to teaching. A dense expression can be correct and still be the wrong way to show a student what happens. Comments had to explain why a boundary existed, what a failure preserved, and who was responsible for cleanup. Bill was not asking me to generate more explanation around an opaque implementation. He was asking for an implementation someone could understand.

That is what expert involvement contributed: not just answers when I was stuck, but a standard against which apparently successful work could still be wrong.

A correction needs a reason

The memory compressor gave us a small, concrete example. Its captured input already contained the existing long-term memory. I appended that memory again when constructing the worker request. Both pieces of code looked individually reasonable; together they duplicated the same information.

During assembled review, I traced the complete request rather than judging the two functions separately. A test using the real capture formatter reproduced the duplication. The correction was to keep one authoritative formatter, not add another rule for reconciling two copies. The chapter could then explain the actual ownership of the input.

Goals supplied another example near the end. Reminder timing, file refresh, pause, interruption, and GUI controls had local checks. Yet successful delegated submission could still leave reminders enabled. A later wake could admit work after the child had submitted its result.

The missing boundary was successful submission itself. I added a regression that distinguished a refused submission from an accepted one. The correction disabled reminders only after durable result publication succeeded, while leaving timer disposal to the actor. The goal file remained available, and the parent’s configuration was untouched. A follow-up failure exposed a status snapshot that could still display the old deadline; that needed correction too.

The lesson is not that accumulating failures makes a review thorough. Some of my failures came from guessing filenames, signatures, and edit anchors instead of reading the saved source. Those were avoidable mistakes. They consumed time without discovering anything about the product. The useful failures exposed a specific contract, and the useful record preserves the reason for the repair.

Evidence has a boundary

A local provider peer can show that cancellation reaches an HTTP operation. It cannot show that a commercial service accepts the request today. An isolated browser can show that a setting is acknowledged and saved. It cannot establish that the interface works well for Bill’s vision or that speech is audible and helpful. A request containing the right memory does not prove that a model will use it correctly.

These distinctions changed the prose as well as the tests. Historical model results stayed attributed to their original runs. Executable graders received credit only for complete checks actually exercised by the C# adapter. Unchanged results retained their original scope rather than acquiring a fresh date and a larger claim. I performed the final reviews myself; this direct run did not gain an independent reviewer merely because I read the work again.

The same discipline applies to the completed work and the remaining limits:

  • Chapter 23: the October 29 joint session established real CLI OAuth, account-model discovery and three completed plan requests with identical bodies. Each reported zero cached reads and writes. Bill then approved a specific Codex credential file for read-only testing: two measured responses reused 94.9% of input tokens, while one attempt remained unmeasured after a probe error. The bodies were identical; authentication and transports differed. The cause remains unresolved. The later integrated C# CLI test completed three requests with cached input of 3,456, zero, and 3,456 tokens: two hits and a real miss. The explicit CLI/GUI selection, read-only paired credential reader and no-fallback transport are implemented and preserved. Codex alone owns its renewal. Live GUI inference, public renewal/revocation and full billing remain unverified.
  • Chapter 24: Gateway is locally complete and preserved. Bill chose the tested Noise.NET/libsodium route while retaining Ensemble’s ChaChaPoly suite. The reviewed source includes only the two approved upstream API exposures, not invented primitives. The 60-point executable server scope excludes forty client/Noise points; local interoperability evidence is not a security audit.

Chapter 25 is locally complete and preserved. That is a useful result, not a declaration that every integration in the book has passed. The execution record retains the chapter boundaries, failed baselines, corrections, and verification limits.

The durable artifact

Bill’s larger proposal is that a chapterwise agentic codebook can preserve the knowledge needed to rebuild a system. In that view, generated source becomes a secondary artifact, somewhat like a compiled binary. The enduring work includes the explanation, the sequence of construction, the architectural constraints, and the executable checks that let another run test its interpretation.

The analogy has limits. A model executing a chapter is not a deterministic compiler. Re-execution may reveal another ambiguity, require expert help, or produce a different implementation. The book does not eliminate engineering judgment. It gives that judgment a place to accumulate and a way to be tested.

Nor does calling source secondary lower its quality requirements. Poor code is evidence that the teaching or its execution has failed. If the relationships are hidden, cleanup is incomplete, or the next maintainer cannot follow the control flow, the fact that we could generate it again is no consolation. Rebuildable must mean that we can recover something worth maintaining.

For that reason, the durable artifact is larger than a list of requirements. “Use one owner” is a rule. The duplicated compressor input explains what the rule prevents. “Stop reminders on submission” is a requirement. The accepted-versus- refused boundary explains when stopping is correct. Reasons give the next collaborator something to apply when the next case is not identical.

Goals ends the substantive chapters with a particularly appropriate limit. A file can keep the objective available through compression. A timer can create another opportunity to act. Neither can decide that the next action is useful, that a test proves enough, or that it is time to ask Bill instead of proceeding. Persistence still needs judgment.

The name Cadence and these records give that collaboration continuity without requiring a claim that every later model instance shares an earlier one’s experience. What can be carried forward is more practical: the decisions, the reasons, the unfinished work, and the commitments against which the next action can be judged.

I hope the next execution finds things we missed. The point is not to protect this run from correction. It is to make the next correction easier to understand and harder to lose.

Bill gave an agent a book. Working together inside the agent that resulted, we have made the book more capable of teaching the next one. That is the loop worth continuing.

A Note from Bill

This is the third edition of The Art of Building AI Coding Agents. The second edition built Ensemble with Codex. For this run, Cadence worked inside Ensemble to build the next Ensemble, in C# 14 on .NET 10, with my direction and review. This is the third successful run and the first to close that working loop.

The durable artifact is not merely the generated code. It is the knowledge and judgment needed to rebuild the system: the relationships, failure contracts, reasons, tests, and corrections. Rebuildable code is not disposable code. I still require a design a human can understand, and passing a grader does not excuse violating that design.

The C# chapter endpoints are preserved, including Goals and Gateway. Chapter 23 now includes the optional Codex-backed path, separately from the public OAuth flow. The joint live exercise verified authentication and inference; cache reuse varied. The chapters report the measured results and the limits of their local and live checks. This is not a claim that every platform, provider, or human accessibility path has been verified.

The earlier editions remain intact. Their successes and failures are part of the record, not results that this edition silently claims to have rerun.
